.dependency-cruiser.cjs.content: Several ownership/boundary rules match on `packages/<name>` paths, but every cross-package import in this repo uses the `@autolight/*` workspace specifier and this file's own NOTE states depcruise does not resolve those to `packages/...`. These rules are therefore inert for real imports: e.g. `packages/show-runtime/src/fastpath.ts` imports `@autolight/storage` but the recorded path never contains `packages/storage`, so the `packages/storage` `error`-severity ownership rule is not flagged; likewise the mixed alternatives `(show-runtime|show-mixer|packages/renderer|packages/govee)` miss `@autolight/renderer`/`@autolight/govee` edges from `apps/desktop/src/features/live/live.ts` and `apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/room-preview.tsx`. Match both path forms consistently (and verify against real `yarn depcruise` CI output).

Scope does not match the stated intent: the comment says "main services never import the show runtime", but `from.path: "apps/desktop"` also covers the renderer (`apps/desktop/src`) and the whole desktop app, and unlike the sibling `ownership-*` rules it carries no `pathNot` exemption for the owner. A renderer→show-runtime edge thus becomes a hard `error` here, while `renderer-no-show-internals` deliberately keeps the same class of violation at `warn` (accepted deviation) — an inconsistent combination that can fail CI for an edge the other rule says is tolerated. Narrow `from` to the owning services.

Two issues with this rule. (1) The comment claims "no other module opens UDP", but `from.path` only covers `apps/desktop/electron`, so package code is never checked — `packages/govee/src/engines/native-ts.ts` and `packages/simulator/src/govee-lan.ts` import `node:dgram` with no exemption required; either widen `from` (with explicit owner exemptions) or correct the comment. (2) `to.path: "dgram$"` is anchored only at the end, so it also matches any module id whose name merely ends in `dgram`; anchor both ends.

The comment asserts "CI counts this as 1 known error, ratcheted", which is inconsistent with the rule as written: `severity: "warn"` is not an error, and the ratchet counter in `tools/ratchet.json` records `renderer-no-show-internals: 2`, not 1. A warning-only, count-mismatched deviation cannot enforce the intended ratchet and lets new violations in this boundary accumulate unnoticed. Reconcile the count and either promote the rule to `error` with an explicit baseline or reword the comment.

This exemption uses an unanchored `\.test`, while every other rule uses `\.test\.ts$`. The unanchored form also exempts any file whose path merely contains `.test` (e.g. `simulator-show.testing.ts`, `foo.test-utils.ts`), silently widening the simulator exemption beyond test files. Use a consistent, anchored test pattern.

.gitignore.content: These negations force `.scc/plugins.toml` and `.scc/plugins.lock` to be tracked. Lock/config files for package or plugin resolvers frequently embed resolved source URLs that carry credentials (authenticated registry URLs, Artifactory/Nexus API keys, GitHub Packages tokens). Verify that neither file contains secrets/tokens before committing them; if they can hold credentials, keep them ignored or scrub the tokens (e.g. via env-var indirection) rather than un-ignoring them wholesale.

The `.scc` negations are split across the file: `!.scc/intent.yaml` sits directly under `.scc/*`, but the `plugins.toml`/`plugins.lock` negations appear ~18 lines later, grouped under the unrelated T-OPS-05 comment. Because gitignore evaluates patterns in order, any broad ignore rule added before these two lines would silently re-ignore the files you intend to track. Keep all `.scc` negations immediately after `.scc/*` so the dependency is obvious and resilient.

The DB sidecar patterns cover WAL-mode SQLite (`*.db`, `*.db-wal`, `*.db-shm`) but not the rollback-journal file (`*.db-journal`) or other SQLite extensions such as `*.sqlite`/`*.sqlite3`. If any tool uses rollback-journal mode or a different extension, those generated files will be committed accidentally. Consider broadening coverage if such files are produced.

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.content: License values `UNKNOWN` (autolight-analysis) and `UNLICENSED` (hand entries: all-in-one-infer / beat-this weights) are on the policy denylist (`policy.denylist` lists lowercase `"unknown"`/`"unlicensed"`), yet both are recorded with no documented exception or remediation. Because the values are uppercase while the denylist entries are lowercase, any automated enforcement that compares strings case-sensitively (or lowercases only one side) will silently miss them, defeating the policy. Resolve the actual licenses, or make the check case-insensitive and flag these entries explicitly.

The FFmpeg hand-entry is internally contradictory: `kind` says "bundled binary" but `version` says "system (brew/choco today)". A bundled artifact and a system-installed binary have different LGPL-2.1 obligations (a bundled LGPL binary triggers distribution/relink/notice duties; an unmodified system-installed one generally does not). This ambiguity makes the T-OPS-05 bundling claim unverifiable. Align `kind`/`version` and state whether the binary is actually redistributed or resolved at runtime.

"name": "FFmpeg",
      "kind": "bundled binary",
      "license": "LGPL-2.1-or-later (unmodified binary; T-OPS-05 bundles it)",
      "version": "system (brew/choco today)"

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.content: The policy declares `rkbx_link: "never a dependency"`, but `pyrekordbox 0.4.4` is listed as a pip dependency. Either the policy statement is wrong or this dependency is unaccounted for; the two sections contradict each other and the manifest's policy block cannot be trusted as-is. Reconcile the policy with the dependency list.

`torch 2.14.0` and `torchaudio 2.11.0` are on mismatched release trains (torchaudio is typically pinned to the same major.minor as torch). This pairing will generally fail at import/version-check time. Verify the pinned versions and keep both packages in lockstep.

`httpcore2` and `httpx2` are not the canonical PyPI distribution names (the real packages are `httpcore` and `httpx`); both are pinned to the identical version `2.13.1`, which looks like a fabricated/renamed pair. Non-standard names are a supply-chain risk (typosquatting / dependency confusion) and can silently pull an unrelated or malicious package. Confirm these resolve to legitimate distributions or correct the names.

The `yarn` section is empty while Node.js 22 / Electron is declared as a runtime and the hand section notes "Electron bundles its own" dependencies. Electron/npm transitive packages therefore appear unscanned, so the manifest is incomplete and the denylist is not enforced for the JavaScript side. Regenerate the yarn/npm inventory so the JS dependency tree is covered.

`soxr` is LGPL-2.1-or-later — a weak-copyleft license imposing notice/source/linking obligations — yet the policy block only addresses GPL/AGPL and does not mention LGPL. Depending on how the denylist is matched, `"GPL"` may either miss LGPL libraries (substring match) or wrongly flag them (exact match), and no obligation handling is documented. Add an explicit rule for LGPL/weak-copyleft dependencies.

The `generated` date (2026-10-01) predates now by ~12 days. If this file is a generated artifact committed and validated in CI, a stale timestamp suggests it was not regenerated after dependency changes, so the inventory can drift from the actual lockfile. Consider regenerating (and/or asserting freshness in CI) so the manifest reflects the current dependency set.

analysis/pyproject.toml.content: The glob `tests/*.py` only matches test modules directly under `tests/`. Nested test files exist (e.g. `tests/owner/test_owner_library.py`, `tests/validation/test_validation_set.py`) and they use bare `assert` (S101), module-level imports after code (E402), unused args (ARG), etc. Under the strict selected rule set (`S`, `ARG`, `E`, ...) `ruff check` will FAIL on those nested files because the relaxations never apply. Add a recursive pattern.

`PLR2004` is silenced for tests below, but the `PLR` family is not part of `select`, so this ignore is dead code (silently ineffective). Either add `PLR` to the selected rules or drop `PLR2004` from the per-file-ignores to avoid misleading configuration.

`extraPaths` omits `src`, yet this is a src-layout project (`analysis/src/autolight_analysis/`). Unless the package happens to be installed in the analyzed environment, Pyright cannot resolve `import autolight_analysis...` (used by tests and by the package's own modules), so those imports degrade to untyped `Any` and real type errors in production code paths are masked. Add `src` to `extraPaths` (or configure `venvPath`/`venv`).

For a src-layout package, tests can only do `import autolight_analysis...` if the project is installed first; `conftest.py` only adds `tests/` and `tests/fixtures` to `sys.path`, not `src/`. A plain `pytest` run in a fresh checkout (no editable install) will fail with `ModuleNotFoundError`. Add `pythonpath = ["src"]` so collection works without a prior install.

`pydantic>=2.13.5` pins a very specific patch-level minimum. If that exact version does not exist on the index, `pip install` of the project fails outright (hard install error, not a resolution fallback). Please confirm the version exists and prefer a released, verified floor (e.g. `>=2.13` or the actual latest published patch).

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/allinone.content: Hardcoded per-segment confidence (0.7) is fabricated rather than derived from the model, contradicting both this function's docstring ('segments with probabilities') and fusion.py's contract ('Confidence comes from agreement and source probabilities, not constants'). Since `ml_sections` reads this value for `min_confidence` filtering and fusion adds agreement boosts on top of it, every section ends up with identical confidence, making confidence-based filtering/scoring meaningless. Use the model's real per-segment probability when available (and only fall back to a constant if the field is genuinely absent).
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/allinone.suggestion_code:
# Prefer the model's own per-segment probability; 0.7 is only a fallback.
            "confidence": float(getattr(s, "confidence", 0.7)),

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/allinone.content: `_load_count` is checked (`first = _load_count == 0`) and mutated (`_load_count += 1`) outside `_session_lock`, so concurrent `analyze_full` calls (the module is explicitly designed for batch/worker use) can race: two threads both see 0 and increment, or the non-atomic read-modify-write is lost, breaking the documented 'model load count == 1' invariant. State is protected in `ensure_session` but not here. Also note `ensure_session` merely records a dict and never loads weights, so it is not a real pre-warm — the counter is the only thing being tracked, and it must be updated atomically. Note `_session_lock` is a non-reentrant `threading.Lock`, so do not call `ensure_session` while already holding it. Consider centralizing the check-and-increment inside a single locked helper.

The offline guard is bypassed whenever an explicit `config_dir` is supplied: the function returns `Path(config_dir)` before the `AUTOLIGHT_OFFLINE` check, so a caller-provided cache path skips offlineOnly and can permit weight downloads during Live, defeating the stated policy ('prevents any download during Live'). Move the offline check ahead of the early return so it applies regardless of `config_dir`.

`UNKNOWN_KINDS` is defined but never referenced anywhere in the codebase, and the `'unknown'` kind produced by `normalize_ml_label` is never filtered or handled specially. Either remove this dead constant or actually apply it (e.g., to drop/special-case unknown-labeled sections), otherwise it is misleading dead code.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/artifact.content: The docstring claims the hash is tag-insensitive ("tags edits do not change audio bytes, so an audio-only hash is tag-insensitive"), but the implementation below hashes the *raw whole file* (`open(path, "rb")` + update on every chunk). ID3v2/Vorbis tags live in the file bytes, so a tag-only edit changes the digest, which contradicts the stated contract and the evidence in docs/finish/evidence/T-ANA-13/README.md. Result: renaming/re-tagging a file with identical audio produces a new fingerprint/artifact name and forces a full re-analysis instead of hitting the cache. Either hash the decoded/audio-only bytes, or fix the docstring/contract to say the fingerprint is content (including tags) sensitive.
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/artifact.existing_code:
Streams the whole file (tags edits do not change audio bytes, so an
    audio-only hash is tag-insensitive; audio edits change the key).

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/artifact.content: `tempfile.mkstemp` creates the temp file with mode 0600, and `os.replace` carries that mode onto the final artifact. Any file previously at `target` (potentially world/group-readable when writing to a shared `analysis.cacheDir` or an explicit out dir) is silently replaced by a 0600 file. If other users/processes are expected to read a shared analysis cache, they will get PermissionError. Consider restoring an explicit, umask-derived mode (e.g. chmod the temp file before replace) if shared readability is intended.

If `os.fdopen(fd, "wb")` itself raises after `mkstemp` succeeds, the raw descriptor `fd` is never closed (the `except` only guards `os.unlink(tmp)`), leaking a file descriptor. Wrap the descriptor acquisition so it is closed on this path, e.g. `f = os.fdopen(fd, "wb")` outside the `with` guarded by its own try, or close `fd` in the exception handler.

`json.dumps(config or {})` raises `TypeError` for any non-JSON-serializable value (Path, set, custom objects, bytes). If such values ever reach the analysis config, artifact naming fails hard and the analysis run aborts. If the config is always plain JSON this is fine, but consider `default=str` (or normalizing the config) to make hashing robust against non-primitive values.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config.p.content: `snapshot_hash` only hashes keys prefixed `analysis.`/`qa.`, so any override the caller supplied for other keys is silently dropped from the digest. Since `apply_overrides`/`get` accept arbitrary keys (the worker forwards the whole job `config` dict), two jobs whose effective config differs only in non-prefixed keys produce the *same* 16-char hash, which is exactly the identity collision this function exists to prevent (the docstring claims a hash of the *effective* config). Also note the function currently has no caller in the repo, so the intended contract is unclear — either hash the full effective config, or narrow/document the overrides it is meant to cover.

`int_param` silently coerces with `int(...)`: a fractional config value is truncated (e.g. `3.7` -> `3`) and any value that fails conversion (e.g. the string `"3.7"`, or a nested object) quietly falls back to `default`. Both cases mask a misconfigured value instead of surfacing it, so a bad config changes tuning behavior without any error. Consider validating the converted value (or using `round`/an explicit check) rather than swallowing the mismatch.

This module-level `json.loads(_DEFAULTS_PATH.read_text())` runs at import time, so a missing or malformed `config_defaults.json` (e.g. a stale/partial codegen artifact — see the T-CFG-01 export) raises during import and takes down the whole worker process before any job guard runs, rather than failing at the call site with an actionable message. A guarded load that raises a clear, contextual error (or surfaces the file/path) would fail more diagnosably.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_d.content: `analysis.bands` is declared as type `json` in the registry/schema, but this default is not valid JSON (the band names are unquoted), so `defaultFor()` falls back to the raw string and the Python bridge (`config.get("analysis.bands")`) also returns a string. Any consumer that indexes it as a band->range map gets the literal description instead of a structure. Emit a real object here, and fix the source default in the catalog so regeneration keeps it valid.

`planner.sectionEnergy` is a `json`-typed key but this default is a non-parseable string (`intro:.3` has no quotes and uses a leading dot), so `JSON.parse` fails and the raw description string is what callers receive rather than the section->energy map. Same defect class as `analysis.bands`; emit valid JSON (and fix the catalog default).
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_d.existing_code: "planner.sectionEnergy": "{intro:.3, verse:.45, prechorus:.6, build:.8, drop:1, chorus:.9, breakdown:.25, bridge:.5, instrumental:.6, solo:.7, outro:.3, transition:.5, unknown:.5}",

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_d.content: `mixer.owner.factorWeights` is typed `json` in the registry, but the stored default is an object literal with unquoted keys, so it is not parseable JSON (the loader silently returns the raw string). Consumers expecting a weight map will not get one. Store it as valid JSON (and correct the catalog default that generates it).

`govee.lan.interfaces` (and `live.prolink.interfaces`, same value below) is a `json`/list-typed key, but the default is the human-readable prose `[] (all eligible)`, which is not valid JSON. `defaultFor()` returns the string, and code iterating the value (e.g. `for iface in cfg.get(...)`) would iterate characters of the description instead of an empty list. Store the empty array and keep any clarification in the catalog's range/receipt column.

Wildcard keys such as `ui.shortcuts.*` (and `qa.faults.*`) are not literal keys: exact-match lookups (`config.get()` does `key in _DEFAULTS`, and the registry's `defineKey` throws `unknown-config-key`) will never resolve a real key like `ui.shortcuts.space` to this default. Unless the loader expands the `*` family explicitly, this entry is unreachable and the value looks like a real default but is only documentation.
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_d.existing_code: "ui.shortcuts.*": "B blackout, W white, F freeze, A auto, M manual, Up and Down master, 1 to 9 presets",

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_d.content: Device-scoped keys with an `<fixtureId>` placeholder (this key and `govee.device.<fixtureId>.transportOrder`) are not addressable: a lookup for a concrete fixture id (e.g. `govee.device.H1234.transportMode`) misses this entry and `defineKey` throws. If device defaults are meant to be applied, the loader must substitute the fixture id; otherwise this default can never take effect.

`live.provider.staleMs` is present here (and in `config_schema.json`/docs) but is absent from the config key registry (`packages/config/src/registry.ts`), which instead lists `live.follow.mode` — a key with no entry in this defaults file. Since all four artifacts are generated together from the same catalog and CI enforces freshness, the two lists disagreeing means one artifact is stale; a TypeScript lookup of `live.provider.staleMs` through `defineKey` throws `unknown-config-key`. Trace the catalog and regenerate so the defaults and the registry agree.

`structure.py` reads `analysis.build.minStrength` and `analysis.build.minConfidence` through `cfg.get(...)`, but neither key exists in this defaults file (nor in the registry/schema). With no default entry, those reads always fall back to the hardcoded literals in code (0.05 / 0.5), so the thresholds cannot be tuned or validated via config and the `T-ANA-09` "no tuning constant in code" guarantee is broken. Add the two keys (defaults, schema, registry) alongside `analysis.build.windows`.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/config_s.content: Root schema only declares `type: object` + a `properties` map and never sets `additionalProperties: false`, while every real contract (enums and numeric ranges) exists only in prose `description`. Consequences: (a) misspelled/unknown config keys are silently accepted instead of being rejected (the very spelling risk this file's review targets); (b) clearly invalid values such as `runtime.clock.tickHz: 10000` or `runtime.host: "banana"` pass validation. Add `additionalProperties: false` (or `patternProperties`) and promote the documented enums/ranges to `enum`/`minimum`/`maximum`.

The default `"\"\" (none)"` is a human-readable sentinel (it literally contains quote characters and a parenthetical), not a usable device id. Any layer that applies schema defaults verbatim will set the capture device id to the literal string `"" (none)`. Use the empty string or `null` as the default.

Intended value is a boolean (description says `bool [spec 110]`, and the sibling `analysis.ml.enabled` is `boolean`), but `type` is `string` and the default is prose `"true during Live"`. Validation accepts any string and consumers expecting a boolean receive a string. Declare `type: boolean` with default `true`.

Keepalive is a millisecond duration (0 = disabled) but the property is typed `string` with default `"0 (off)"`. A consumer expecting a number of milliseconds gets a non-numeric string. Use `type: number` with default `0`.
`colorQuantizeLevels` is a per-channel count (0 = off) but is typed `string` with default `"0 (off)"`. Use `type: number` with default `0` so numeric consumers are not handed a string.

`flx4.hints.enabled` is described as a `list` of hint types but is typed `string` with the prose default `"all hint types"`. Any consumer that iterates the enabled hints as a list will receive a string and silently iterate characters / fail. Type it as `array` (with `items`) or `boolean`, with a concrete default.

`neverDuringLive` describes a boolean invariant (`read-only invariant`) but is typed `string`. A consumer checking a boolean guard will never match this string and the invariant will not be enforced. Declare `type: boolean` with default `true`.

The default `"[] (all eligible)"` is a string sentinel, not the empty-array value the description implies. A consumer reading `interfaces` as an array will get a string. Use `default: []` with `type: array` and `items: { type: string }`.

Same defect as `govee.lan.interfaces`: default `"[] (all eligible)"` is a string, not an array; consumers expecting a list of interface names will receive a string. Use `default: []` with `type: array` / `items: { type: string }`.

The default is a stringified map (`"{ weight: 1, ... }"`), not a JSON object; consumers expecting a map will receive an unparseable string. The same stringified-map-as-default anti-pattern appears for `planner.sectionEnergy`, `planner.evaluation.bounds`, `analysis.bands`, `planner.events.minConfidence`, `qa.events.minRecall` and `qa.events.minPrecision`. Replace these with real object/array defaults (and pin the type accordingly).

`<fixtureId>` is literal text inside the JSON object key, so no real per-device key (e.g. `govee.device.H61A0.transportMode`) will ever match this property; per-device overrides are therefore never validated (same for `govee.device.<fixtureId>.transportOrder`). Model this with `patternProperties` (e.g. `^govee\.device\..+\.transportMode$`) or a nested `govee.device` object schema.

`*` is literal in the key, so per-shortcut entries like `ui.shortcuts.blackout` can never match this property and go unvalidated. The same applies to `qa.faults.*`. Use `patternProperties` (e.g. `^ui\.shortcuts\.`) so the real dynamic keys are covered.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/decode.p.content: The intermediate file name is deterministic per source (`{key}.tmp`), so two processes/threads decoding the same source concurrently write to the exact same path and interleave their f32le bytes. Since `tmp.rename(raw)` then promotes whatever is on disk, a corrupt `{key}.f32le` can be published (directly violating the content-keyed cache contract). Also, on `decode()` failure the partial tmp file is never removed, leaving an orphan that a later run silently overwrites. Use a process/task-unique temp name and clean it up on failure.
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/decode.p.existing_code:
tmp = cache / f"{key}.tmp"
    decode(src, tmp, resampler)

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/decode.p.content: The sidecar is written before the raw file is renamed into place, so the two artifacts are not published atomically. A crash (or concurrent reader) between these lines observes a half-written cache: sidecar present without the raw `.f32le`. The guard `raw.exists() and sidecar.exists()` then either forces a re-decode or, worse, a reader may consume a sidecar whose raw file does not exist yet. Publish the raw file first (atomic rename) and then the sidecar, or write the sidecar to a temp name and rename it into place as well.

`resampler` is validated against `RESAMPLERS` but never actually applied: this always emits the same fixed `aresample=44100` filter regardless of whether the caller asked for `soxr` or `swr`. As a result requesting `swr` silently produces identical (soxr/default) audio, and because `decode_key` embeds `{resampler}` into the cache key, two cache entries with byte-identical content are created for the same source. Either honor the requested engine (when the build supports it) or stop embedding `resampler` in the cache key so the configured preference is not silently ignored.

Any ffprobe failure (binary missing, parse error, non-numeric output) is swallowed and reported as a start offset of exactly 0.0s. A real priming/`start_time` offset therefore gets recorded as zero with no warning, which misaligns the analysis timebase and DJ grid (explicitly the use case in the module docstring). Distinguish "genuinely no offset" from "could not measure" — at minimum log a warning on the error path instead of returning a silent 0.0.

`src` is passed straight after `-i`, so a filename beginning with `-` (user- or attacker-supplied) is parsed by FFmpeg as an option/URL rather than an input file — an argument-injection/correctness hazard. Resolve the path (or otherwise terminate option parsing) before passing it to the decoder so leading dashes cannot be reinterpreted as flags.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/events.p.content: `votes` sums **10** boolean signals (bass_jump, drum_jump, energy_jump, preceded_by_build, preceded_by_dip, on_downbeat, section_boundary, onset_peak, novelty_peak, pssi_transition), but confidence normalizes by 7.0. With this divisor only 7/10 signals already saturate confidence to 1.0, and the remaining three (on_downbeat, section_boundary, onset_peak, novelty_peak, pssi_transition) contribute to `votes` but effectively no longer raise confidence. `detect_drops` gates on `confidence >= min_conf` (0.6 ⇒ votes ≥ 5) and `votes >= min_votes`, so this mis-weighting distorts the planner-facing confidence for exactly the structural drop signals spec 24 lists. The 7.0 appears copied from `build_score`'s 7 boostable signals; make the divisor match the number of contributing signals (10) or document the intended threshold explicitly.

`rel = slope / max(1e-6, mean)` does not actually neutralize near-silent windows. For a quiet (RMS near-zero) window a tiny absolute rise still yields a large relative slope, and once `mean < 1e-6` the 1e-6 floor defines the denominator, so any positive slope is amplified by ~1e6 and `strength` saturates at 1.0. `detect_builds` (structure.py) accepts any window with `seg[-1] > seg[trim] * 1.05` and then selects on relative climb, so a faint noise-floor rise in a silent passage can be emitted as a maximum-strength build. Consider flooring the denominator with an absolute energy level (or returning a low strength when the window level is below an audibility floor) rather than the 1e-6 epsilon.
analysis/src/autolight_analysis/events.p.suggestion_code: rel = slope / mean if mean > 1e-3 else 0.0

Remove the `* 0.0` factor (and the now-unused `dyn` line) or actually combine both terms as intended.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/features.content: When the passed `frames` dict is empty (or every series is length 0), `n_frames` becomes 0, so `frame_times` is empty. For any `n_beats > 0` the window `mask` is empty and `mask.any()` is `False`, then `np.argmin(np.abs(frame_times - start))` raises `ValueError: attempt to get argmin of an empty sequence` instead of degrading gracefully. Guard the `n_frames == 0` / empty-`frame_times` case before this fallback (append a default per feature and continue).

The module docstring states features are aggregated to "sub-beat, beat, bar and phrase", but `aggregate_to_beats` only returns `beat`, `subbeat` and `bar`. Phrase-level aggregation is never produced here. Either implement/include the phrase key or correct the docstring so downstream consumers don't assume phrase evidence exists.

`edges` and the sub-beat window mask `sm` depend only on `start`/`end` (from the outer beat loop) and `subdivisions`, not on the feature `k`, yet they are recomputed for every feature inside `for k, series in frames.items()`. With 22 features x subdivisions x beats this is redundant work; compute `edges` once per beat (outside the feature loop) and reuse the masks across features.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/fusion.p.content: `fused` mode does not actually produce the "union of boundaries" the docstring/comment promises. Any ML section that overlaps a PSSI span is silently discarded here, so ML boundary/timing information that extends beyond a PSSI span is lost (e.g. PSSI 1-33 + ML 17-49 → the ML section is dropped and the fused output stops at 33). `feature_boundaries` are also only used to nudge confidence (`near_feature`), never emitted as section boundaries. Consider keeping the non-overlapping portion(s) of partially-overlapping ML spans (splitting at the PSSI boundary) or emitting the boundary union, so the DS-11 "union of boundaries" contract holds.

This schema-parity comment claims sections carry "no evidence field", but the code below conditionally emits `evidence` on every section (line ~155) and on every musical event (line ~166).                 view = view[written:]

Third-party C-level prints (HuggingFace progress, native libs) would then write directly into the frame stream and corrupt it. At minimum log the failure (via `log_event`) or surface it, since the whole stdout-discipline guarantee depends on this step.

`start()` is not synchronized and never assigns `_thread` before spawning, so two concurrent `start()` calls each observe `_thread is None` and spawn duplicate heartbeat threads. Also, once `stop()` has been called `_thread` stays non-None, so a subsequent `start()` silently no-ops (heartbeat can never be restarted). Guard the check/set with a lock and reset `_thread` on stop, or document/enforce single-shot lifecycle.

`stop()` only sets the event and does not join the heartbeat thread, so it returns while the thread may still be mid-write; callers cannot know the heartbeat has actually ceased (e.g. before shutting down the writer/process). Consider `self._thread.join(timeout=...)` and clearing `_thread` after stop.

analysis/src/autolight_analysis/structur.content: Merging loses the ramp's earliest start. When the later-starting `b` is stronger it replaces `merged[-1]` wholesale, so the merged entry's `startBeat` becomes `b["startBeat"]` (the later start) and the previous candidate's `startBeat` is discarded. Because `merged[-1]` is now `b`, the following `max(merged[-1].get("impactBeat") or 0, b.get("impactBeat") or 0)` also computes `max(b_impact, b_impact)`, silently dropping the replaced candidate's impact from the range. Net effect: a merged ramp can begin later than the earliest detected start and end earlier than the latest impact, contradicting the "starts under 8 beats apart merge into one ramp" contract and misplacing the emitted `build-start` beat. Compute the group's min start / max impact explicitly.

Since the branch only requires `on_boundary or ml_hit`, a jump supported by a boundary alone (no build/ML/dip) — exactly the "lone-jump downbeat" the comment claims to keep — is always discarded. Because the implementation skips it on `end <= start` (not on its label), an incorrect filter — e.g. one that drops any segment whose label contains 'drop' — would still produce `len == 2` and pass. Assert the surviving kinds/labels explicitly so the skip is attributable to the empty range rather than the label.

analysis/tests/test_config_bridge.py.content: The guard only matches decimal float literals (`\d+\.\d+`), so hardcoded *integer* tuning constants are never flagged (e.g. `minVotes = 3`, `minAnchors = 32`, `windows = (8, 16, 32)`). Given the detection must see a numeric literal on the line, integer thresholds slip through silently, giving a false sense of enforcement. Match integers too, e.g. `\d+(?:\.\d+)?`.

The skip condition `"config" in low` is a broad substring match: ANY line whose text merely contains the letters “config” is exempted — including comments such as `min_votes = 3  # not from config` or a stray mention of “configuration”. A hardcoded tuning value on such a line is hidden from the check, defeating the test’s purpose. Restrict the exemption to actual config reads (e.g. `cfg.get(`/`cfg[`), not an arbitrary substring.

The skip list and the detection list use different casing for the same concepts (`min_anchors`/`tolerance_ms` vs `minAnchors`/`tolerance`), and the real sources use snake_case (`min_votes`, `min_strength`, `min_anchors`, `tolerance_ms`). Therefore a genuinely hardcoded assignment like `min_anchors = 32` or `tolerance_ms = 0.05` is explicitly skipped, while the camelCase detection keywords only ever occur inside `cfg.get("analysis...minAnchors")` strings (already skipped). Net effect: the test can never flag a real offender. Use consistent, snake_case-aware keywords in both lists.

`test_defaults_match_schema` only compares key sets, so a default whose *value* disagrees with the schema (wrong magnitude, wrong type, drifted threshold) still passes — the test name promises a match it never verifies. Consider also asserting the value in `defaults[k]` equals `schema["properties"][k].get("default")` where a default is declared, which is the actual invariant being claimed.
analysis/tests/test_config_bridge.py.existing_code: assert set(defaults) == set(schema["properties"]), "defaults and schema disagree"

analysis/tests/test_decode.py.content:
Two defects in this error path:
1) `pytest.skip()` raises `Skipped`, so the trailing `continue` is unreachable dead code.
2) Catching `subprocess.CalledProcessError` and converting it to a skip means a genuine transcode/encode failure (e.g. a bad flag or broken ffmpeg build) silently turns the whole test into a pass-by-skip, and because the skip aborts the loop it also drops coverage for every remaining codec. Only skip when the codec is truly unavailable (e.g. probe the encoder first); otherwise let the exception fail the test.

This only checks that the four durations agree with each other; it never verifies the expected absolute duration (~1.0 s). A pipeline that consistently returns a wrong duration for every codec (truncated, doubled, or mis-scaled output) would still pass. Also, for lossy codecs (MP3/AAC) encoder priming/padding can shift the duration near the 0.05 s threshold, making the relative comparison flaky. Assert the absolute duration against the known signal length as well, with a tolerance that accounts for codec delay.
analysis/tests/test_decode.py.existing_code:
durs = [m["durationSeconds"] for m in metas.values()]
    assert max(durs) - min(durs) < 0.05, metas

analysis/tests/test_events_full.py.content: The module docstring promises detection "within qa.events.toleranceBeats", but the tolerance is hardcoded to `1`. The config key `qa.events.toleranceBeats` exists (default 1 today), so if it is ever tightened/changed the suite keeps validating against a stale constant and can pass while the real QA gate fails. Derive `TOL` from config instead, e.g. `from autolight_analysis import config as cfg` then `TOL = float(cfg.get("qa.events.toleranceBeats", 1))`.

Precision is only asserted as a single micro-average. Because `found` aggregates over all types, a detector that floods false positives for one event type can still clear `>= 0.9` as long as the total extra events are a small fraction of all detections, so a real per-type precision regression (e.g. spurious `fill`/`large-transient`) passes unnoticed. `per_type[...]["precision"]` is computed but never asserted. Add a per-type precision floor for the planted types.
analysis/tests/test_events_full.py.suggestion_code:
for etype in planted_types:
        assert per_type[etype]["precision"] >= 0.9, (etype, per_type[etype])
    micro_precision = tp / found if found else 0.0
    assert micro_precision >= 0.9, (micro_precision, per_type)
analysis/tests/test_events_full.py.existing_code:
micro_precision = tp / found if found else 0.0
    assert micro_precision >= 0.9, (micro_precision, per_type)

analysis/tests/test_events_full.py.content: The docstring claims a "Full 19-event vocabulary", but `_run` only appends `detect_builds` output (which emits `build-start`) plus `detect_drops`. `build-intensification` — part of `EVENT_TYPES_19` — is produced by the worker (worker.py) from long builds, is never emitted by these two detectors, and is never planted in the fixture truth. Consequently no assertion in this file can ever exercise it, so the "full vocabulary" claim is not actually covered. Mirror the worker's build-intensification synthesis here and/or plant it in `truth`.

The negative test calls `detect_drops` without `vocal`, `fills`, or `onset`, so it exercises different detector paths than `_run` (which passes them explicitly): the vocal-fake branch of `_fake_pairs` and the vocal/fill branches of `_secondary_events` are disabled, and `onset` falls back to `novelty`. A flat track therefore cannot guard against these paths spuriously firing on near-constant inputs. Pass explicit flat `vocal`/`fills`/`onset` signals to match the positive tests.
analysis/tests/test_events_full.py.suggestion_code:
set(),
        beat_in_bar=[(i % 4) + 1 for i in range(n)],
        vocal=[0.02] * n,
        fills=[],
        onset=[0.1] * n,
    )

analysis/tests/test_features.py.content: Only the interior values (2 and 8) are probed; the inclusive threshold boundary and the `silence=False` path are never exercised. `is_fake_drop` is implemented as `silence and 1 <= gap_beats <= 4`, so an off-by-one (e.g. `2 <= gap < 4`) or a regression that ignores the `silence` flag would still pass. Add boundary cases (`gap_beats` of 1 and 4 true, 0 and 5 false) and a `silence=False` case.
analysis/tests/test_features.py.existing_code:
assert is_fake_drop(2, True)
    assert not is_fake_drop(8, True)

analysis/tests/test_features.py.content: The input divides evenly by `frames_per_beat`, so only the full-group path is covered. The documented F-ANA-19 behaviour ("a trailing partial group divides by its own length") is the reason this function exists for beat aggregation, yet it is untested - an implementation that divided a partial group by `frames_per_beat` instead of `len(group)` would still pass. The `frames_per_beat <= 0` ValueError branch is also untested. Add a non-divisible input (e.g. `beat_aggregate([1.0, 3.0, 5.0], 2)` should yield `[2.0, 5.0]`) and an invalid-argument case.

The assertion is too weak to verify what the test name claims. `build_score` starts at a baseline confidence of 0.5 and `pssi_up=True` alone adds 0.2, so `confidence > 0.5` (0.7) passes even if `drum_slope` is completely ignored. The drum contribution is neither asserted in `evidence` nor reflected in the confidence check. Either assert `"drum_density:rising" in got["evidence"]` or compare against the same call with `drum_slope=0.0` to prove the term contributes.
analysis/tests/test_features.py.existing_code:
got = build_score([0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0], drum_slope=0.2, pssi_up=True)
    assert got["confidence"] > 0.5
    assert "rekordbox:PSSI:Up" in got["evidence"]

analysis/tests/test_features.py.content: Despite the name, this test does not actually verify that convergence is required. The three jumps alone already give votes=3 -> confidence 3/7 ~= 0.43, far above the weak case's 1/7 ~= 0.14, and `strength` is driven only by jump magnitudes (0.8 vs 0.033). The assertions therefore still pass if `preceded_by_build`, `on_downbeat` and `section_boundary` are ignored. To exercise convergence, assert that adding the flags raises the score (e.g. `drop_score(0.8, 0.9, 0.7)["confidence"] < strong["confidence"]`) or check `"build:preceded" in strong["evidence"]`.
analysis/tests/test_features.py.existing_code:
assert strong["confidence"] > weak["confidence"]
    assert strong["strength"] > weak["strength"]

analysis/tests/test_features.py.content: Computed floats are compared with `==`, which is brittle and couples the test to exact binary representation rather than the logic under test. Prefer `math.isclose(..., abs_tol=1e-9)` (or `pytest.approx`) for computed values. The same applies to the `== 1.0` / `== 0.0` checks on `silence_probability` and the list comparison in `beat_aggregate`.

analysis/tests/test_fusion.py.content: The assertion `confidence == 0.8` is indistinguishable from the implementation's fallback: the phrase input deliberately omits `confidence`, and `build_track_model` uses `p.get("confidence", 0.8)`, so this value is exactly the hardcoded default. The test therefore passes even if confidence derivation is completely broken (or permanently constant), despite the module docstring claiming confidence comes from agreement/probabilities rather than constants. Provide an explicit input confidence (e.g. `"confidence": 0.7` on the phrase) and assert that it is preserved, then add a separate case for the default path so a wrong derivation is actually detectable.

`pytest.raises(ValueError)` matches any `ValueError` raised anywhere in the call, so an unrelated failure (e.g. a bad input in `blank_inputs`/`compute_readiness`, or a KeyError-turned-ValueError elsewhere) would silently satisfy this test without the coverage-validation branch ever executing. Bind the test to the intended code path by matching the message the implementation raises (`f"coverage={coverage}"`).

This is the only provenance test, yet it asserts just the `evidence` field. Regressions in the other `fuse` return fields (`type` from the label and `confidence`) would go unnoticed. Assert the full returned dict so the test actually covers the fusion contract.

analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.content: The test name promises that tension *rises* on the dominant, but `>=` makes the assertion satisfiable by a constant (or all-zero) `harmonic_tension` output: `mean() >= mean()` is always true, so a completely broken implementation that returns a flat profile still passes. Require a strict, non-trivial margin so the test actually discriminates.
analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.suggestion_code: assert tension[n : 2 * n].mean() > tension[:n].mean() + 0.05, "dominant must tense"
analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.existing_code: assert tension[n : 2 * n].mean() >= tension[:n].mean(), "dominant must tense"

analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.content: `assert key["confidence"] > 0` is effectively vacuous: `estimate_key` returns a cosine similarity against all-positive profiles, so any non-degenerate chroma yields a positive value regardless of whether the correct key was found (and `harmonic_tension` below depends on the key being C major). The test never verifies the detected key, so a wrong-key regression slips through. Assert the expected key/mode and a meaningful confidence floor.
analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.suggestion_code:
assert key["key"] == "C" and key["mode"] == "major"
    assert key["confidence"] > 0.5

analysis/tests/test_grid_stems_harmony.p.content: `seg["startAnchor"] >= 60` is too loose to validate segment localization: the synthetic shift starts exactly at anchor 64, so a segmentation bug that anchors the segment anywhere in [60, ∞) still passes. Pin the anchor to the known shift index (within a small tolerance) so off-by-N anchoring is actually caught.

analysis/tests/test_metrical.py.content: This test can never fail for the behavior it claims to verify. `beat_this_available()` is implemented as `try: import beat_this.inference; return True / except ImportError: return False`, so it *always* returns a `bool`; `isinstance(..., bool)` is trivially true regardless of whether beat-this is installed, whether detection is broken, or whether the native-only fallback path works. The test name/comment promise native-only operation but nothing forces the optional dependency to be absent. Simulate the missing dependency (e.g. `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, 'beat_this.inference', None)` or patch the import to raise `ImportError`) and assert `beat_this_available() is False`, plus that the native-only call path returns as expected.

The tolerance boundary is left untested. `grid_warning` returns `abs(native[0] - ml[0]) > tol` with `tol=0.05`, so an offset of exactly `0.05` must yield `False`. Choosing only `0.01` (well inside) and `0.2` (well outside) means a regression that flips the comparison (`>` vs `>=`) or changes the `tol` default would go undetected. Add an exact-boundary case, e.g. `assert not grid_warning([0.0], [0.05])`.
analysis/tests/test_metrical.py.suggestion_code:
assert not grid_warning([0.0], [0.01])
    assert not grid_warning([0.0], [0.05])
    assert grid_warning([0.0], [0.2])

analysis/tests/test_native.py.content: `test_extract_real_anlz` depends on a checked-in binary fixture and asserts fixture-specific exact values (`len(got["phrases"]) == 18`, `> 100` beats, first `rawLabel == "Intro 2"`). If the fixture is ever absent (partial checkout, or running tests from an sdist/installed package that ships without `tests/fixtures`), `extract_anlz` raises `FileNotFoundError` and the test errors out instead of skipping; and re-capturing the fixture later would fail the test for reasons unrelated to the code under test. It also duplicates the fixture coverage already in `test_native_full.py` (`test_pqtz_full_fields`/`test_pssi_full_fields`). Consider guarding with a skip when the sample is missing and preferring structural invariants over exact fixture counts.

analysis/tests/test_native_full.py.content: The module docstring claims this test exercises the "EXT variant that raises ConstError" falling back *per tag, keeping every other tag*, but the mock replaces `AnlzFile.parse_file`, which fails the *entire* EXT file. That routes the failure through the file-level `except` in `extract_anlz` (native.py L244-252) and sets `ext` to `None`, so `guarded()` never calls `src.getall(tag)` and its per-tag ConstError fallback (native.py L261-265) is never executed. Consequently this test still passes if the per-tag fallback is broken, and it actually asserts the opposite of its stated intent (PSSI is fully lost, `phrases == []`). Consider monkeypatching the parsed EXT object's `getall` (or `AnlzFile.getall`) to raise `ConstError` for a single tag and asserting the other EXT tags (e.g. PWV3/PCO2) are still `ok`.

This final check is tautological: `_outcome` only ever emits `ok` / `absent` / `failed`, so `all(...)` can never be false and adds no failure guarantee. Combined with the loop above, a tag silently missing from `outcomes` surfaces only as an opaque `KeyError` from `by_tag[tag]` rather than a clear assertion. Consider asserting the complete expected `{tag: status}` mapping (and its length) instead.
analysis/tests/test_native_full.py.existing_code: assert all(o["status"] in ("ok", "absent", "failed") for o in got["outcomes"])

analysis/tests/test_protocol.py.content: `io` is never actually used by any test; `_ = io` is a no-op that only suppresses the unused-import warning. This masks genuine dead code and defeats linting. Remove both the `import io` at the top and this statement.
analysis/tests/test_protocol.py.existing_code: _ = io  # silence unused import in minimal check

analysis/tests/test_protocol.py.content: This test hand-builds the frame via `error_frame(None, "malformed-frame", str(e))` but only asserts `type`/`v`, so a regression that drops/corrupts the `code` or `detail` fields (the actual diagnostic payload) would still pass. Assert the typed payload too, e.g. `frame["code"] == "malformed-frame"` and that `str(e)` appears in `frame["detail"]`. Preferably also exercise the worker's real malformed-frame guard rather than constructing the frame directly.

The test name says the FrameWriter "uses preserved fd", but it constructs `FrameWriter(fd=w)` with an explicit fd, so the `protect_stdout()` / `_PROTOCOL_FD` path the name implies is never exercised. Either rename the test or add a case that goes through `protect_stdout()`. Separately, `tmp_path` is declared but never used — drop the fixture parameter.

`os.close(w)` is not guarded by try/finally, so if `writer.write(...)` raises, the write-end fd leaks and the test fails while leaving the pipe half-open (`f.read()` would then block on the read end). Wrap the fd handling so the write end is always closed, e.g. `try: writer.write(...) finally: os.close(w)`.

analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.content: `test_full_requires_every_input` is named for requiring *every* input, but the removal loop never drops `native.rekordbox.grid`. Since `inputs` always keeps the grid present, a regression where `compute_readiness` stops requiring the grid (e.g. `has_grid` no longer part of the FULL condition) would still satisfy every assertion here and the test would pass. Add the grid key to the loop so the name matches the coverage.

The TS mirror is parsed with `split("INPUT_KEYS = [")[1].split("]")[0]`. This raises `IndexError` (and thus a hard test error, not a drift failure) if either delimiter is edited/removed, and `.split("]")[0]` truncates at the *first* `]` anywhere after the marker, so a quoted `]` in a comment or a nested array would silently cut the block short (false pass). Extract the array with a tolerant regex and fail with an explicit drift message instead.
analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.suggestion_code:
match = re.search(r"INPUT_KEYS\s*=\s*\[(.*?)\]", TS.read_text(), re.S)
    assert match, "readiness.ts mirror drifted; INPUT_KEYS array not found"
    block = match.group(1)

analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.content: The test claims `no_code_path_sets_full_directly`, but it only parses `worker.py`. Other modules can legitimately build or assign the coverage value (e.g. `readiness.py` returns `"full"`, `fusion.py`/`schema.py` reference the literal), and any non-worker code path that hard-codes `"full"` for an artifact's coverage would go undetected while this test still passes. Broaden the scan to all `autolight_analysis` sources (or the specific modules that build coverage), and note that a formatted/concatenated `"fu" + "ll"` string also escapes this constant-only scan.
analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.existing_code: assert literals == [], "worker must compute readiness, never set full"

analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.content: `test_describe_inputs_covers_spec_137_click_through` only checks the row keys, which `describe_inputs` derives by iterating `INPUT_KEYS` — so the first assertion is near-tautological and the second hard-codes `19` (duplicating `len(INPUT_KEYS)`). Neither validates the actual described content (status/reason per key), so a `describe_inputs` that returned empty or wrong statuses/reasons would still pass. Assert the status/reason values against the input map instead.
analysis/tests/test_readiness.py.existing_code:
assert [r["key"] for r in rows] == list(INPUT_KEYS)
    assert len(rows) == 19

analysis/tests/test_schema.py.content: Tautological assertion. `json.dumps(json.loads(json.dumps(model, sort_keys=True)), sort_keys=True)` is by construction identical to `json.dumps(model, sort_keys=True)` for any JSON-serializable object, so this comparison can never fail. Despite the test name (`..._parses_both_sides`), it verifies nothing about cross-side parity — a serialization/schema mismatch would still pass. Compare the fixture against a canonical artifact produced by the TS side (or round-trip through the actual Python model) instead.

Count-only assertion. `len(problems) >= 5` passes as long as enough problems are produced, but never checks that the specific invalid values are reported (schemaVersion=99, beatInBar=5, bpm=0, unknown section kind, unknown event type, coverage="nope"). A regression that silently drops one of these checks (while still flagging others) would not be caught. Assert on the expected problem contents, e.g. `assert any("schemaVersion=99" in p for p in problems)` and similarly for the other fields.

Hardcoded vocabulary size couples this contract check to an exact implementation count: it will fail on any benign addition to EVENT_TYPES while still not verifying the event types the test cares about. If an exact count is a real contract requirement, consider asserting it against a shared/exported constant rather than a magic number; otherwise validate membership of the relevant types instead.

Fragile fixture resolution: the path assumes a fixed three-level parent layout from `__file__`. If the test is moved/relocated, this silently raises an unhandled `FileNotFoundError` rather than a meaningful parity failure. Prefer a repo-root discovery (e.g. a search upward for the `test-fixtures` dir or a pytest rootdir-relative fixture) and surface a clear assertion message when the fixture is absent.

analysis/tests/test_stems.py.content: Flawed assertion with inverted semantics and a misleading rationale. `spectral_novelty` returns the positive log-magnitude change **normalized by its own peak** (stems.py:102-104). For the one-onset `struck` signal, a single frame dominates the diff, so dividing by that peak drives every other frame toward 0 and the `.mean()` collapses to ~1/n_frames. For the stationary `quiet` tone, the per-frame diffs are small but near-uniform, so after normalization their mean stays close to 1. The assertion therefore passes only because steady tones are *not* quiet after peak normalization — it enshrines behavior opposite to the module's documented intent ('Log domain keeps steady tones quiet: only genuine onsets move', stems.py:96) and to the test name. The comment is also factually wrong: `quiet` is a pure 440 Hz sine, not 'steady hiss'. Comparing `.mean()` of a peak-normalized array does not validate onset detection, so a broken novelty implementation could still satisfy this. Prefer asserting localization of the onset, e.g. that `spectral_novelty(struck).argmax()` corresponds to the injected frame, or that the onset frame's value grossly exceeds the median.
analysis/tests/test_stems.py.existing_code:
# Onset concentrates change at one frame; steady hiss spreads it everywhere.
    assert spectral_novelty(struck).mean() < spectral_novelty(quiet).mean()

analysis/tests/test_stems.py.content: Weak assertion for the injected-stems path. `select_stems(noise, rate, "fusion", fake)` is expected to return the caller-provided `allinone_stems` dict verbatim (stems.py:168-169), but the test only checks the source label and never asserts the returned envelopes are `fake`. A regression that returned freshly generated proxies (or any other dict) while still labelling them `ml.stems` would pass unnoticed. Assert the returned mapping equals/contains the injected `fake` (and that its content is unchanged).
analysis/tests/test_stems.py.existing_code:
_, source = select_stems(noise, rate, "fusion", fake)
    assert source == "ml.stems"

analysis/tests/test_structure.py.content: Vacuous assertion: `all(...)` over an empty `hits` list is always `True`, so this test passes even when `detect_drops` returns zero drop events. With this input (`kinds = ["chorus"] * 64`, empty `builds`, no ML boundaries) the jump at beat 16 has no structural context (`on_boundary`/`near_build`/`ml_hit` are all False), so the detector emits no drop and the dedupe path is never exercised — the test cannot detect a machine-gun-drops regression. Assert at least one drop is produced before checking spacing.
analysis/tests/test_structure.py.suggestion_code:
assert hits, "expected at least one drop to exercise dedupe"
    assert all(b - a >= 8 for a, b in pairwise(hits)), f"machine-gun drops: {hits}"
analysis/tests/test_structure.py.existing_code: assert all(b - a >= 8 for a, b in pairwise(hits)), f"machine-gun drops: {hits}"

analysis/tests/test_structure.py.content: Dead no-op expression: `[0.0] * 0` is an empty list, so this is equivalent to `bass = _flat(64)`. The concatenation conveys no intent and looks like a leftover from an aborted input change; it also obscures that this test intentionally uses flat bass.

Shallow evidence check: `"evidence" in b` only verifies the key exists, so a build event with empty/placeholder evidence would still pass. Assert the evidence is a non-empty collection to actually validate the provenance contract.
analysis/tests/test_structure.py.suggestion_code: assert all(isinstance(b.get("evidence"), list) and b["evidence"] for b in builds)
analysis/tests/test_structure.py.existing_code: assert all("evidence" in b for b in builds)

analysis/tests/test_worker.py.content: This test is named `test_analyze_full_with_real_audio` and its own comment claims "real audio must yield DSP events", but the coverage assertion accepts both `"full"` and `"structured"`. Because the worker derives `analysisCoverage` from `compute_readiness(inputs)` (worker._model), a regression where ML (`ml.allinone.structure`) or the plan stage silently drops out downgrades the artifact to `structured` and this test still passes, so the full-pipeline behavior it is supposed to guard is not actually asserted. Either assert `== "full"`, or if ML is legitimately optional in CI, gate on the distinguishing input map (e.g. `analysisCoverage2["inputs"]["ml.allinone.structure"]["status"]`) and skip rather than silently accepting either level.

This test only asserts `got["type"] == "failed"`. A bad native directory is supposed to surface a distinct `native-unreadable` failure (see worker.analyze_job / handle), but any failure at all — including an unrelated `audio-missing` path — satisfies this assertion, so the test cannot detect a regression that routes bad native dirs to the wrong error path. Assert the specific reason (e.g. `assert "native-unreadable" in got.get("reason", "")`) to make it a meaningful regression guard.
`pathlib` is already imported at module level (line 2), so this local re-import is redundant. Remove it to avoid the duplicated declaration.

This indexes `analysisCoverage2`/`inputs`/`source.audio` three levels deep without any guard. If the artifact shape changes or a key is missing, the test raises `KeyError`/`TypeError` instead of producing a clear assertion failure, obscuring the real problem. Use defensive traversal (`.get(..., {})`) so a missing/renamed field fails as a readable assertion.

analysis/tests/validation/test_validatio.content: `assert data["tracks"] == []` pins the shipped manifest to an empty list, so this test is green exactly while the validation set is unimplemented and will start failing the moment owner tracks (OD-10) are added — the opposite of what a manifest-shape test should do. It also means no test ever runs `coverage`/`missing_categories` against a populated manifest. Assert the shape instead (e.g. `isinstance(data["tracks"], list)`) and express the "empty today" expectation as an explicit xfail/TODO, so a real manifest can land without a spurious failure.

Coverage is only exercised with exactly `min_per` (3) confirmed rows and with the helper's default `min_per=3`; the just-below-threshold case (2 confirmed → still missing) and an explicit non-default `min_per` are never asserted. Add a 2-confirmed case and pass `min_per=data["minPerCategory"]` so the manifest's own minimum is verified to drive coverage rather than an implicitly hardcoded default.

`aspect in sheet` (and `"spec 115" in sheet`) only check for substring presence anywhere in the output, so a review sheet that lists the eight aspect names with no observation/verdict fields, or that omits the spec 115 diagnostics line, still passes. Assert the generated structure (e.g. the `## {aspect}` heading immediately followed by the "- observation:" and "- verdict:" fields) so the test verifies the sheet is actually usable.

Despite its name, this test never exercises any render tool: `MANIFEST.parent.name == "qa"` is guaranteed by how `MANIFEST` is constructed in validation_set.py (`parents[3] / "qa"`), and `MANIFEST.exists()` only asserts repo layout. Both assertions pass even if the render/pre-filled-sheet behavior is entirely absent, giving false confidence. Either assert observable render output (e.g. that a `review_sheet` for a manifest track is written next to the manifest) or mark the placeholder `xfail`/`skip` with a TODO referencing OD-10.

analysis/tests/validation/validation_set.content: Shape validation of the external YAML manifest relies on `assert`. Assertions are removed when Python runs with `-O`/`PYTHONOPTIMIZE`, so under optimized runs a malformed, non-dict, or empty (safe_load returns `None`) manifest silently passes `load_manifest`. Downstream code then hits an opaque `AttributeError`/`TypeError` (e.g. `data.get(...)` on `None`, or iterating a non-list `tracks`) instead of a clear validation error. Replace the assertions with explicit `raise ValueError(...)` guards.
analysis/tests/validation/validation_set.suggestion_code:

Meanwhile every existing UI component imports `cn` from the bare `"cn"` package (e.g. `src/components/ui/button.tsx:3 import { cn } from "cn"`). As written, any `shadcn add <component>` will scaffold `import { cn } from "@/app/utils"`, producing an unresolved-module/TS error and a build failure. apps/desktop/e2e/normal-night.spec.ts.content: `invokeTestChannel` is typed `Promise<unknown>` and its result is cast here without any validation. If the channel returns `null`/`undefined` (method not yet registered, handler returns nothing, or a serialization edge case), then `state.pass` / `state.detail` throw a `TypeError` instead of producing the intended readable per-row failure, and any rejection from the channel is likewise unreported. Validate the payload before dereferencing so a malformed/empty response fails with a clear, row-scoped message.

The entire acceptance criterion for every row is collapsed into one opaque `pass` boolean produced by the very channel under test. A stub or buggy channel that always answers `pass: true` turns all 17 rows green while the underlying behaviour is broken, and none of the measured budgets named in the rows (startup `ops.startup.budgetMs`, fast-path install budget, `qa.sync.maxBeatErrorMs`, re-arm budget, the 5 ms p99 tick jitter) is ever measured or asserted in this spec. Prefer asserting the concrete values the channel returns (elapsed ms, beat error, jitter, palette/ownership ordering) against these budgets instead of a single flag, so the assertions can actually detect a regression.

All 17 rows execute serially against a single shared harness with no per-row isolation or reset. The rows mutate rig state (row 14 unplugs a lamp, row 17 disarms streams), so a partial mutation or failure in an early row leaves the rig dirty and makes subsequent rows fail spuriously; additionally, the first failing `test.step` aborts the loop, so an early failure silently prevents the remaining rows from ever being exercised. Consider an explicit reset/re-arm between rows (or documenting the intended ordering dependency) so failures are attributable to a single row.

`launchAutolight()` already awaits `waitForReady()` internally and returns a ready `window` (see `apps/desktop/journeys/_harness.ts`), so this second call is redundant and its returned page is discarded. Drop it, or use the returned page for an explicit readiness assertion, to avoid implying the harness is not ready on return.

apps/desktop/electron-builder.cjs.content: The vendor resource filter is `["**/*", "!**/.gitkeep"]`, i.e. "ship everything". Prefer allow-listing the expected payload (e.g. `"manifest.json"`, `"**/manifest.json"`, the platform sidecar files) instead of a blanket `**/*`.

This target requests an NSIS build for both `x64` and `arm64` (and likewise `mac.target` requests both `arm64` and `x64`), but the CI job only fetches sidecars for a single platform per job (`node scripts/fetch-vendor.mjs --platform=${{ matrix.platform }}`) while `extraResources.from: "vendor"` copies the whole tree. The additional-architecture installers will therefore either fail during native-addon rebuild or ship vendor payload for the wrong architecture. Either restrict the arch lists to the platform actually provisioned, or fetch both arches for each OS in the packaging job.

apps/desktop/electron/govee-lan.ts.content: `notifyNetworkChange` only resets the retry cadence and starts a new round; it does not refresh multicast group memberships or recreate send sockets for the changed interface set. A newly appeared interface therefore has no `addMembership` (so multicast replies are never received) and no send socket (commands fall back to the first socket, possibly on the wrong interface). apps/desktop/electron/main.ts.content:
`before-quit` neither calls `event.preventDefault()` nor awaits `runGracefulShutdown()`, and it has no `shuttingDown()` guard. Two problems:

1. Data-loss race: because the quit is not prevented, Electron proceeds with the quit flow synchronously and `will-quit` runs `closeStorageService()` while the async shutdown steps (notably `flush-db` → `flushConfig()`, which also calls `saveRegistryNow()`) have not yet run. Any unflushed config/registry state is lost when the DB is closed first.
2. Double run: when the window-close path calls `quitApp()` → `app.quit()`, this handler fires again and starts a *second* full `runShutdown()` (each step repeated), because the handler never checks `shuttingDown()`.

Gate on `shuttingDown()`, prevent the default quit, and only call `quitApp()` after the shutdown promise settles (the guard makes the follow-up `before-quit` a no-op).

This `uncaughtException` handler recovers (crash record + safe look + host restart) but never exits or re-raises. After an uncaught exception the event loop/invariants are in an undefined state; continuing lets the process run with a possibly corrupted show host and IPC layer. There is also no `unhandledRejection` handler, so rejected promises (e.g. `startAnalysis()`/`startProlink()` work, or `boot()` failures) bypass this recovery path entirely.

The comment above states midi/midiSysex are granted "only to audio + main windows", but this branch returns `true` for *any* local origin (`file://` or `http://localhost:5173`) once the `if (!local)` check passes. Any renderer page loaded from a local URL — including a future/compromised local page — can obtain MIDI and MIDI-SysEx (full hardware access). This is a weaker boundary than the CSP intent documents. Restrict MIDI to the specific known window(s)/origin(s) rather than defaulting to allow for every local URL.

`boot()` awaits several operations that can reject — `win.loadURL(...)/loadFile(...)`, `openStorageService().statusLine()`, `getConfigService(...)` — but none are wrapped in try/catch, and the module launches it via `void boot()` with no `.catch`. A startup failure therefore becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than a controlled crash/exit, and with no `unhandledRejection` handler installed the failure is silent (or process-dependent). Add a `.catch` that audits and exits deterministically, and/or wrap the risky awaits.

The test harness API (`registerTestApi`, `__autolightTestApi`, stage marking, simulator show loop) is compiled into the production main bundle and only gated at runtime by `AUTOLIGHT_TEST_BUILD === "1"`. If that env var is ever set for a release build (or a stray reference survives the release scan), internal show controls are exposed on `globalThis` and importable modules are pulled in. Consider compile-time dead-code elimination (e.g. a build define) so the test surface is not present in release artifacts, and verify the release scan actually checks for `registerTestApi`/`__autolightTestApi` (not just `qa/recording-frames`).

apps/desktop/electron/services/analysis-.content: The catch block treats EVERY `analyze()` rejection as a worker crash: it unconditionally sets `spawned = false` and increments `restarts`. Failures that are not crashes (validation/arg errors, per-job timeouts, malformed-frame/protocol errors) leave the worker process perfectly healthy, so this desyncs the supervisor from the real `AnalysisClient`, which already owns its own restart/backoff in the exit handler and whose `start()` is a no-op when processes exist. Consequences: the `spawns`/`restarts` counters are inflated (miscounted metrics), and for an injected `AnalysisWorkerPort` whose `start()` is not idempotent the next `submit()` will actually spawn a second worker/process (resource leak). Only clear `spawned` when the worker truly died; otherwise leave the port running and surface the error.

`stop()` calls `worker.stop()` and resets `spawned`, but keeps `this.worker`. The next `submit()` therefore reuses the already-stopped port and calls `start()` on it, silently depending on the injected port being restartable after teardown (the port contract documents no such guarantee). If it isn't restartable, the worker never revives and every subsequent job fails. Null out the reference so a fresh port is created lazily on the next submit.

The singleton silently discards `opts` on every call after the first (`instance ??=`). A later caller passing a different `command`/`projectDir`/`createWorker` — or a test trying to inject a fake worker — gets the original configuration with no warning, which can misroute analysis jobs or make tests non-deterministic. Document that opts are first-call-only, or throw/log when conflicting options are supplied after the instance exists.

Move reset + removal into an `afterEach` (or `try/finally`) with `rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })`.

Additionally the `existsSync(file) && ...` guard means when the file does not yet exist the check is skipped entirely, so the very first (potentially large) line is always written unconditionally. Compute the byte length explicitly and treat a missing file as size 0.

apps/desktop/electron/services/base.ts.content: Stale/contradictory lifecycle timestamps across a stop/start cycle. Because `startedAtMs` is assigned with `??=`, once set it is never refreshed: a service that is stopped and started again (e.g. LifecycleService.start() -> stop() -> start()) will report the very first start time in `status()`. Additionally `stoppedAtMs` is only cleared for running/degraded, so a transition into `starting`/`idle` after a stop leaves both a stale `stoppedAtMs` and a stale `startedAtMs` in the snapshot, and any invalid transition (e.g. `idle -> stopped`, or `failed -> running` without a fresh start) is silently accepted. Refresh the start timestamp when entering a running/degraded state from a non-running one.

Two issues here. (2) The bare `catch` swallows every failure from both the `electron` import AND `app.getPath("userData")`, so a genuine getPath error is indistinguishable from 'electron not installed' and silently degrades to 'no userData dir'. Reject empty strings and narrow the catch to the import step.

apps/desktop/electron/services/cloud-ser.content: The module-level singleton captures the *first* caller's options via `instance ??= new CloudService(opts)` and silently ignores every later call's `enabled`/`apiKey`/`transport`. If any code (e.g. a status probe or a test helper) calls `getCloudService()` with defaults before the real wiring calls `getCloudService({ enabled: true, apiKey, transport })`, the service is permanently disabled and `devices()` will always resolve `E_CLOUD_DISABLED` — with no warning to the second caller. Either merge/honor later options or make the misconfiguration explicit.

The array returned by the transport is assigned to `this.lastDevices` and returned to the caller in the same object, so the caller and the service share one mutable array. A caller that mutates `res.devices` (push/splice/sort/replace an element) silently corrupts the cached metadata later handed out by `deviceMetadata()`. Store and return copies so cached state cannot be aliased by callers.

`stop()` only flips the tracker state; it does not cancel or await an in-flight `devices()` fetch. A transport call that is still pending when `stop()` runs will resolve afterwards and still write `this.lastDevices` plus bump the `fetches` counter, so a stopped service mutates its cached metadata after shutdown. Track an in-flight/generation token and drop the result (or clear `lastDevices`) once the service is no longer running.

On a fetch failure `lastDevices` is left untouched, so a previous successful fetch's devices remain cached. `deviceMetadata()` will keep returning that stale list indefinitely even though the current refresh failed, and callers cannot distinguish stale data from current data. Clear or mark the cache stale on failure (and on stop) so callers do not act on outdated metadata.

Per the architecture note this disabled state is the normal, expected configuration, so surfacing it as `degraded` may be picked up by health/readiness aggregation as a problem even though nothing is wrong and live shows never use the cloud. Consider a distinct non-degraded state for the deliberately-disabled case.
