apps/desktop/electron/services/config-se.content: `resetConfigServiceForTest()` only nulls the reference without calling `stop()`, so the previous service's store subscription, accumulated history, and any unsaved state (the store's `save()` is only invoked from `stop()`/mutating calls) are left behind, and the old store keeps notifying the orphaned listeners. This is a likely source of test cross-contamination and lost writes. Call `stop()` (or at least `flush()` and unsubscribe) before clearing.

`history` is appended on every store change and never trimmed, while `changes()` copies the entire array. For a long-running desktop session (and because the shared store can also be mutated by show-service) this grows without bound. Consider a bounded ring buffer or a cap with eviction.

apps/desktop/electron/services/fault-inj.content: This assertion (and every other `staleFrames` assertion in the suite: tests 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and `m.staleFrames`) can never fail. `runFaultSuite` hardcodes `staleFrames: 0` in the returned result (line 151) and in each measurement (line 146) — the value is never derived from actual deliveries. So the suite's headline promise ("goes red if ... stale frames ... regress") is not actually verified by these tests. Either make the engine compute `staleFrames` from real delivery/tick state so this assertion is meaningful, or assert on something the port can actually observe (e.g. that every delivered frame index is strictly increasing per device).

The `workerkill` scenario is registered but its measurement is never asserted — only `hostkill` is checked. A regression in worker-kill recovery (wrong `recoveryFrames`, no `othersContinued`, frames continuing to the killed device) would leave this test green. Also, the reload assertion only counts deliveries at frame 30; it does not verify the payload, so a broken reload that emits `"held"`/all-off while still delivering two frames would pass. Add assertions on the workerkill measurement and on the reload payload.

This aggregate count over the combined duplication+reorder window is a masking assertion: 20 deliveries over frames [30,50) can still be 20 if, e.g., duplication caused extra deliveries on some frames while reorder dropped the same number on others. It proves nothing about per-frame duplicate resolution. Assert per-delivery identity instead, e.g. that each (device, frame) in the window appears exactly once.

`toHaveLength(120)` is effectively tautological here: port-conflict and multicast-blocked are discovery-plane faults that never touch the delivery path in `runFaultSuite`, so this count is always frames × devices regardless of whether frames actually "kept flowing" correctly. The `discoveryDegradedFrames` check below is the only meaningful assertion. Consider asserting per-device frame continuity (every device delivered on every frame in the window) so a broken failover that stalls delivery would be caught.

`sourceSilent` is derived from all active scenarios without applying `affects()`, so it ignores device scoping. A `dj-silence` scenario targeted at one device (e.g. `deviceId: "a"`) forces `"held"` payloads onto every other device too, diverging from the per-device scoping (`deviceFaults`) used everywhere else in this loop. Compute silence per device against `deviceFaults` (or filter with `affects`) and pass the per-device result to `port.deliver`.
apps/desktop/electron/services/fault-inj.suggestion_code: // (moved into the device loop, see below) const deviceSilent = deviceFaults.some((s) => s.kind === "dj-silence");

apps/desktop/electron/services/fault-inj.content: `pending` is incremented here and then unconditionally reset to 0 in every reachable branch below (congested skip, malformed drop, and successful delivery). As a result `pending.get(device)` is never greater than 1, so `maxPending` can only ever be 0 or 1 and the queue-depth metric is meaningless — a real accumulation regression would go undetected. Either model the queue honestly (only reset on delivery, keep depth while superseded frames are pending) or remove the misleading `maxPending` field.

`staleFrames` is hardcoded to the literal 0 for every scenario and for the aggregate result, and `recoveryFrames` is a fixed constant (0 for renderer-reload, 1 otherwise). These values are never measured from the port, so the suite reports success even if the port actually emits stale frames or a recovery gap. This defeats the exact behaviors specs 105/106/108 claim to guard. Derive `recoveryFrames`/`staleFrames` from the recorded deliveries instead of hardcoding them.

`framesDuringFault` is computed theoretically as `during * (targeted ? 1 : deviceCount)` and does not subtract frames that were skipped by throttle/latency/loss, dropped as malformed, or superseded. It therefore contradicts the actual delivered count recorded in the loop (e.g. an untargeted `malformed`/`throttle` scenario reports `during * N` even though zero frames were delivered). Count frames actually delivered to the affected device(s) during the window.

`othersContinued` is not a real measurement. `othersSeen` is only set from an unaffected device's delivery, and the fallback `!hasOthers` returns `true` whenever the scenario is untargeted (all devices affected) or targets a single/unknown device — even though no peer ever actually delivered. For an untargeted fault, or a `deviceId` absent from `opts.devices`, the flag reports `true` despite the fault applying to nothing or everything. Track per-device continued delivery during each scenario window rather than relying on this fallback.

The `discoveryDegradedFrames` counter is incremented once per logical frame while a discovery-plane fault is active, but the interface comment (line 62) states it "counts the frames delivered while one was active". With N devices there are N deliveries per tick, so the reported value (frames) understates deliveries by a factor of N. Align the comment with the implementation or count deliveries.

apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.content:
The memoization key is built from only the FIRST present identifier, but `resolveIdentity` (packages/track-model) uses a different precedence (rekordboxId → fileHash → pcmFingerprint → path). This makes the cache return identities that a fresh resolution would never produce. Concrete reproducible failure:
1) `resolve({ canonicalPath: "/a/b" })` → key `"/a/b"`, caches identity `id: "path:/a/b"` (no fileHash).
2) Later `resolve({ canonicalPath: "/a/b", fileHash: "H" })` → same key `"/a/b"` → cache HIT, returns the old path-only identity, even though `resolveIdentity` would now yield `id: "hash:H"`.
Same issue with `{ rekordboxId: "r1", fileHash: "H1" }` then `{ rekordboxId: "r1", fileHash: "H2" }`: the stale H1 identity is served. Also note the key precedence here (seratoPath/canonicalPath before fileHash) diverges from the id precedence in resolveIdentity, so a hit can even drop/replace source ids (`sourceIds.seratoPath` vs `canonicalPath`). Derive the key from all present identifiers (or from the resolved `identity.id`) so an upgraded input set re-resolves instead of returning a stale/weaker identity.
apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.existing_code: const key = parts.rekordboxId ?? parts.seratoPath ?? parts.canonicalPath ?? parts.fileHash ?? parts.pcmFingerprint;

apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.content: Empty-string identifiers are treated as present because the `??` chain and this `=== undefined` guard do not filter falsy values. `parts = { rekordboxId: "", canonicalPath: "/a/b" }` yields `key = ""`, which short-circuits the fallback to the valid `canonicalPath`, and `resolveIdentity` then throws its `!key` guard. Result: a track with a blank native id but a perfectly valid path fails with `E_IDENTITY_RESOLVE` instead of resolving via the path (broken failover). Use a falsy check and reject empty/whitespace keys (mirroring `resolveIdentity`'s `if (!key) throw`, which itself must be fixed consistently).

The cache is an unbounded `Map` with no eviction or size cap. In a long-running session resolving many tracks, it grows without limit (and `cachedIdentities()` materializes an ever-growing array), leaking memory. Consider an LRU / max-size bound, or clear it in `stop()` so a session restart does not retain every resolved identity.
apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.existing_code: private readonly cache = new Map<string, TrackIdentity>();

apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.content: This re-implements `messageOf` from `./base.js`, which exists precisely to avoid this duplication (used by analysis-supervisor, cloud-service, config-service, library-service, lifecycle, matter-bridge, midi-service, secrets-service, show-host-supervisor). Import and use `messageOf(err)` instead to keep error normalization consistent.
apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.existing_code: const message = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);

apps/desktop/electron/services/identity-.content: The exact `TrackIdentity` object created by `resolveIdentity` is stored in the cache and also returned to the caller (both on the miss path here and via `cache.get` on the hit path), so the cached entry is aliased and mutable. Any caller that mutates the returned identity (e.g. `identity.sourceIds`) silently corrupts every subsequent cache hit. Store a defensive copy/read-only object, or return a clone.

apps/desktop/electron/services/ipc-route.content:
The IPC trust boundary is fail-open and prefix-based, so it can be spoofed.

1) Fail-open: `event.senderFrame` is `null` for destroyed/unknown frames (and nullable in Electron), and an empty URL makes this return `true`, granting access to the privileged channels (`config/set`, `config/import`, `master/*`, `show/*`) instead of denying.
2) Prefix match: `startsWith("http://localhost:5173")` also matches `http://localhost:5173@evil.com/…` (the string after `@` is the real host) and `http://localhost:5173.evil.com`, letting a spoofed frame pass the allowlist. `file://` likewise accepts any local file origin.

Compare the parsed exact origin instead and fail closed when the frame is unknown. Note the same prefix pattern also lives in `main.ts` (allowedNavigation/onBeforeRequest), so the string should be a single shared constant rather than a hardcoded literal here.

Request validation, handler execution, and response validation all share one `try`/`catch`, so every failure collapses into the same `E_HANDLER` code at the bottom of `dispatch`. Consequences:

- A malformed/absent request payload (a renderer bug) is reported as an `E_HANDLER` server fault, making client/server faults indistinguishable in status and in the audit log.
- A response that violates the channel's response schema (a real protocol/handler bug) is reported identically to a thrown handler error, hiding response-schema mismatches.
- The response is validated *after* the handler's side effect has already run. If a handler mutates state (e.g. `setMasterBlackout`) but returns a shape the response schema rejects, the router returns `{ ok: false }` even though the action applied, so the renderer may retry/report a false failure.

Use distinct error codes (e.g. `E_REQUEST` for `request.parse`, `E_HANDLER` for handler throws, `E_RESPONSE` for `response.parse`) and audit them separately so protocol mismatches surface in the UI/status.

apps/desktop/electron/services/library-s.content: `stop()` clears the debounce timer but never clears (or flushes) `this.pending`. Any change events detected before shutdown are silently dropped, and the leftover entries are carried into the first batch emitted after a subsequent `start()` — with their pre-stop `atMs` timestamps — delivering stale changes to consumers and corrupting downstream state (`status().counters["pendingChanges"]` also keeps reporting them while stopped). Clear `pending` here (or flush it to listeners before shutting down if drop-on-stop is not intended).

No per-listener error isolation: a single throwing listener aborts the loop, so every later listener silently misses the batch, and the exception is thrown inside a `setTimeout` callback (after `this.debounce` was already nulled) where it becomes an uncaught exception. Wrap each invocation so one bad subscriber cannot break delivery to the others.

An async watcher 'error' only sets the tracker to degraded: the watcher object stays in `this.watchers` and is never closed. Combined with the `if (this.watchers.length > 0) return` guard at the top of `start()`, a later `start()` will short-circuit and refuse to re-establish a working watch, so a root can remain permanently unwatched while `start()` still returns without doing anything. Close/remove the failed watcher so recovery is possible.

`FileSystemWatcher` may report a null filename, and the interface type is `string | Buffer`. Substituting `eventType` ('rename'/'change') puts a bogus non-path value into `LibraryChange.file`, and passing a Buffer violates the declared `file: string` contract, breaking consumers that treat it as a path. Normalize: skip/omit the file when unknown and coerce Buffer to string.

`start()` sets the tracker to 'degraded' when a watcher cannot be opened (both the catch block and the 'error' handler), but the tail of the method unconditionally overwrites it with 'running' whenever at least one root is readable. The result: a service whose watch setup failed reports a healthy 'running' state, masking the degradation from callers and from the status machine. Preserve/aggregate the degraded state (e.g. only set 'running' when all readable roots were actually watched).

The lazy singleton memoizes the instance built from the first caller's options and is never reset, so later callers passing different `roots`/`watchRoot`/`debounceMs` (notably tests) silently get the original configuration, causing cross-test watcher/timer leakage and tests that exercise the wrong code path. Consider exposing a reset (or ignoring stale options explicitly / documenting the single-config contract) so callers cannot be silently misconfigured.

apps/desktop/electron/services/lifecycle.content: Singleton captures only the first caller's options. `instance ??= new LifecycleService(opts)` means that if `getLifecycleService()` is invoked before `userDataDir` is known (e.g. a module-level call during boot), every later call passing `userDataDir` is silently ignored and `crashPath()` returns `null` forever, so crash-record persistence is permanently disabled. Either make `userDataDir` injectable/updatable on the singleton, or require the caller to resolve `userDataDir` before the first access.

The crash-hold timer is `unref`'d, so it does not keep the event loop alive. If the crash occurs on the last thing keeping the process up (or the app begins quitting), Node/Electron can exit before the timer fires, meaning `safeLook("dim")` never runs and the returned `dimmed` promise never resolves. That defeats the "hold then dim" crash contract. Remove the `unref()` so the dim phase is guaranteed to run, or document that callers must keep the process alive.
apps/desktop/electron/services/lifecycle.suggestion_code:
// Do NOT unref: the safe-look dim must run even when nothing else keeps
  // the loop alive, otherwise `dimmed` never resolves.

apps/desktop/electron/services/lifecycle.content: On timeout `Promise.race` settles but the `port()` promise is never cancelled; the wedged step keeps executing concurrently with all subsequent teardown steps (e.g. `flush-db` runs while `analysis` is still shutting down), which can cause data races/lost writes. Additionally, if that still-running promise later rejects, the rejection is unhandled. Attach a rejection handler and/or await the underlying promise with its own guard so a timed-out step cannot corrupt later steps.

`nextStage()` selects any stage that is not `ok`/`degraded`, which includes terminal `failed` states. A stage already marked `failed` will be returned again, so callers that loop `advance(nextStage(), ...)` can retry a permanently dead stage or spin forever instead of surfacing the terminal failure. Exclude `failed` (and only return `pending`/`running`).

`advance()` has two timing/state problems: (1) it overwrites `startedAtMs` on every `running` call, so a re-entry resets the measured duration; (2) it only records `ms` when `startedAtMs` already exists, so a stage that transitions straight to `ok`/`degraded`/`failed` without a prior `running` reports no duration. There is also no guard against illegal transitions (e.g. `ok` back to `running`). Guard the transition and seed `startedAtMs` on first entry so timing is always meaningful.

apps/desktop/electron/services/live-show.content: Machine-specific absolute paths committed into the suite. `cpSync` throws ENOENT synchronously when the source is missing, so every test that copies from these paths errors on CI or any other developer machine — the suite is non-portable and unreliable. Also note the ANLZ bucket name `fb47d-24bc-49c5-b5e7-ce275ed46465` is not a well-formed UUID (first segment truncated), which suggests a corrupted copy/paste. Move the fixtures into the repository (checked-in test fixtures) or resolve them from an env var and `describe.skipIf` when absent.

The mock ignores all of its arguments (`audioPath`, `nativeDir`, `trackId`) and always returns the same artifact. Because `resolveDeck` passes the discovered ANLZ dir and a `trackId` into `analyze`, a bug that associates the wrong directory/track with a deck (wrong title matching, broken cache keying across decks) would not be caught. Assert the call arguments and vary the return per track/deck to actually exercise identification logic.

Only the "analyzer resolves to null" failure path is covered. The more likely real failure is the analyzer rejecting/throwing, and `resolveDeck` has no try/catch around `await this.analyze(...)`, so a rejection propagates to the caller (potential unhandled rejection). Add a case where `analyze` rejects and assert the expected behavior of `resolveDeck`, otherwise this error path is entirely untested.

    // assert resolveDeck either rejects or returns null per the intended contract

apps/desktop/electron/services/live-show.content: `supervisor.start()` has no corresponding `stop()` and the `afterEach` only resets the bridge, so this instance is left in the `running` state. The trailing `start()` also serves no assertion purpose here (the failure was already asserted before it). Either remove it or pair it with `supervisor.stop()` to guarantee no worker/timer is left behind if this test is later extended to submit after start.

Claim dedup compares incompatible keys, so the fallback always returns `dirs[0]`. The `claimed` set is built from `d.track.identity.id`, which is always the synthetic `live-deck${deckId}` value (see `trackId` below), never a filesystem path. `dirs` contains `nativeDir` paths, so `claimed.has(dir)` is always `false` and `dirs.find(...)` always yields `dirs[0]`. Because the only production caller (`readLiveShow`) passes `title = null`, the title-match branch never runs either, so *every* deck on first sight binds to the same first ANLZ directory and reports the same TrackModel/ShowPlan. This silently duplicates one track across all decks. Fix by recording the resolved `nativeDir` per deck and excluding those directories from the candidate list.

apps/desktop/electron/services/live-show.content: Singleton silently discards `BridgeOptions` after first construction. `getLiveShowBridge` only applies `opts` when `bridge === null`; a later caller that is the first to supply `analyze` (or a different `styleId`/`shareDir`) is ignored. Concretely, if any code calls `getLiveShowBridge()` with no options before `readLiveShow`, the analyzer is permanently absent and every `resolveDeck` hits the `no-analyzer` miss path, so no deck ever resolves. Consider merging/overriding options on each call, or lazily binding the analyzer on first use so a later provider can supply it.

apps/desktop/electron/services/live-show.content: Concurrent first-sight resolution for the same deck duplicates work and races the cache. The first-sight path checks `this.decks.get(deckId)` before the `await this.analyze(...)` with no in-flight dedup, so two concurrent AX readings for a new `deckId` (e.g. `Promise.all` over rapidly repeated polls in `readLiveShow`) both launch analysis; the analyzer artifacts are then written and the cache/state is overwritten last-writer-wins. Track an in-flight `Promise<BridgeDeck|null>` per deck and return it to coalesce concurrent calls.

apps/desktop/electron/services/live-show.content: Bidirectional substring title matching can bind a deck to the wrong ANLZ set. `readTrackTitle` picks the longest printable run from arbitrary UTF-16 binary data (a heuristic, not a real tag parse), and the match accepts `lower.includes(t.toLowerCase())` in addition to the forward containment, so a short/noisy extracted string can false-positive against an unrelated directory. Since the resulting TrackModel/ShowPlan looks valid, there is no fallback to the honest `no-anlz-match` path. Tighten matching (exact/normalized equality, minimum length, or prefer the true PSSI/PQTZ title field) to avoid silently binding the wrong track.

Parse/plan failures are swallowed without any audit entry, unlike the other miss paths (`bridge.miss`). A malformed artifact or schema mismatch thrown by `JSON.parse`, `trackModelSchema.parse`, `showStyleSchema.parse`, or `planShow` becomes invisible and undiagnosable, and the deck stays silently unresolved on every subsequent poll (the caught error is discarded). Add an `audit("bridge.miss", { deck: deckId, reason: "analysis-failed" /* or "plan-failed" */ })` (and log the error) in this catch to keep failures observable.

apps/desktop/electron/services/matter-br.content: `stop()` kills the process and nulls `this.port`, but the port's `onExit` handler (registered in `start()`) fires asynchronously and unconditionally calls `this.start()`. Because there is no `stopped`/lifecycle flag, a `stop()` issued while a running controller is killed will respawn the utility process right after intentional shutdown, leaving an orphaned/zombie process that the service no longer tracks. Add a `stopped` flag (set in `stop()`, cleared in `start()`) or a generation token that `onExit` checks before restarting.

The exit closure is not bound to the specific `port` instance, so an exit event from a previously replaced or killed port will null out `this.port` (which may already point to a freshly started port) and then call `this.start()`, spawning a duplicate controller while orphaning the live one. Capture `port` in the closure and guard with `if (this.port !== port) return;` before clearing/restarting.

`this.restarts` is never reset, so it accumulates across the entire process lifetime. After `maxRestarts` crashes spread over months (even with long healthy runs in between), the bridge is permanently pinned to `degraded` with no way to recover. Reset the counter after a healthy uptime window (e.g. the process stayed alive for N seconds) or expose an explicit reset so transient crashes don't cause permanent degradation.

`postMessage` is called with no error handling. If the controller process has crashed but `onExit` hasn't run yet (the exit is asynchronous), `this.port` is still non-null and `postMessage` throws a raw exception to the caller, contradicting the `boolean` contract that implies `false` on failure. Wrap the call in try/catch and return `false` on failure.

A throwing listener aborts delivery to the remaining listeners and propagates the exception into the port's message callback (potentially killing message dispatch entirely). Wrap each invocation in try/catch so one faulty subscriber cannot break message relay for others.

Options are only applied on the first invocation (`instance ??= new MatterBridge(opts)`). Any later caller passing `spawn` or `maxRestarts` is silently ignored, which can yield a non-functional bridge that never wires the utility process. Document that options are first-call-only, or merge/override options on subsequent calls.

apps/desktop/electron/services/midi-serv.content: Resource leak on backend open failure. If `backend.open()` throws (e.g. it acquires the OS MIDI handle/port and then fails subscribing), the `catch` only marks the service degraded — the half-initialized backend is never `close()`d and `this.backend` stays `null`. The leaked OS handle survives, and a subsequent `start()` call (which sees `this.backend === null`) will invoke `openBackend()` again and open a second handle. Declare the backend outside the `try` and close it in the `catch` before degrading.

The lazy singleton silently ignores `opts` on every call after the first: `instance ??= new MidiService(opts)` returns the existing instance and drops the caller's `openBackend`. Tests or capture tooling that call `getMidiService({ openBackend })` with a different backend will unknowingly bind to a stale/default one and exercise the wrong code path. Either assert that `opts` is empty when an instance already exists, or provide an explicit reset/reconfigure seam for tests.

Listener fan-out is not failure-isolated. A single listener that throws aborts the `for` loop, so every listener registered after it silently misses the hint (and the exception propagates back into the MIDI backend callback / `handleCc` / `handleNote`). Iterate over a snapshot and guard each invocation so one bad subscriber cannot break delivery to the rest, nor corrupt hint ingestion.

`find` returns the first match, and the imported `NOTE` map has duplicate values (PLAY_1/PLAY_2 = 0x0b, CUE_1/CUE_2 = 0x0c, SYNC_1/SYNC_2 = 0x58). As a result `controlForNote` can only ever return the `*_1` control (PLAY_1, CUE_1, SYNC_1); the deck-2 controls are unreachable and transport hints for deck 2 are mislabeled as deck 1. If deck separation is required, use the deck-aware `decodeMessage`/`FLX4_CONTROLS` path from the package instead of this channel-blind reverse lookup.

Telemetry is inconsistent: the backend callback increments the `messages` counter, but the direct injection paths `handleCc`/`handleNote` never do, so injected traffic is invisible in `status()`. Additionally `status()` is a query that mutates tracker counters (`setCounter`) on every read, coupling observation to state. Move the counter bookkeeping into `publish()`/the injection helpers and make `status()` read-only (e.g. snapshot counters at publish time).

apps/desktop/electron/services/provider-.content: `prolinkBindError` is a module-level flag that is only ever *set* (on `error`) and never cleared. After one transient bind failure, `providers()` will permanently report `deaf on :50001` even if a later `start()` binds successfully and `observation.peerPresent` becomes true. Clear the flag once the bind is confirmed via the `listening` event (and reset it in `stop()`/on the cleanup path).

On a bind error the socket is never closed/destroyed. The observer is left in a half-configured, unbound state and the fd is only released when `stop()` happens to run (the returned closer is the only teardown). On repeated start/stop or reset cycles (e.g. `resetProviderManagerForTest`) this leaks file descriptors. Destroy the socket inside the error handler.

Race: `boot()` is fire-and-forget and its promise is not tracked. If `stop()` runs while the boot is in flight, `stop()` sets `this.composite = null` / `compositeStarted = false`, but the late-resolving `.then` then re-assigns `this.composite = result`, resurrecting composite state after shutdown (so `providers()` reports `composite-flx4` running again). Guard the continuation against the current lifecycle (e.g. an epoch/generation counter incremented in `stop()`).

`setInterval` fires `tick` every `pollMs` regardless of whether the previous `await poll()` has settled. A slow osascript/helper call (up to 8s/3s timeouts) overlaps with subsequent ticks, so several polls run concurrently and a late-finishing earlier poll can overwrite `this.readings` with stale data; `axTicks` is also over-counted. Add an in-flight guard so only one poll runs at a time.

The osascript fallback flattens all static texts from every Rekordbox window into one comma-joined stream, matches clock pairs with a global regex, then maps them positionally (`decks[deckId - 1]`). Any extra/missing text or a different window/deck ordering silently shifts readings onto the wrong deck instead of being reported unreadable. Since the regex already discards all positional metadata, deck identity cannot be recovered reliably; at minimum validate the expected count and mark unreadable otherwise.

apps/desktop/electron/services/secrets-s.content: This plaintext-persistence assertion is effectively vacuous. `SecretVault.flush()` writes `toBase64(crypto.encryptString(...))`, and `PLAIN` contains `-`, which cannot appear in the base64 alphabet, so `bytes.includes(PLAIN)` can never be true regardless of whether encryption actually happened. Combined with the transparent fake cipher (`encryptString` returns `enc(<plaintext>)`, so the "encrypted" bytes still contain the secret verbatim), the test would still pass even if encryption were removed and the vault wrote `toBase64(JSON.stringify(persist))` directly. Make the fake cipher opaque (e.g. XOR each byte with a fixed key) and assert against the base64-decoded blob so the check genuinely detects a missing/identity encryption step.

Test name promises the cloud key is retained ("keeps the cloud key"), but the body only sets/checks the memory-only agent token — the cloud key is never set and never asserted. The test can pass regardless of a cloud-key persistence regression, so the stated guarantee is unverified. Set `govee.cloud.apiKey` before the restart and assert it is still retrievable (in addition to the agent token being gone), or rename the test to match what it actually verifies.
apps/desktop/electron/services/secrets-s.existing_code: it("loses the agent token across a restart but keeps the cloud key", async () => {

apps/desktop/electron/services/secrets-s.content: Removal durability is never verified across a restart. The test checks only the in-memory `getSecret` after `removeSecret`, then stops. `removeSecret` ultimately calls `flush()`, which for an empty persistent set writes `clearBlob()` ("blob": null). If `clearBlob` were a no-op (or wrongly rewrote the old blob), the value would remain in the on-disk file and a subsequent start would resurrect it — yet this test would still pass. Add a third `started(file)` cycle and assert `getSecret("govee.cloud.apiKey")` is missing after restart.

The test is titled "redacts every live value at log boundaries" but only the persisted cloud key (`PLAIN`) is set before calling `redactSecrets`/`liveValues()`. The memory-only agent token is a live value too (`liveValues()` returns both ids), yet it is never exercised, so a leak of in-memory secrets through redaction would go undetected. Also set `agent.apiToken` and assert its value is redacted from the same line.

Inconsistent error contract: `getSecret` declares a structured-error return (`{ ok: false; error: {...} }`) but `requireVault()` throws `Error("secrets-service not started")` when the service has not been started (or was stopped), and the call is not wrapped. Unlike `setSecret`, this escapes as an uncaught exception across the API/IPC boundary instead of the documented error shape. apps/desktop/journeys/m1-slice.journey.t.content: Two issues with the blackout deadline: (1) `t0.wallMs` is `Date.now()` captured in the Playwright test-runner process, while `zero.sentAtMs` is the recording transport's timestamp from the main process — if the transport uses a monotonic/app-relative clock (the `RecordedFrame` type gives no guarantee), the `< 100 ms` subtraction mixes clock domains and is meaningless. (2) `frames` is read once immediately after the keypress with no retry, so the blackout frame may not be recorded yet, making `expect(zero).not.toBeNull()` flaky. Confirm both timestamps share one epoch and poll/wait for the zero frame before asserting the deadline.

This assertion is tautological: `resume.wallMs` and `t0.wallMs` are both `Date.now()` and the A press necessarily happens after the B press, so it can never fail and validates nothing about "resume on the next bar". Either drop it or assert something meaningful (e.g. that a non-black frame resumes after `resume.wallMs` in the next recorded frames).

The P-56 continuity check is too weak: it only requires at least one frame with `sentAtMs > lastBefore` and pairwise gaps `< 500 ms` starting from index 1. A single frame emitted right after the freeze begins satisfies it, and the gap between `lastBefore` and the first "during" frame is never checked, so a stall at the start of the pause goes undetected. Also, nothing computes that frames actually span the full 5 s freeze window (or the expected frame count for the qualified rate), and the negative-gap case (unsorted `sentAtMs`) would also pass. Assert frame coverage across the whole pause window (first/last timestamps vs. the freeze duration and expected count).

apps/desktop/journeys/night.journey.ts.content: This assertion cannot tell a working blackout from a broken one. `renderFrame` (packages/renderer/src/index.ts:108-137) already returns an all-zero frame for any cell not covered by an active lighting cue, and the only cue here is the blackout itself. If the `blackout` type were dropped/ignored (or `intensity: 1` were mishandled) the fixtures would still render `rgb(0,0,0)` and this test would pass green. Add a lower-priority lit look on the same cells (e.g. a `section-look` on `PRIMARY` with `priority: < 100`) so the frame is black *only because* blackout overrides it, and assert those cells are non-black without the blackout cue.

The test claims to prove crossfade "hands over ownership", but it never asserts `owner`, and it cannot observe which deck dominates: the single fixture (`makeFixture("f", 4)` + `groups: ["PRIMARY", "SECONDARY"]`) belongs to both target groups, so deck A and deck B paint the *same* cells and `brightness` counts the same lit cells on both sides. The only real check is the weight ordering, which would still pass even if ownership failed to transfer. Assert the handover explicitly, e.g. `expect(left.owner).toBe("a")` / `expect(right.owner).toBe("b")`, and give A and B distinct fixtures so the dominant deck's cells can be distinguished.

In production `deckA` and `mixA.state` are the *same* object (`resolve-live.ts:80` builds `mixA: { state: deckA, ... }`), but here `makeDeck` is called twice, so `deckA !== mixA.state` (and `deckB !== mixB.state`). The view-model reads `deckA` for `weights` and `mixA.state` inside `mixDown`, so these duplicated-but-identical instances no longer mirror the production shape and could mask a state-synchronization regression. Build one instance per deck and reuse it for both `deckX` and `mixX.state`.

apps/desktop/package.json.content: `electron-builder` is invoked by these scripts but is not declared in this package's `devDependencies` (only in the root `package.json`). Resolution currently relies on hoisting via `nodeLinker: node-modules`; if the linker is switched to PnP or the root dep is removed, packaging breaks. Declare the tool in this package's `devDependencies` (e.g. `"electron-builder": "^26"`) so the dependency is explicit and version-consistent.

`dist:package:dir` omits `node scripts/fetch-vendor.mjs`, but `electron-builder.cjs` unconditionally lists `vendor` under `extraResources`. On a clean checkout (no `apps/desktop/vendor/`) electron-builder will fail because the `extraResources.from: "vendor"` directory does not exist, so this script produces a broken/incomplete package. Run `fetch-vendor` here as well (matching `dist:package`).

All internal workspace packages are referenced with a semver range (`^0.1.0`) instead of the `workspace:` protocol. Because `^0.1.0` allows `<0.2.0`, any workspace package bumped to `0.2.0` would silently stop matching the local workspace and be resolved from the registry, causing version/schema drift between packages in the same monorepo. Prefer `workspace:^0.1.0` (this repo uses Yarn 4) to guarantee local linking and an explicit version contract.

apps/desktop/playwright.config.ts.content: `testDir: "./journeys"` restricts test discovery to the `journeys/` directory, and `testMatch: "**/*.journey.ts"` only accepts `.journey.ts` files. As a result `apps/desktop/e2e/normal-night.spec.ts` (the T-QA-11 17-row acceptance spec for 99-final-acceptance.md section 3) is never collected by `yarn workspace @autolight/desktop test:e2e` — it can never pass or fail. This contradicts docs/finish/evidence/T-QA-11/README.md, which states "the e2e spec is picked up by the same `test:e2e` command", and it matches the documented run ("5 passed": m1-slice + night(2) + soak + live-session = 5 tests over 4 files, i.e. the spec is silently skipped). A silently-unrun acceptance suite means real regressions in those 17 rows go undetected. Either relocate the spec under `journeys/` (e.g. `normal-night.journey.ts`, consistent with e2e/README.md which says the `e2e/` dir stays empty), or widen discovery, e.g. `testDir: "."` with `testMatch: ["**/journeys/**/*.journey.ts", "**/e2e/**/*.spec.ts"]`.

`retries: 0` is set but there is no `forbidOnly` guard. Several journeys (m1-slice, normal-night) are intentionally-red probes whose whole purpose is to fail until dependencies land. If a developer leaves a stray `test.only(...)` on a green test (night/soak/live-session) and pushes, Playwright silently skips all other tests, so CI passes green while the red probes are never evaluated — tests passing despite unverified behavior. Suggest adding the standard CI guard so a committed `.only` fails the run.

apps/desktop/scripts/build-main.mjs.content: The top-level `await`s (`context`, `watch`, `build`) run without any error handling. If `workspaceSrc` is missing or a build fails, the script surfaces an opaque unhandled rejection. Wrap the run logic in try/catch to emit a clear message and exit non-zero deterministically (important for CI/packaging).

apps/desktop/scripts/build-preload.mjs.content: The alias map is built from every raw entry returned by `readdirSync`, with no filtering for directories or for the existence of `src/index.ts`. Stray entries (e.g. `.DS_Store`, stray files, or a non-package directory) produce bogus aliases, and any workspace entry whose directory name differs from the actual package name (or that has no `src/index.ts` barrel) yields an alias that either never matches the import specifier or points at a non-existent file, causing opaque `Could not resolve` build failures that appear only once that package is imported. Filter to real directories whose barrel exists before generating aliases.

`workspaceSrc` hardcodes the relative path `../../packages` with no existence check. If the script is ever run from a different layout (monorepo moved, file relocated, `packages` renamed/removed), `readdirSync` throws a raw `ENOENT` that gives no hint about the expected workspace layout. Consider validating the directory exists and emitting an actionable error.

More importantly, `ctx.watch()` performs the initial build internally and only logs failures (with `logLevel: "warning"`), so a broken first build still prints `watching ...` and looks successful. Surface the initial build result/errors and dispose the context on termination signals.

apps/desktop/scripts/build-preload.mjs.content: Both branches `await` esbuild at top level without any `try/catch`, so a build failure bubbles up as an unhandled promise rejection instead of a clean, diagnosable exit; the `bundled ...` log is only reached on success, but there is no `catch` to print a user-facing message or set a non-zero exit code. Wrap the build/watch invocation in a `try/catch` that logs the error and sets `process.exitCode = 1`.

apps/desktop/scripts/fetch-vendor.mjs.content: The script never actually fetches the sidecars it advertises. `FFMPEG_MAC`/`FFMPEG_WIN` are only written into the manifest as `url` fields (no download occurs), and `uv`/CPython are installed into the `uv` cache rather than being placed under `vendor/<platform>/`. Combined with `apps/desktop/electron-builder.cjs` copying `vendor` → `vendor`, packaging can ship a `manifest.json` that advertises FFmpeg, uv and CPython binaries that do not exist in the bundle. The header comment ("Downloads pinned uv + Python ... + FFmpeg into vendor/<platform>/") contradicts the implementation. Add real download/copy steps (with checksum verification) and a post-fetch existence assertion before writing the manifest.

`ffmpeg-release-essentials.zip` is a moving "latest" URL, so the vendored binary is non-reproducible and changes without any review, directly contradicting the "Pinned sidecars" comment. There is also no checksum/verification. Pin an immutable, versioned URL and verify a SHA-256 digest after download.

Two problems here: (1) `uv python install` installs the *host-arch* interpreter, so fetching `mac-x64` on an `mac-arm64` host (or vice versa) seeds a Python whose architecture does not match `vendor/<platform>/`, producing an unrunnable/mislabeled bundle. (2) `execFileSync` throws when `uv` is missing (the manifest note admits uv may not be present on dev machines), and the throw is uncaught, aborting the whole run with a raw stack trace. Skip the install when the target arch differs from the host, and wrap the call so failures surface as an actionable message.

The header comment claims the FFmpeg build is the "static GPL-conformant build", but the manifest note records it as "LGPL-recorded" and `tools/license-check.mjs` hand-lists FFmpeg as `LGPL-2.1-or-later`. The referenced builds (evermeet.cx and gyan.dev "essentials") are in fact GPL builds, so the recorded license may diverge from the actual shipped binary and the license hand list — a real compliance risk. Reconcile the header comment, the manifest note, and the license-check hand list with the actual build's license.

apps/desktop/src/features/diagnostics/di.content: The promise chain has no `.catch`/`.finally`. `invoke()` itself never rejects (it swallows errors and returns `null`), but any throw inside this `.then` callback — e.g. `JSON.stringify(d?.ax)` on a payload containing `BigInt` or a cyclic structure that structured-clone preserved (the IPC schema is `z.unknown()`, so nothing is stripped) — rejects an unobserved promise and silently aborts the whole update (no `setSeenAt`, no `setSessionEvents`, no user-visible error). Prefer an `async` IIFE with `try/catch`.

`seenAt` is stamped on every resolved fetch regardless of outcome. When `diagnostics/all` fails, `invoke` returns `null`, so `d` is `undefined` and this block still rebuilds the map with empty values (`AX: [] PROLINK: {}`, `Transport: "no decks"`, …) and then marks the fetch fresh. The `stale` badge therefore can never indicate a failed/absent fetch — the panel silently reports success on stale/empty data. Only stamp `seenAt` (and rebuild) when `envelope?.ok !== false && d !== undefined`, otherwise leave the previous timestamp/state intact.

`isFresh` is evaluated with a `Date.now()` captured only at render time and there is no timer in this component. After a successful fetch `seenAt ≈ now`, so `stale` is `false`, and it will never flip to `true` as time passes unless some unrelated store change re-renders the view (>2s later, per the default `staleAfterMs`). The freshness indicator is effectively dead. Drive it from a ticking state (e.g. a 1s `setInterval` updating a `now` value) or a `useSyncExternalStore`-style clock.

These deps (`live` in particular is replaced frequently by beat/status updates during a show) re-run the whole effect and fire a fresh `diagnostics/all` IPC request on every change. The `cancelled` guard keeps the results correct, but this is a request-per-beat storm. Additionally each re-run resets `seenAt`, which masks the staleness detection. Consider narrowing to primitives (e.g. `live?.source`, deck titles) or sourcing the refresh from a dedicated interval instead of store reactivity.

The `fallback` path is unreachable: `TabMetrics` only reaches it when `found.length === 0`, and every tab in `TAB_ROWS` (Transport, Beat Clock, Track Resolver, Analysis, Planner, Renderer, Fixtures, Latency) always has a matching label in the inline `rows` array (Logs returns early). So the per-tab strings written into the store by the effect (`Transport`, `Beat Clock`, `Planner`, …) are never read, while the same values are recomputed inline in `rows` with different formatting (`"deck1=…"` vs `"· deck 1 …"`). This duplicated source of truth will silently drift and one of the copies is dead code. `set({ diagnostics: {…} })` replaces the entire `diagnostics` map rather than merging. As written the assertion (`DROP IN 16`) would still pass if the drop/breakdown/build ordering or the `priority` field handling regressed, so the stated behavior is unverified. Add a `build-ramp` cue to the fixture and assert the full ordering explicitly (and decide whether precedence should actually be driven by `priority`, which the fixture implies with 100 vs 40).

Fallback and boundary paths are untested. `predictiveLabel` is never exercised with an empty cue list, a drop beyond the horizon, or a breakdown-only set (its `BREAKDOWN IN`/`BUILD`/null branches are never asserted), and `nextPhraseBeat` is only checked mid-phrase (33). Add cases such as `predictiveLabel([], 0) === null`, a breakdown-only case, and the exact boundaries `nextPhraseBeat(32) === 32` and `nextPhraseBeat(64) === 64` so off-by-one regressions at phrase boundaries are caught.

The "labels missing data instead of guessing" case asserts only title/nativeBpm/nextEvent, omitting `section`, `analysisQuality`, and derived `bar`/`phrase`. Missing-data guessing for those fields would go undetected. Assert `idle.section === null` and `idle.analysisQuality === "NEEDS ANALYSIS"` (and the beat-0 bar/phrase values) to cover the degradation contract fully.

Drop cue is selected by type priority (earliest `white-hit` first), not by nearest start time, and there is no re-search after the horizon check. Two failure modes:
1) A far-away white-hit/impact masks a nearer `drop` (e.g. `[{white-hit,200},{drop,40}]`, beat=32 → says "DROP IN 168"... actually fails horizon and falls through, hiding the drop at 8 beats).
2) If the matched drop is beyond `horizonBeats`, `drop` is still non-null so the branch is skipped and the code falls to breakdown/build, returning `null` even though a plain `drop` sits inside the horizon.
Concrete: `predictiveLabel([{type:'white-hit',startBeat:200},{type:'drop',startBeat:40}], 32)` returns `null` instead of "DROP IN 8".
Select the earliest cue among all drop-family types (which `after` is already sorted for):

This violates the module contract stated at the top ("Missing data renders as null ... never a guessed number"). Guard for a positive, finite rate and emit `null` otherwise.

`nativeBpm` is always taken from the first grid anchor (`grid[0]`), which ignores per-beat tempo and is wrong when the current beat lies in a different grid segment (the contract's `nativeBeatSchema.bpm` is per-anchor and adaptive grids carry an empty `beats` array). Derive the BPM from the anchor at/around the current position (falling back to `grid[0]`) instead of the first element.

`nextPhraseBeat` returns the boundary `at` the beat, not the next one: when `beat` is exactly on a phrase boundary (e.g. 32) it returns `32`, so a caller like `invoke("show/trigger-build", { at: nextPhraseBeat(s.liveBeat) })` can schedule at the current beat instead of the upcoming phrase. Negative beats also silently clamp. If strictly-next semantics are intended, add `phraseBeats` to the floored boundary.

Since `upcoming` only contains cues with `startBeat > beat`, the difference can be < 0.5 and rounds to 0, producing a misleading "<type> in 0 beats" while the cue is still in the future. `predictiveLabel` guards this with `Math.max(1, ...)` but this branch does not — apply the same clamp for consistency.

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content:
`intent.channel in channels` walks the prototype chain and only tests key existence, so a bogus/non-implemented name that happens to be inherited (e.g. `"toString"`, `"constructor"`, `"valueOf"`) would still make this assertion pass. The test name claims to verify "only implemented typed channels" but does not. Use an own-property check and, ideally, validate the payload against the channel's request schema so a channel/payload mismatch is also caught. E.g.:
```ts
expect(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(channels, intent.channel)).toBe(true);
```

These `toMatchObject` assertions only inspect a subset of keys, so they cannot detect a wrong/missing intent channel or extra payload fields. Notably `blinderIntent(64)` is asserted solely on `payload.at` while its channel is actually `"show/trigger-build"` (and that channel's request schema is `z.object({ version: v1 })`, which has no `at`); a mis-wired channel or a stripped/unexpected payload field would go unnoticed. `palettePickIntent` is only checked for `custom` and `flashIntent` only for `channel`. Assert the full intent (`channel` + `payload`) for each helper, and for helpers bound to a channel validate the payload with that channel's request schema.

This assertion pins the clamp result at `2` for input `9`, but the `master/intensity` request schema in `@autolight/ipc` is `z.object({ version: v1, value: z.number().min(0).max(1) })` — a value of `2` is outside the contract and would be rejected at runtime. `manual-intents.ts` clamps with `Math.min(2, Math.max(0.5, value))`, so the test locks in a contract-violating bound instead of catching it. Assert a value within `[0, 1]` (and add negative/NaN/lower-bound cases) so the mismatch surfaces.

The fabricated `as unknown as TrackModel` fixture is never validated against the real model, and `toHaveLength(2)` only counts entries — it does not verify the returned colours, so an incorrect `SWATCH_BY_KIND` mapping (or falling back to the white default) would still pass. Also, because the two kinds are distinct this never exercises the de-duplication logic the description implies. Assert the actual swatch values and include a repeated `kind` to cover dedup.

const track = { sections: [{ kind: "chorus" }, { kind: "verse" }] } as unknown as TrackModel;
    expect(trackPalette(track)).toHaveLength(2);

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: `flashIntent(true)` only exercises the resume branch; the `false` branch (`master/freeze` with `payload.frozen: true`) and the payload shape of the true branch (`{ version: 1, at: "bar" }`) are never asserted, so a swapped branch or wrong freeze payload would not be caught. Add an assertion for `flashIntent(false)`.

Clamp range [0.5, 2] is incompatible with the `master/intensity` request schema. `packages/ipc/src/index.ts:34` declares `value: z.number().min(0).max(1)`, and `ipc-router.ts:140` runs `channels[name].request.parse(payload)` before dispatch. Any sensitivity > 1 (e.g. `sensitivityIntent(9)` → 2, or the `sensitivityIntent(1.5)` used in the test) yields a value above the schema max, so `parse` throws a ZodError and the router returns `{ ok:false, error:{ code:'E_HANDLER' } }` — the control simply fails instead of applying intensity. Additionally, `Math.min/Math.max` propagate `NaN`, so a non-finite input yields `value: NaN` (also rejected by the schema) rather than a safe default. Clamp to the schema bounds and guard non-finite input.

  return { channel: "master/intensity", payload: { version: 1, value: clamped } };

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: The `at` field is silently discarded, so the blinder is indistinguishable from a plain build. The `show/trigger-build` request schema (`packages/ipc/src/index.ts:64`) is `z.object({ version: v1 })` — there is no `at` — and zod's default object parsing strips unknown keys, so `at: nextPhraseBeat` never reaches the backend. The router handler `triggerBuild()` (`ipc-router.ts:43`) also takes no argument. Result: the "restraint-aware blinder carrying the next-phrase beat" advertised by the header comment is a no-op; the intended phrase-synced blinder fires as an immediate full build. If the blinder needs a distinct action/beat, it requires its own channel + schema (the `ManualChannel` union has no blinder/at-bearing channel today).

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: The `custom` flag never reaches the backend. The `venue/set-color` request schema (`packages/ipc/src/index.ts:80`) is `z.object({ version: v1, rgb: z.tuple([z.number(), z.number(), z.number()]) })` — no `custom` — and zod strips unknown keys during `request.parse`, so the "explicit custom free-colour opt-in" is a no-op and the handler `setVenueColor(req.rgb)` never sees it. Also, `rgb` is forwarded unvalidated: the schema only requires three `number`s, so floats, negatives, or values > 255 (and `NaN`) are accepted and forwarded to the driver. Add `custom` to the channel schema (or drop it here) and clamp/round rgb components to 0-255 integers.

apps/desktop/src/routes/live/manual-inte.content: Semantics of a momentary `flash` look inverted/unbalanced. `flashIntent(true)` maps to `master/resume` (run) and `flashIntent(false)` to `master/freeze` (persistent stop). A momentary flash control releasing to `master/freeze` would leave the master latched-frozen rather than releasing to the prior state, and the name "flash" does not match resume/freeze. Both payloads are individually schema-valid (`master/resume` `at: "bar"`, `master/freeze` `frozen: true`), so this is a behavioural/polarity concern rather than a schema error — confirm the intended on/off action before shipping.

Unknown section kinds silently resolve to white, masking contracts schema drift. If `@autolight/contracts` adds a new section kind (or the kind casing changes), `trackPalette` will quietly emit a white swatch with no signal that the `SWATCH_BY_KIND` map is out of date. Consider surfacing unmapped kinds (log/dev warning) so missing mappings are detectable.

apps/desktop/src/routes/routes.test.ts.content: The `library` marker is not unique to the Library screen: SetupView renders each step's `title` from `STEP_LABELS`, and the `"library"` step title is literally `"Library"` (see `apps/desktop/src/features/setup/setup-view.tsx` line 12 + the `SETUP_EVIDENCE_STEPS.map` list). Because the assertion uses `toContain`, a mis-wiring such as `library: () => <SetupView />` in `routes/index.tsx` would still produce markup containing "Library" and the test would pass, defeating the "a mis-wired import fails here" intent in the comment above. Use a screen-unique marker (e.g. the `aria-label="Library"` table / "Preanalysis queue" heading) or combine positive markers with a negative check against the other screens.

The `"Lights"` marker is a generic substring that also appears on other screens' static markup: SetupView renders the `"lights"` step title `"Lights"`, and DiagnosticsView renders a `"Lights"` metric row/TAB_ROWS label (line 97). A mis-wiring like `venue: () => <DiagnosticsView />` (or SetupView) would still satisfy `toContain("Lights")`, so the test cannot detect that failure. Prefer a marker unique to the Venue screen (e.g. the "Find lights" heading or the `aria-label="Venue sections"` tablist).

Typing MARKERS as `[Route, string][]` does not enforce exhaustiveness: it only guarantees each entry's first element is a valid Route, so a newly added Route member (or an accidentally deleted entry) compiles and silently loses coverage, contradicting the comment claiming the table is exhaustive. Keying the table by Route makes the compiler require every member, e.g.:

```ts
const MARKERS: Record<Route, string> = {
  live: "No show loaded",
  library: "Library",
  inspector: "Track inspector",
  venue: "Lights",
  setup: "Follow mode",
  diagnostics: "Diagnostics",
  settings: "Search settings",
};
```
then iterate `Object.entries(MARKERS)`.

Only the `live: null` prop path is exercised, and `renderToStaticMarkup` never runs effects. Screen content that is produced in `useEffect` (e.g. DiagnosticsView's metric rows, InspectorView's lane loading) is not rendered by SSR, so these assertions only validate the static shell text and would not catch a route that throws or renders nothing once data arrives. Consider also rendering a route with a populated `LiveState` so the non-null live branch is covered.

A malformed registry — duplicate entries, a renamed/removed scenario id that keeps the count at 5, or wrong ordering — would still pass while `SIMULATOR_SCENARIOS` is actually broken. Assert the exact set of ids instead of just the count.

Protocol mismatch: the `simulator/mode` request schema in `packages/ipc/src/index.ts` declares only `{ version, enabled }` (no `scenario`), and the main-process handler calls `setSimulatorMode(req.enabled)` which records/persists only `enabled`. The `scenario` field produced here is therefore not part of the channel contract and is silently stripped by the zod `parse` in the IPC router (unknown keys are dropped by default), so the selected scenario never reaches the backend. A consumer that wires this intent into `invoke` will believe the scenario is transmitted when it is not. Either extend the `simulator/mode` request schema + handler to carry `scenario`, or drop `scenario` from the payload so the intent matches the wire contract.

F-UI-13).

The comment overstates the guarantee: the function only checks the 95th percentile, so up to ~5% of samples may still exceed one frame. A negative regression that flips an unrelated flag to `true` (e.g. `controller`, which the model currently hardcodes to `false`) would not be detected. `controller` is hardcoded `false`, but it is ordered 2nd (right after `dj`). Since `setupProgress` returns `next` as the first step whose evidence `!== true`, once `dj` completes `next` is permanently pinned to `controller` and can never advance to `library`/`lights`/…; likewise `next === "ready"` is unreachable in the real UI, so "All steps ready" never shows. `controller`'s route is `"setup"`, so no "Open" button is rendered either — the user is left with a non-actionable "Next: controller" forever even when later steps are satisfied. Either drop `controller` from the ordered readiness steps until an IPC source exists, or make `setupProgress` skip steps that have no evidence source.

`placement` and `orientation` are both derived from the single `roomSaved` boolean, so they can never disagree or be measured independently. Per `STEP_LABELS`, `orientation` is "DJ anchor facing" — a saved-room record does not necessarily prove the anchor/orientation was set, so a saved room falsely marks `orientation` ready and defeats the per-step gating the file header claims. Give `orientation` its own evidence source, or keep it pending until distinct evidence exists.

`library` readiness is inferred from a presentation sentinel: any deck whose title is not the literal em-dash `"—"` counts as a resolved track. This couples the evidence model to a UI placeholder string (also used in `resolve-live.ts`/`library-rows.ts`). If the placeholder ever changes, or a deck legitimately carries an empty-string title, `library` is reported incorrectly. Prefer a data-level signal (e.g. non-null track identity) rather than filtering by the magic `"—"` string.

apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/room-canva.content: The DJ facing arrow is mirrored in X relative to the engine's facing convention. `computeFields` (packages/venue/src/fields.ts:176-181) rotates into the DJ frame with `rx = dx·cos f + dy·sin f`, `ry = -dx·sin f + dy·cos f` and defines the front side as `frontBack = ly >= 0` (fields.ts:268), i.e. the engine's forward vector is `(-sin f, cos f)`. This arrow tip uses `(+sin f, +cos f)`, so the rendered arrow agrees with the engine only for f = 0 or ±π; for the ±90° values the "DJ facing (deg)" input produces, the arrow points at the region the engine marks as back. Align the arrow with the engine (or fix the convention consistently) so the picture matches the computed front/back field.

apps/desktop/src/routes/venue/room-previ.content: `referenceById(roomId)` throws for any id that is not present in `REFERENCE_ROOMS` (`if (!found) throw new Error(...)` in packages/venue/src/reference.ts). The result is dereferenced immediately (`ref.room`, `ref.zeroS`, `ref.runs`), so a mistyped/misconfigured `roomId` (e.g. the future wizard passing a user/non-reference room id) will crash the whole venue route during render instead of degrading gracefully. The `useMemo` depends on `beat`, so `referenceById`, `fieldCellsForReference` and `computeFields` — all of which depend only on `roomId` and allocate large typed arrays (see computeFields) — are recomputed on every beat tick even though only `sampleSpatial` actually consumes `beat`. Since `beat` is driven by the numeric input, this re-runs all the static field math on each keystroke/step. Split this into a memo keyed on `[roomId]` that produces `{ cells, fields }`, then a second cheap memo keyed on `[built, beat]` that only maps `sampleSpatial` over the cells.

The `min`/`max` attributes on the input are declarative only and do not constrain typed or programmatically set values; `onChange` maps only `NaN` (via `Number(...) || 0`) to 0, so negative or `> 16` beats pass straight into `sampleSpatial`. Clamp the parsed value to the declared range before storing it, e.g. `const v = Number(e.target.value); setBeat(Number.isFinite(v) ? Math.min(16, Math.max(0, v)) : 0)` (or use `e.currentTarget.validity.valid`).

The preview overrides the room's own configuration: `perimeterDirection` is hardcoded to `"clockwise"` and the Orbit `params` (`heads`, `beatsPerRevolution`, `tailCells`, `tailCurve`, `phase`) are fixed constants. If the referenced room is counter-clockwise (or the caller expects the real primitive params), the preview silently disagrees with the actual venue configuration. At minimum, derive direction from `ref.room.perimeterDirection` and document that the sampling params are preview-only placeholders.

apps/desktop/src/styles/globals.css.content: `app-region` is used without the vendor prefix here and on `.app-no-drag`. The unprefixed `app-region` property is only honored by recent Chromium (129+); older Chromium/Electron builds (and many tooling pipelines) only understand `-webkit-app-region`. Because `chrome.tsx` relies on these classes for the frameless-window title bar, if the prefix is ever unsupported the region silently stops being draggable (no error, no fallback). Since the project pins Electron `^41.10.6` it currently works, but declaring both keeps it robust and self-documenting.

`--ok`, `--warn`, `--bad` are the only color tokens that are not re-exported through `@theme inline` (compare `--color-accent: var(--accent)` etc.). As a result Tailwind generates no `text-ok` / `bg-warn` / `text-bad` utilities and none of the opacity-modifier support (`text-bad/60`) that the other tokens enjoy; consumers are forced to fall back to raw `var(--ok)` inline styles (see `tokens.statusOk` in `app/tokens.ts`). Mapping them keeps the token vocabulary consistent and usable from class names.

Every other theme token (`--background`, `--border`, `--chart-*`, sidebar tokens, …) is re-declared in `.dark`, but the semantic status colors `--ok` / `--warn` / `--bad` are only declared in `:root`. Since the app always renders with `.dark` on `<html>` (`src/index.html`), the status dots in `kit.tsx` (`StatusDot`, `tokenForTone`) resolve to the light-theme values. Either add dark-tuned values here or document that these tokens are intentionally theme-independent, so a future light/dark toggle doesn't silently reuse the wrong palette.

`body` is declared twice: this top-level (unlayered) rule and again inside `@layer base` with `@apply bg-background text-foreground`. Unlayered rules always win over layered rules regardless of specificity, so the `@layer base` body declaration is effectively dead and the two rules now define the same `background`/`color`. This is confusing for future edits (changing the layered one would appear to have no effect). Consolidate the base body styling into a single rule.

apps/desktop/tsconfig.json.content: The `@/*` → `./src/*` alias is inert and misleading in this config. This file sets `rootDir: "electron"` and `include: ["electron"]`, and no `electron/**` source uses an `@/` import (verified: the only aliases in play are `@autolight/*`, resolved to package `dist/index.d.ts`, plus a `@/` alias used in the *renderer* `src`/`tsconfig.typecheck.json`). Because esbuild's `alias` in `scripts/build-main.mjs`/`build-preload.mjs` does not map `@/` either, this declaration affects only type checking. If a developer adds an `@/…` import here (expecting parity with `tsconfig.typecheck.json`), tsc will resolve it to a file under `./src`, which is outside `rootDir: "electron"`, producing TS6059 ("File is not under 'rootDir'") and corrupting the outDir layout. Remove the alias from this emit config (it is already defined where it is actually usable, in `tsconfig.typecheck.json`).

`include: ["electron"]` also matches the co-located test files (`electron/services/*.test.ts`, `electron/updater/index.test.ts`). Since this config has no `noEmit` and is run in the production `build` script (`tsc -p tsconfig.json`), those tests are compiled and written into `dist/electron-tmp/…` (relying on a later external `rm -rf dist/electron-tmp` to clean up) and the production build now depends on test-only devDependencies such as `vitest`. Type checking of tests is already covered by `tsconfig.typecheck.json`. Recommend excluding tests, e.g. add `"exclude": ["electron/**/*.test.ts"]`, or make this config `"noEmit": true` for the type-check step.

apps/desktop/tsconfig.typecheck.json.content: The `include` list misses the directory that actually holds the Playwright suite. `playwright.config.ts` sets `testDir: "./journeys"` with `testMatch: "**/*.journey.ts"`, so the runtime tests are `journeys/*.journey.ts` (and the `e2e/normal-night.spec.ts` listed here is not even collected by Playwright). Only `journeys/_harness.ts` gets pulled in transitively via the spec's import; the sibling journey specs (`night.journey.ts`, `soak.journey.ts`, `m1-slice.journey.ts`, `live-session.journey.ts`) are never included and therefore escape `yarn typecheck`, allowing broken imports/type errors in the E2E suite to ship undetected. Add `journeys` to the include set.

`moduleResolution: "bundler"` is applied to the whole program, including the `electron`/`e2e` code that is Node-executed (the Playwright specs and their `journeys/_harness.ts`, which import `node:fs`/`node:path` and rely on explicit `.js` ESM specifiers). Bundler resolution does not enforce Node's ESM extension/`exports` rules, so an extensionless or mis-resolved import can pass `tsc --noEmit` yet fail at runtime under Playwright. The current specs happen to use `.js` extensions, but the config cannot catch a regression. Consider a separate NodeNext config for the Node-executed sources instead of a single bundler-mode config which is only correct for the (esbuild/Vite-bundled) `electron` main and `src` renderer.

apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.content:
The subpath regex `^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)$` matches exactly one flat segment and hardcodes the `.ts` extension. Consequences:
1. A deeper import such as `@autolight/pkg/sub/module` does NOT match, so `resolve.alias` falls through to the next entry — the **string-form barrel alias**. Vite/`@rollup/plugin-alias` replaces string matches by prefix, so `@autolight/pkg/sub/module` becomes `.../pkg/src/index.ts/sub/module`: a bogus path that only fails at bundle time. That is precisely the fall-through the surrounding comment says this block prevents.
2. Subpath modules that are `.tsx`, or subdirectories whose entry is `index.ts`, can never resolve because `$2.ts` is forced.
Consider allowing nested segments and letting Vite's extension resolution handle the leaf, e.g. `find: /^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/(.+)$/` with `replacement: join(workspaceSrc, "$1", "src", "$2")`.

`readdirSync(workspaceSrc)` is called without `withFileTypes`, so every entry (including non-directories such as a stray `.DS_Store`, README, or lock file) becomes an alias, and no check is made that `<pkg>/src/index.ts` actually exists. A package directory that hasn't added a barrel yet, or any file entry, therefore produces a dangling `@autolight/<entry>` alias that only surfaces later as a confusing "failed to resolve import" at module load. Filter to entries that are directories and verify `join(workspaceSrc, p, "src", "index.ts")` exists before adding the alias.

These `execSync` git calls run synchronously at config-load time with no `timeout` and default `maxBuffer`; a git that hangs (index.lock contention, slow network filesystem) blocks the entire Vite startup. The bare `catch` also swallows every failure, so a genuinely broken git invocation is indistinguishable from "not a git checkout" and silently ships `sha: "unknown"` — defeating the stated goal of proving which commit is running. Pass `{ cwd: root, timeout: <ms>, maxBuffer: <bytes> }` and at least warn once when the lookup fails.
apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.existing_code: sha = execSync("git rev-parse --short HEAD", { cwd: root }).toString().trim();

apps/desktop/vite.config.ts.content: `fs.allow` is widened to the monorepo root (`join(root, "..", "..")`), so the dev server will serve any file in the repository — including `.env`/credential files and unrelated apps — to anything that can reach `localhost:5173`. Restrict the allow list to the renderer root plus only the aliased package `src` directories that are actually needed (e.g. `join(workspaceSrc, "*")` or the resolved package src paths), rather than the whole repo.

apps/desktop/vitest.config.ts.content: `include` only collects `src/**/*.test.ts`, so every Electron unit test under `apps/desktop/electron/**` is silently dropped: `electron/services/audit-log.test.ts`, `fault-injection.test.ts`, `live-show-bridge.test.ts`, `secrets-service.test.ts`, `simulator-show.test.ts` and `electron/updater/index.test.ts` all exist but are never collected here. Because `apps/desktop/package.json` runs `vitest run` in the package cwd and Vitest resolves the nearest config (`apps/desktop/vitest.config.ts`), the root `yarn test` (`yarn workspaces foreach --all run test`) executes this config and reports green while those suites are skipped — while the root `vitest.config.ts` explicitly includes `apps/desktop/electron/**/*.test.ts`. Add the electron glob so both entry points stay consistent.

This regex only matches a single subpath segment (`@autolight/<pkg>/<module>`). A deeper specifier such as `@autolight/<pkg>/a/b` does not match, falls through to the string alias `@autolight/<pkg>` (Vite/@rollup/plugin-alias treats string `find` as a prefix match), and is rewritten to `<packages>/<pkg>/src/index.ts/a/b` — a mangled, nonexistent path (or a silently wrong module) rather than an error. The repo already uses multi-segment specifiers (e.g. `@autolight/simulator/dist/govee-lan.js` in `packages/govee/src/index.test.ts`), so any such import reachable from a desktop test resolves incorrectly. Widen the capture (e.g. `/^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/(.+)$/`) or make deep paths fail loudly instead of resolving to a bogus path.

`readdirSync` is unfiltered here, unlike the root `vitest.config.ts` which uses `{ withFileTypes: true }` plus an `isDirectory()` filter. Any non-directory entry in `packages/` (a stray file, `.DS_Store`, a shared config file) produces a bogus `@autolight/<name>` alias, and every entry is assumed to expose `src/index.ts` — a package with a different entry point resolves to a nonexistent file, which then silently falls back to the installed `node_modules` copy (exactly the stale-dist behavior this config exists to avoid). There is also no guard around the read, so a missing/unreadable `packages` directory aborts config loading with an opaque stack trace. Filter to directories and guard the read.

readdirSync(workspaceSrc, { withFileTypes: true })
    .filter((e) => e.isDirectory())
    .map((e) => [`@autolight/${e.name}`, join(workspaceSrc, e.name, "src", "index.ts")]),

docs/finish/evidence/T-MAT-02/measuremen.content: Derived value inconsistency: `timerFloorMsPerTick` is 1.1, but the recorded sample average `timerFloorSampleMs / timerFloorIterations` = 1134.5 / 1000 = 1.1345 ms/tick. docs/finish/evidence/T-QA-05/measurement.content: Two rows in this file use `pass: false` for states that are not real gate failures: `ui.frameTimeLive` is recorded as unmeasured (its statistic is p95 with p95 0 vs threshold 50.1, which numerically passes), and `showHost.tickJitterWith20msStall` is a deliberate fault-injection negative control that fails by construction (p99 18.42 ms > 15 ms). `queue.maxDepth` is recorded from a single sample (`samples: 1`) whose `max` equals the threshold exactly (`max: 1`, `threshold: 1`). packages/analysis-client/src/index.ts.content: On any single process exit this selects *every* pending entry with a timer, including jobs actively running on sibling processes. Those jobs are requeued and re-executed even though their worker is still alive, producing duplicate execution and duplicate completion/failure for the same job (and potentially double resolution of the same promise). packages/analysis-client/src/index.ts.content: `start()` spawns workers but never calls `drain()`. The crash/restart path (`exit` handler → `restartWithBackoff()` → `start()`) requeues interrupted jobs into `this.queue`, but nothing dispatches them until some later `analyze()` happens to call `drain()`. After a worker crash the requeued jobs sit idle indefinitely — a liveness bug that also defeats the spec-109 requeue guarantee. Call `this.drain()` at the end of `start()` (or after requeuing in the exit handler).

packages/analysis-client/src/index.ts.content: `stop()` kills the processes but leaves in-flight job timers armed and never rejects pending promises. Two consequences: (1) the per-job `setTimeout` callbacks still fire after stop, calling `failEntry` + `restartWithBackoff()` and resurrecting a supervisor that was explicitly stopped; (2) the `exit` handlers run asynchronously after `this.procs = []`, observe `procs.length === 0`, and also call `restartWithBackoff()`. Any later `setTimeout(() => this.start())` can then spawn workers after an explicit `stop()`. `stop()` should clear all pending job timers, reject/resolve pending entries, and set a `stopped` flag that the `exit` handler (and `start()`) honor.

Any routed frame that is neither `progress` (with `stage`) nor `complete` (with `artifactPath`) falls through to the failure branch and rejects the job. A `progress` frame lacking `stage`, a `complete` frame lacking `artifactPath`, or any other frame type addressed to a known job id (e.g. an ack/started frame) will incorrectly fail a healthy job. Explicitly ignore/handle non-terminal frame types instead of treating them as failures.

`restartWithBackoff()` is not idempotent and races with the asynchronous `exit` handlers: `stop()` clears `this.procs` synchronously, then each killed proc's `exit` handler sees `procs.length === 0` and calls `restartWithBackoff()` again, incrementing `this.restarts` and scheduling multiple stacked `start()` calls. Also `backoffMs` is only ever doubled and never reset to `restartBackoffMs[0]` after a healthy run, so backoff monotonically escalates to the max even for isolated, widely-spaced failures. Add a restart-in-progress guard and reset `backoffMs` once the worker has been healthy.

`lastHeartbeat` is never reset when workers are (re)spawned or stopped. After a restart, the stale timestamp is still compared against `Date.now()`, so `checkHeartbeat()` can immediately declare a fresh worker unhealthy (before it emits its first heartbeat) and trigger a restart loop that never stabilizes. Reset `this.lastHeartbeat` in `spawnOne()`/`start()` and in `stop()`.

Fallback lookup by `trackId` returns the first matching entry. When the same track is analyzed again while a prior job for that track is still pending, multiple entries share the same `trackId` and messages addressed by track id can be routed to the wrong job, resolving/rejecting an unrelated promise. Prefer the unique job id for routing and treat the trackId fallback as ambiguous.

In-flight detection is derived solely from `entry.timer !== undefined`, which conflates a job that has actually been dispatched with one that was requeued after a crash (timer cleared). Combined with the concurrency/`send()` bug this makes `capacity` unreliable. Consider tracking an explicit `dispatchedTo`/`inFlight` flag on `PendingEntry` rather than inferring state from the presence of a timer.

packages/analysis-client/src/protocol.ts.content: `parseFrame` only checks that the parsed value is a non-null object, so it never validates the protocol contract: `v` is not compared against `PROTOCOL_VERSION`, `type` is not required to exist/be a string, and JSON arrays (`typeof [] === "object"`) also pass the guard and get cast to `ProtocolFrame`. A worker speaking an incompatible protocol version, or a non-frame payload, is silently accepted and cast, which can be misinterpreted downstream. `frameId` treats only null/undefined as absent (`??`), so an empty-string `id` is returned as `""`, and a non-string id is coerced to `"[object Object]"`. Job ids are derived from a module-level, in-memory counter (`jobSeq`). It resets on every process restart and is not persisted, so ids can collide with records already stored in a persistent queue; given the spec 109/139 requeue/idempotency requirements this can break dedup and correlation of results back to jobs across restarts. Use a durable/unique id source (e.g. UUID or a persisted sequence).

`toJob` defaults `configHash` to `""` when omitted.
