`describeInputs` diverges from the Python mirror `describe_inputs` (readiness.py:107-112), which returns `{"key": key, **inputs.get(key, input_entry(ABSENT, "unknown"))}`. Two concrete differences that consumers of the Inspector rows can observe:
1. Missing keys: Python injects a default `reason: "unknown"` (via `input_entry(ABSENT, "unknown")`); the TS version emits no `reason` at all, so a row for an absent input renders without the "unknown" placeholder.
2. The Python spread copies every entry field, so rows carry `version` and `durationMs`; the TS return type/impl strips them, silently dropping data that the input map provides.
Because the drift test only checks `INPUT_KEYS` ordering, this parity gap is not caught by CI. Consider mirroring the Python row shape (default `reason` + spread of all entry fields) and widening the return type accordingly.

`statusOf(inputs, key)` is evaluated twice for every key (once for the `reason === undefined` test branch, once more inside each returned object). Besides the redundant lookups, having two independent call sites means the `status` and `reason` of a row are resolved separately, which is easy to make inconsistent during future edits. Resolve the entry once and reuse it (see the spread suggestion above), which also preserves `reason`/`version`/`durationMs` and matches the Python `describe_inputs` semantics.

packages/analysis-client/tsconfig.json.content: `include: ["src"]` globs the entire source directory, which also matches `src/index.test.ts`. The `build` script (`tsc -p tsconfig.json`) will therefore type-check and emit test artifacts (`dist/index.test.js` / `dist/index.test.d.ts`) into the published output. This is undesirable because: (1) the package's `main`/`types` publish `dist`, so consumers receive compiled tests, and (2) the emitted `.js` imports `vitest` (a devDependency) that will not be present in consumer installs. Exclude test files from the build program (vitest picks up tests via its own config, so this does not affect testing).

packages/analysis-client/vitest.config.t.content: `readdirSync(packages)` returns every entry in `packages/`, not just package directories. Non-package entries (e.g. `.DS_Store`, `README.md`, `.gitignore`, any file or stray folder) each become an `@autolight/<name>` alias pointing at a non-existent `<name>/src/index.ts`. This can mask genuine "module not found" errors with a confusing resolution attempt into a bogus path. The root `vitest.config.ts` guards against this with `readdirSync(workspaceSrc, { withFileTypes: true }).filter((e) => e.isDirectory())`; do the same here.

Vitest/Vite alias `find` values are prefix-matched, so the plain string alias `@autolight/foo` also rewrites deep imports like `@autolight/foo/subpath` to `<foo>/src/index.ts/subpath`, producing a wrong (non-existent) module path. The root `vitest.config.ts` deliberately places a regex subpath alias (`/^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)$/`) before the barrel aliases ("T-TRU-04 spine fix") so barrels never swallow `/subpath` imports. Mirror that ordering here, or use an exact-match regex for the barrel alias.

packages/ble/package.json.content: With `"type": "module"`, the package only exposes `main`/`types` and has no conditional `exports` map. Node/bundlers prefer `exports` when present, and its absence prevents any subpath or explicit ESM/CJS condition resolution for consumers of this scoped package. Sibling `@autolight/config` already declares an `exports` map; add one here for consistency and future-proof resolution.

There is no `files` allowlist, and `dist/` is listed in the repo `.gitignore`. With no `.npmignore` and no `files` field, npm falls back to `.gitignore` when packing, which would exclude `dist/` from the published tarball — leaving `main`/`types` pointing at non-existent files. Conversely, without the fallback the build output plus `src`/`tsconfig` would be published wholesale (TS config has no test exclusion, so compiled `*.test.js` land in `dist/`). Declare a `files` allowlist (or add an explicit `.npmignore`) so the published surface matches the build output.

`frame.slice()` is not guaranteed to copy. The channel then holds a live view of the caller's buffer, so later in-place mutation of the source frame silently changes what `take()` returns and defeats the latest-wins copy intent. Use an explicit copy that is subclass-safe: `Uint8Array.from(frame)` / `new Uint8Array(frame)`.

Consider resetting `primaryReason` to `null` on a successful primary scan, and keep per-device reasons in `overrides` separate from the scan-level cause.

`noteFallback()` silently discards the typed reason when there is no secondary adapter (`return` without recording anything). Either store the reason/decision even without a secondary, or make the no-op explicit to callers (throw/return a boolean) so the drop is not silent.

`available` is hardcoded to `true` and there is no code path that can ever set it to `false`, even when `primaryReason` shows the primary backend failed to load/scan. packages/ble/src/link.test.ts.content: This test does not reproduce the "burst / catch-up" scenario it claims to cover. `clock.advance(100)` between sends is exactly the 10 Hz budget spacing, so `BleLink.send()` always takes its immediate-flush fast path (`now - lastFlushAt >= spacing`) and the queue/`pump()` path is never exercised. As a result `stalled === 0` holds trivially even if the catch-up/burst guard is removed, and `send()`'s queueing logic is untested. Send several frames with no clock advance (or advance less than the spacing) so writes must be paced through `pump()`, then assert the burst is bounded. Also assert `peripheral.metrics.writes` (and `writesDroppedBudget === 0`): `writesSent` is incremented before the write is issued, so a silently dropped write would still leave `writesSent === 30`.

The assertions are too weak to prove newest-wins actually replaced the queued frame. `pendingWrites <= 1` and `peripheral.metrics.writes <= 2` both have no lower bound, so they pass when zero writes ever fire; and `writes <= 2` explicitly permits the very "queued behind" behaviour (two writes) the test name says must never happen. Most importantly, nothing verifies *which* frame reached the peripheral, so writing the stale first frame (0x01) instead of the newest (0x00) would still pass. Assert exact values and inspect `peripheral.written`.
Add a lower bound and verify the payload written is the newest frame, not the superseded one.

This test never exercises the drain hold during `close()` that its name promises. By the time `close()` runs, `clock.now()` (100320) is already past `lastWriteAt + drainMs` (100010 + 300 = 100310), so the `wait > 0` branch in `BleLink.close()` is skipped and no drain timer is scheduled — only the `busy` getter is verified. A regression that disconnects immediately inside the drain window would not be caught. Add a case that calls `close()` while still inside the window and asserts the disconnect is deferred until `writeDrainMs` elapses.

The reconnect assertions don't verify the behaviour under test. `reconnects >= 1` is incremented in `reconnect()` before the backoff wait, so it would also pass with a zero/broken backoff and even if the final connect never succeeded; the 500 ms `backoffMs` schedule and the `advertiseGapMs` trigger are never checked. Tighten to `toBe(1)` and assert timing (e.g. that `peripheral.metrics.connects` only advances after the 500 ms timer fires). Separately, driving the async chain with exactly two `await Promise.resolve()` per iteration and fixed 600 ms advances couples the test to the current microtask resolution order; use `await vi.runAllTimersAsync()`-style advancement or a helper that drains until the state settles so it does not silently break when `link.ts` adds/removes an `await`.

The test name says the budget stays unmeasured "until the wizard records one", but the test never covers the measured transition — it only checks the unmeasured state before and after `open()`. If a measurement path exists (or is added), add an assertion that the badge clears once a measured budget is supplied, otherwise the stated requirement is only half-verified.

packages/ble/src/link.ts.content: `wallClock.clearTimeout` is a no-op that ignores its handle, so in production neither `cancelReconnect()` nor the drain-timer reset in `close()` actually cancels anything. A pending backoff timer will still fire after `close()`, driving a reconnect attempt on a closed link, and the drain timer handle can never be cleared. The test clocks implement this correctly, so tests pass while production leaks timers. Delegate to the real clearTimeout.

On the fast path `writesSent` is incremented and `lastFlushAt`/`lastWriteAt`/`lastSeenAt` are advanced even when `connection` is null (i.e. while `state` is `connected`/`reconnecting` during a reconnect). The frame is then silently discarded: it is never sent and never queued, so `writesSent` over-reports real transmissions, the drain/`busy` accounting is corrupted, and the command is lost. packages/cloud/vitest.config.ts.content:
`readdirSync(packages)` returns every entry name, including plain files (`README.md`, `.DS_Store`, lockfiles) and non-package directories (e.g. `.cache`, `.turbo`). Each one is turned into an `@autolight/<name>` alias pointing at a nonexistent `<name>/src/index.ts`. A bogus alias can silently shadow a real module resolution (especially with a file/extensionless name) and produces confusing errors instead of failing fast.

The repo's root `vitest.config.ts` already guards against this with `readdirSync(workspaceSrc, { withFileTypes: true }).filter((e) => e.isDirectory())`; mirror that here (optionally also skip hidden dirs).

Two problems with this alias set:
1. Every alias maps a package name to a concrete *file* (`<pkg>/src/index.ts`). Vite string aliases match on `<find> === id || id.startsWith(find + '/')`, so a subpath import such as `@autolight/contracts/schema` does not resolve to `<pkg>/src/schema.ts` — it is rewritten to `<pkg>/src/index.ts/schema`, an invalid path. The root `vitest.config.ts` adds a dedicated regex subpath alias (`/^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)$/` → `packages/$1/src/$2.ts`) precisely to avoid this.
2. Blindly assuming `<pkg>/src/index.ts` exists means any package whose entry differs (root `index.ts`, an `exports` map, or no `src/`) silently resolves to a missing file. Prefer a subpath/directory alias or validate the entry exists when building the map.

Supplying `exclude` replaces Vitest's default exclude list rather than extending it. The patterns here are also root-relative and unanchored (`node_modules/**`, `dist/**`), whereas Vitest's defaults use `**/node_modules/**` / `**/dist/**`. As a result, nested `node_modules`/`dist` directories under `src` (e.g. `src/<nested>/node_modules/...`) are no longer excluded and could be collected as tests, and defaults like `**/*.config.*` are dropped too.

Anchor these globs (use `**/` prefixes) or extend the defaults instead of overriding them.

packages/config/package.json.content: `--passWithNoTests` makes the test step exit 0 even when zero tests are discovered (e.g. if the `src/**/*.test.ts` files are removed/renamed, or a bad `include` glob stops matching). CI would then silently report success for a broken/missing suite. Since the package already ships tests, this flag buys nothing and only hides regressions — drop it so a missing suite fails the build.

This package is publishable (no `"private": true`) yet declares no `files` allowlist. `npm pack`/`npm publish` will therefore include `src/` (incl. `*.test.ts`), `tsconfig.json`, `vitest.config.ts`, and `scripts/export.mjs` alongside `dist/`, leaking internals and potentially shipping stale sources. Add an explicit `files` allowlist (or mark the package private if it is internal-only).

`main`/`exports` all target `./dist/*`, but nothing builds `dist` before it is consumed/published: there is no `prepare`/`prepublishOnly`/`prepack` script. A consumer installing from a symlink/git ref, or a publish that forgets `yarn build`, gets a package whose entry points do not exist (ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for `@autolight/config` and the `./registry` subpath). Add a build-before-publish hook.

Vacuous assertion: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(v))` cannot throw for any value `defaultFor` can return (it either returns a parsed value or, on parse failure, the raw string — registry.ts:276). packages/config/src/secrets.ts.content:
Data-loss bug in `flush()`: the persisted blob is rebuilt exclusively from `this.memory`, so any persistent id that is on disk but not currently loaded into memory is silently dropped, and if the resulting map is empty the whole blob is wiped via `clearBlob()`.

Concrete failure: a vault whose blob contains `govee.cloud.apiKey` and whose memory is empty (no `get`/`presence` call yet this session) receives `set("agent.apiToken", token)` (a MEMORY_ONLY id) or `remove("agent.apiToken")`. `persist` ends up empty, so `clearBlob()` erases the stored Govee key. A later `get("govee.cloud.apiKey")` returns `null` even though the user had stored it. The same structure breaks whenever more persistent ids are added: a `set` of one id overwrites the blob with only the ids currently in memory.

Fix: merge with the decrypted on-disk blob and only drop ids explicitly removed (e.g., track a `removed` set), instead of deriving disk state solely from live memory.

Two problems here:
1) `set()` mutates `this.memory` *before* `flush()` can throw. In degraded mode (`isEncryptionAvailable()` false, e.g. no OS keychain), `set("govee.cloud.apiKey", v)` throws from `flush()`, but the value stays in memory — so `get()`/`has()`/`presence()` report it as "stored" even though the caller was told the write failed. Worse, that retained persistent value makes every later `set("agent.apiToken", ...)`/`remove(...)` throw again (`persist` is non-empty), so the memory-only token can never be set.
2) `flush()` runs unconditionally even for MEMORY_ONLY ids, causing a needless disk write for the agent token and tying its success/failure to unrelated persistent state.

Validate encryption availability before mutating memory, and only persist when a persistent id actually changed.

Silent failure: any `decryptString`/JSON parse error is swallowed and reported identically to "not set". A corrupt blob or a keychain/OS-account mismatch therefore shows the key as `missing` in Settings, and the next `set()` silently overwrites the unrecoverable ciphertext (see the `flush()`/`clearBlob()` path), destroying the last chance to recover it. At minimum distinguish "unreadable" from "absent" (log/return a diagnostic) so corruption is not masked as an unset secret.

Sequential `split`/`join` replacement leaks part of a secret when one secret is a substring of another: with `secrets = ["abc", "abcdef"]`, replacing `"abc"` first turns `"abcdef"` into `"[redacted]def"`, then the `"abcdef"` pass matches nothing, leaving `def` in the output. This helper is the guard that keeps secrets out of logs/exports/crash reports, so a partial leak is a real exposure. Sort secrets by descending length (and de-duplicate) before redacting.

`toBase64`/`fromBase64` rely on the browser globals `btoa`/`atob`. This module deliberately avoids importing Electron to stay unit-testable, so it may be loaded in a Node/main context where these globals are absent (older Node/runtimes). When missing, `fromBase64` throws inside `get()` → swallowed by the catch → silently reported as "not set", while `toBase64` throws out of `flush()` → hard failure on every write. Use a runtime-agnostic base64 codec (e.g. `Buffer` when available, or feature-detect `btoa`) instead of assuming the globals exist.

The secret id list is duplicated across four places (`SECRET_IDS`, `SECRET_TABLE`, `MEMORY_ONLY_TABLE`, and these hardcoded keys in `presence()`). Adding a new secret requires editing all of them; forgetting `SECRET_TABLE` makes `isSecretId` reject the new id, and forgetting `presence()` silently hides it from Settings/diagnostics. Derive `SECRET_TABLE`/`MEMORY_ONLY_TABLE` and build `presence()` by iterating `SECRET_IDS` so the id set has a single source of truth.

packages/config/src/store.ts.content: `save()` overwrites the config file in place. If the process crashes, the disk fills, or another writer truncates mid-write, the file is left partially written; `readLayersFile()` then fails JSON.parse / schema validation and silently returns `null`, so ALL persisted config is discarded on next startup with no error or backup. Write to a temp file and rename atomically (rename is atomic on the same filesystem). Also note this call is uncaught: a write error (ENOSPC/EACCES) propagates out of `set`/`reset`/`importJson` AFTER the in-memory state and mirror were already mutated and the change was emitted, leaving memory and disk diverged.

`emit()` invokes listeners without isolation. A subscriber that throws aborts the loop, so later subscribers never receive the change; worse, in `set`/`reset`/`importJson` `emit()` runs BEFORE `this.save()`, so a throwing listener also skips persistence entirely, leaving the in-memory state changed but the file stale (change silently lost on restart). Wrap each listener call in try/catch (and/or move `save()` before `emit()`).

When `importPayloadSchema.safeParse` fails, `check.success` is false and `values` silently falls back to `{}`. Combined with `bad.length === 0`, the method returns `{ ok: true }` for malformed payloads that were never imported (e.g. `"hello"`, `42`, `{ "values": [1,2,3] }`), so callers believe the import succeeded while nothing changed. Return a failure when the schema does not match instead of coercing to an empty object.

packages/config/src/store.ts.content: `save()` rewrites the whole file from this instance's `mirror` with no lock and no read-merge-write. Multiple `PersistentConfigStore` instances can point at the same path (e.g. show-service always constructs one on `userData/config.json` and config-service falls back to constructing its own when `opts.store` is not passed), so each instance's `set/reset/load` clobbers the other's persisted changes (last-writer-wins), silently dropping data that the other instance still holds in its stale mirror. Consider a file lock or a read-merge-before-write, or enforce a single shared instance.

`load()` mutates the layers and mirror but never emits `config:changed`, so any subscriber (e.g. ConfigService's history, renderer caches) that has already subscribed keeps stale values when `load()` is invoked after construction. Additionally, keys whose `defineKey` throws are silently skipped, so renamed/unknown persisted overrides are dropped without any signal; and the surrounding `readLayersFile` returns `null` on any corruption, which is indistinguishable from an empty config. Consider emitting per-key changes and surfacing dropped keys.

packages/config/vitest.config.ts.content: `readdirSync(packages)` returns every entry, including plain files and non-package directories (e.g. a stray `README.md`, `.DS_Store`, `node_modules`, or a future cache dir). Each such entry is turned into a `@autolight/<name>` alias pointing at a nonexistent `src/index.ts`, producing broken/ambiguous aliases that can silently shadow or fail resolution. The root `vitest.config.ts` avoids this by using `withFileTypes: true` and filtering `isDirectory()`; mirror that here.

packages/contracts/package.json.content: The declared entrypoints resolve into `./dist`, but the repo `.gitignore` ignores `dist/` and there is no `.npmignore` or `files` allowlist. npm falls back to `.gitignore` when packing, so a published/installed tarball would exclude `dist/` entirely, leaving `main`/`types` pointing at non-existent files (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for consumers). There is also no `prepare`/`prepublishOnly` script, so `dist` may not even be built at publish time. Add a `files` allowlist including `dist` and a build hook, e.g. `"files": ["dist"]` plus `"prepublishOnly": "yarn build"` (or `"prepare": "tsc -p tsconfig.json"`).

Unlike sibling packages that define an explicit `exports` map (e.g. `packages/controller-flx4/package.json`), this `"type": "module"` package exposes only `main`/`types`. Any future subpath entry (or tooling that requires an `exports` field) will fail to resolve, and there is no conditional `require`/`import` boundary. Consider adding an `exports` map for consistency and forward-compatibility.

packages/contracts/src/index.ts.content: `beatGridSchema` is non-strict while `adaptiveBeatGridSchema` is `.strict()`, yet both are alternatives of the same union field `beatGrid` in trackModelSchema. Extra/unknown properties on a grid are therefore silently accepted for one branch and rejected for the other, making the contract's strictness depend on which union arm happens to match (and, because `beatGridSchema` is first, unknown keys also survive parsing). Make strictness consistent across both branches.

`.max(0)` forces an adaptive grid to always be an empty array, which conflicts with the superRefine rule below that reports `"adaptive must carry an empty grid"` when `n > 0`. In practice a non-empty grid with `analysisCoverage === "adaptive"` is accepted by the (non-strict) `beatGridSchema` arm of the union and only later flagged by superRefine, so the meaningful diagnostic never depends on this branch; and validating `adaptiveBeatGridSchema` directly rejects non-empty grids with a generic array-length error. Align the two so the empty-grid invariant is expressed in exactly one place.

The superRefine only enforces grid emptiness vs `analysisCoverage`; it omits range/ordering invariants that malformed data can violate without any error: `startBeat <= endBeat` for sections/phrases, events falling within the grid, and consistency between `readinessLevel` and `analysisCoverage`. Invalid state transitions thus pass the contract boundary unchecked. Consider adding these cross-field checks (or a dedicated refine) here.

`catchall(z.unknown())` makes the entire cue payload unvalidated: any properties beyond the declared optionals are accepted as `unknown` and reach consumers unchecked, so native-source schema drift (renamed/renumbered cue fields) cannot be detected at the contract boundary. Enumerate the expected cue fields (or at least narrow the catchall types) so malformed rekordbox cues fail fast.

`markers` is typed as `z.array(z.unknown())`, so malformed or unexpected Serato markers pass validation and are handed to consumers with no type information. Define a concrete marker schema (mirroring `rekordboxCueSchema`) so Serato payload mismatches are caught at the contract boundary.

packages/contracts/vitest.config.ts.content: The alias matches only the bare specifier `@autolight/<name>`, so deep subpath imports such as `@autolight/rekordbox-live/follow` or `@autolight/config/registry` (patterns that actually exist in this repo) are NOT aliased and fall through to Node/pnpm resolution, i.e. they resolve against a package `dist`/`main` build instead of the current sources. This directly contradicts the stated goal of exercising the code the app bundles. `apps/desktop/vitest.config.ts` adds a `subpathAlias` regex (`/^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/([^/]+)$/`) for exactly this reason; this config should mirror it (or drop the alias entirely if unused, since the current contracts tests import no workspace packages).

The include glob collects only `src/**/*.test.ts`. Files named `*.test.tsx`, `*.spec.ts`, or tests placed outside `src/` are silently skipped. Combined with the `vitest run --passWithNoTests` script in this package, a renamed/misplaced test file would make the suite report green rather than failing, hiding lost coverage. Broaden the pattern (e.g. `src/**/*.{test,spec}.{ts,tsx}`) or add the extra directories if any are intended.

packages/controller-flx4/package.json.content: `build` runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json`, whose `include` is the whole `src` directory (which contains `*.test.ts`) and which has no test exclude; combined with the absence of a `files` allowlist or `private` flag here, the build emits `dist/*.test.js` / `dist/*.test.d.ts` and a publish would ship test artifacts, source maps and `vitest.config.ts`. Add an `exclude` for test files in tsconfig, or constrain the publish surface with a `files` array (e.g. `["dist"]`) / `"private": true` if the package is internal-only.

packages/controller-flx4/src/backend.ts.content: Overlapping-poll / stop race. The interval callback fires `poll()` without awaiting it and without any in-flight guard, so a slow `listPorts`/`open` can overlap with the next tick. More seriously, there is no `stopped` flag: if `stop()` runs while a `poll()` is suspended on an await, the resumed `poll()` will fall through to `selectAndOpen()` and re-open the port, leaving the service `connected` (and leaking a new input) after teardown. Even in the connected branch, `this.input` becomes null during the await, so the comparison after `await` mis-detects a loss and emits a spurious `lost` status after stop. Serialize polls and add a stopped/generation guard checked after every await; also have `stop()` notify listeners.

Any error from `listPorts` is swallowed and coerced to an empty list, which the hotplug branch then interprets as "the controller port disappeared". A transient backend hiccup (driver busy, temporary failure) therefore produces a false `lost` transition, closes a still-valid input, and discards the real cause. Distinguish a real failure from an empty list (e.g. only treat it as loss when the call actually succeeded and the port is absent, otherwise surface the error).

Failover state is misclassified. `lastUnavailable` is overwritten by every later probe/open failure, so the final `unavailable-on-this-device` classification reflects the *last* failure rather than a real "held by another client" condition. Consequences: (a) when all backends simply fail to load/probe (e.g. nothing installed), the service still reports `unavailable-on-this-device` instead of `failed`/`searching`; (b) on macOS a Windows-only probe failure can become the user-facing reason, so the remedy tells the user to install Windows MIDI Services. Also, if a port *was* matched but only the open failed, the `sawPort` branch is unreachable because `lastUnavailable` is set, so a genuinely openable-port failure is reported as a device-availability problem. Track availability separately from load/probe failures and prefer the `sawPort`→`failed` classification when a matching port existed.

packages/controller-flx4/src/integration.content: The drain result is only checked for existence (`drained > 0` plus `some(...)` membership), so duplicated, missing, or misordered composite events still pass. Also `toHaveLength(3)` hardcodes the assumption that partial 14-bit MSBs surface as `unknown` rather than being paired, so a pairing/protocol regression silently changes the count. Unbounded growth of the `unknown` store (memory leak). Every unmapped, incomplete or `type: "unknown"` event is appended here and the array is never trimmed, never cleared by `drain()`, and `unknownEvents()` hands back the live internal array. During a long live session this grows without bound. Worse, routine events the composite simply doesn't consume are classified as "unknown": a `sync`/`loop-in`/`hotcue`/`beat-loop` button *release* returns `null` from `feedEventFromDecoded`, and every 14-bit MSB half is incomplete, so the store fills with normal traffic (see the session test where 3 of 8 messages land here). Suggest a bounded ring (or clear on `drain()`) and/or a separate counter, and return a copy from `unknownEvents()` so callers cannot mutate internal state.

`seen` accumulates every derived signal for the lifetime of the subscription and is never cleared or bounded (`signals()` just returns the internal array). In production `subscribeServiceToComposite` is wired once per session and receives a signal per MIDI event, so this is an unbounded memory leak. Consider capping it (ring buffer) or exposing a clear/reset, and returning a defensive copy.

Eviction tracks *first-insertion* order, not recency, so it can defeat the documented latest-wins contract. `order` only gets a new slot when a bucket key is first seen; updating an existing deck+control leaves the stale slot in place. When capacity is exceeded, `shift()` deletes the key that was *created* earliest — even if it currently holds the freshest data. E.g. with `capacity: 2`, a continuously updated `crossfader` retains its original slot and is evicted before a rarely-touched bucket that was created later. Either re-append the key on every push (true LRU/latest-wins) or document that eviction is by first-seen key, not by recency.

Filter-sweep direction assumes `history` is strictly ascending in `atNs`: `trail[0]` is treated as the oldest sample of the window. If a caller passes history newest-first (or unsorted), the direction sign (and therefore the sign of `strength`/`detail` open vs close) is inverted. The window filter also has no upper bound, so history entries with `atNs` after the current event leak into the trail and can fabricate a sweep. Either sort/filter the trail by `atNs` here, or document and enforce the ordering contract on the parameter.

Fader-rise treats the last matching entry of `history` as the "previous" value via `reverse().find()`. This only yields the immediately preceding fader event if `history` is sorted oldest-to-newest; an unsorted or newest-first history picks the wrong baseline and reports a phantom (or suppressed) rise. Consider selecting the max-`atNs` entry with `atNs < event.atNs` explicitly.

EQ re-entry is detected against *any* prior kill found in `history`, with no time bound and the same reverse-order assumption. A bass kill from minutes earlier (or an unrelated stale entry) will be treated as the predecessor of the current raise, emitting a spurious `re-entry` hint. Constrain the lookup to a bounded window ending at `event.atNs` (and pick the newest entry by `atNs` rather than relying on history order).

The "no fallback left" reclaim can strand the machine in an inconsistent `failed-over` state whose `current` is the *preferred* transport, and the very next tick turns a healthy fixture dark.

Walking it through: the reclaim calls `moveTo(open.transport, ...)` but never promotes the state to `on-preferred` (`moveTo` only sets `failed-over`, and the only state fix-up here is `probing-preferred -> failed-over`). So after reclaiming `lan-razer`, `state === "failed-over"` while `current === "lan-razer"`.

On the next tick the fallback section unconditionally executes `if (preferred !== null) down.add(preferred);`, so `held` excludes the preferred even though it is reachable -> `held.transport === null`. Then `open.transport === this.current`, so the `!== this.current` guard skips the reclaim, and control falls through to `if (held.transport !== this.current) this.moveTo(held.transport=null, ...)`, emitting "All frame transports down; fixture dark." and clearing `current` while the preferred LAN path is verified+reachable.

Repro: (1) `machine.select()` (current=lan-razer); (2) mark lan-razer/lan-json/ble-segmented/ble-single unreachable and tick -> current becomes ble-segmented; (3) mark only lan-razer reachable, tick -> reclaim sets current=lan-razer with state still failed-over; (4) tick again with `signal="ok"`, `atBarBoundary=false` -> fixture goes dark. This branch is not covered by machine.test.ts, so it is unverified.

Fix: promote to `on-preferred` when the reclaimed transport is the preferred one, and hold (don't `moveTo(null)`) when `open.transport === this.current`.

`probing-preferred` is never cleared when the preferred transport drops again. When `preferredUp` becomes false the code simply falls through to the fallback section, which only resets the state inside the narrow reclaim branch. Consequences: (a) `machineState` (exposed to the tile/status bar) keeps reporting `probing-preferred` even though the preferred path is down; (b) the `probeIntervalMs` gate is only evaluated for `failed-over`, so once the preferred path recovers the machine can switch back at the next bar boundary without re-arming the probe interval. Reset to `failed-over` whenever the preferred transport is no longer up while probing.

The LAN transport ids are hardcoded and duplicated three times: `down.add("lan-razer"); down.add("lan-json")` appears in both the on-preferred and fallback branches, plus `new Set<TransportId>(["lan-razer", "lan-json"])` in the reclaim selection. If the transport union is ever renamed/extended these sites will silently drift from `TRANSPORTS`/`FRAME_CLASS`. Extract a module-level `const LAN_TRANSPORTS: readonly TransportId[] = ["lan-razer", "lan-json"];` and reuse it.

A stray non-package entry (a file such as `README.md`/`.DS_Store`, a `.cache`/`node_modules` dir) silently produces a bogus alias, and any package whose entry is not `src/index.ts` resolves to a nonexistent module, causing confusing import-resolution failures instead of a clear error. This package has real tests under `src/**/*.test.ts`, so the flag only masks the zero-test failure mode; drop it so an empty run fails loudly (and wire the suite so it cannot silently report success).

`@types/node` is not declared, yet `src` imports Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:dgram`, `node:os`, `node:path`, `node:url`) and uses `Buffer`/`process`, and both `build`/`lint`/`typecheck` compile `src` (including the `*.test.ts` files) with `tsc`. It only resolves today because other workspace packages (e.g. `@autolight/show-host`) hoist `@types/node` into the root `node_modules`. Under an isolated / PnP install `yarn typecheck` fails with `Cannot find module 'node:fs'`. Declare it explicitly as a dev dependency.

The package is `"type": "module"` but exposes only the legacy `main`/`types` fields and has no `exports` map or `files` allowlist. Bare-specifier ESM imports fall back to `main`, but subpath imports (`@autolight/govee/engines`) and modern resolvers rely on legacy behavior, and without `files` a publish would ship `src/`, tests, and `tsconfig.json`/`vitest.config.ts`. packages/govee/src/actions.ts.content: The unarmed flash never powers the unit on before sending white `colorwc`. The restore branch is explicitly written for an off unit (`else if (!observed.onOff) { ... turnCommand(false) }`), which only makes sense if the flash turned it on first — but no `turnCommand(true)` is sent. On a unit that is currently off, `colorwc` alone does not light it (the transport in `govee-lan.ts` sends `turn(true)` before the white `colorwc` for exactly this reason), so IDENTIFY produces no visible flash and the user cannot identify/name the unit; the subsequent `turn(false)` restore is then a no-op. Add a power-on before the white command (mirroring the production transport), which the off-state restore already compensates for.

The flash is performed and then restored as a single unguarded sequence. If any `sendRaw`/`sendJson`/`wait(options.flashMs)` rejects (a `Waiter` that rejects, a transport error, or a `paint()` RangeError from a malformed `currentFrame` or `zones > 255`), control jumps out of `identify` and the restore step never runs, leaving the unit stuck in white RGB — the exact state the function's contract promises to undo. Wrap the flash+restore in `try { ... } finally { restore }` so the previous look is re-applied on every exit path.

The stream-vs-`colorwc` path and the restore strategy are chosen from `fixture.armed`, a snapshot taken by the caller before this call. If the unit's real armed state has changed (e.g. a show opened/closed between snapshot and action), the unarmed branch will send a white `colorwc` — and the off-state restore sends `turnCommand(false)` — while the channel is actually armed. Both are documented as capable of terminating the razer channel, which is the data-loss case the module header warns about. Re-confirm armed state at action time (read B2 status, or take the live stream/`armed` value) before deciding the path instead of trusting the stale boolean.

packages/govee/src/actions.ts.content: `testChase` never restores the look that preceded it. In the single-zone unarmed branch the ramp ends on `colorwc(255,255,255)`, i.e. the fixture is left at full white indefinitely; the segmented branch leaves the last travel frame (only one zone lit) on the unit. Unlike `identify`, there is no read-back/restore and no blackout, so the previous static look is lost after every test chase unless the caller re-paints. Consider capturing the pre-chase state (or re-sending a blackout/last known frame) at the end of the walk as `identify` does.

`zones` here is `Math.max(1, fixture.zones)` without flooring, while `chaseFrames` floors internally (`Math.max(1, Math.floor(zones))`). For a non-integer zone count the frame loop uses the floored count but `zoneOrder` is computed with the raw value, so the reported zone order drifts from the bytes actually sent (e.g. reverse step yields `3.5`). There is also no bound check: a zone count > 255 makes `paint` throw `RangeError`, aborting the chase mid-walk. Floor/validate `zones` once and use the same value for both the frames and `zoneOrder`.

When the pre-flash read-back times out, no restore is issued at all and `restored` is `"no-read-back"`, so the unit is left permanently at `colorwc(255,255,255)` (full white) — contradicting the function's stated contract to restore the previous look. A slow/silent unit therefore ends up visibly white until the next command. At minimum this should be surfaced/compensated (e.g. a deterministic blackout or the last known frame) rather than silently leaving the fixture white; document the trade-off if it is intentional.

`restoreFrame` (`fixture.currentFrame`) is passed straight to `paint` with no length check. The flash was sent with `zones` segments, but `paint` derives its segment count from `restoreFrame.length / 3`, so a frame captured at a different resolution paints a different number of zones than the flash (and a length not divisible by 3 throws `RangeError`, leaving the unit white). Guard that `restoreFrame.length === zones * 3` and fall back to the blackout frame otherwise, as the production transport does.

packages/govee/src/engines/index.ts.content: Concurrent `openStream` calls for the same device are not serialized. Two overlapping calls both read `engineFor(deviceId)` before either records an override, so both invoke the toolkit; if both fail (or one fails after the other already fell back) each call independently runs `noteFallback` and opens its own native stream. The result is two live streams for one device and a leaked/armed toolkit stream, violating the 'one stream per device' invariant. Add a per-device in-flight promise (or a lock keyed by deviceId) so opens for the same device are serialized and the decision is re-read after the await.

On the toolkit error path the code records the override and opens a native stream, but never closes the toolkit stream that may already be open for this device from an earlier successful `openStream`. The old toolkit pacing loop keeps running and its channel stays armed, so the device is driven by two engines at once (and `metrics()` later double-reports it). Close/disarm the device's existing stream before returning the native one.

If `primary.close()` rejects, `native.close()` is never invoked, leaking the native engine's sockets/streams (and vice-versa is impossible only because primary runs first). Isolate the two shutdowns, e.g. `await Promise.allSettled([this.deps.primary.close(), this.deps.native.close()])`, so one failure cannot strand the other engine's resources.

The typed reason class is discarded here. `isUnavailableError(err)` narrows to `ToolkitUnavailableError`, which carries the real `reasonClass` ('load' | 'context' | 'platform'), yet the code hard-codes 'context'. A `load`/`platform` failure surfacing during a stream open (e.g. propagated from `handleFor` -> `sdk()`) would be mislabeled as "unavailable in this context" on the device tile, contradicting the DS-02/§44 requirement that the typed reason is preserved. packages/govee/src/engines/native-ts.ts.content: The previous PacingStream for this device is snapshotted but never closed before it is overwritten in `this.streams`. Since PacingStream only clears its interval and writes `arm(false)` inside `close()`, the replaced stream keeps its pacing interval alive and never disarms, leaking a timer and leaving the unit armed. Anyone still holding the old stream handle will also paint concurrently with the new stream (duplicate/interleaved arm(true)+frames on the same device). Close the existing stream before replacing it.

The one-shot stream created here is never stored in `this.streams` (nor any other collection), so: (1) `close()` cannot disarm it, and the unit can be left armed after the engine closes; (2) its `setTimeout` handle is unmanaged and cannot be cancelled; (3) repeated `segment()` calls for the same device create overlapping concurrent streams that both arm and paint, producing duplicate frames; (4) it is invisible to `metrics()`. Track transient streams (e.g. a dedicated field) so `close()` can cancel/disarm them and so a new `segment()` can supersede the previous one.

The restore timer is never stored or cancelled, and `restore` is captured from `stream.currentFrame`, which is updated by `setAll` (PacingStream sets `current = latest` on every set). A second `identify()` within `identifyFlashMs` therefore captures the white flash as `restore` (`stream.currentFrame` is already white), and its own timer restores white again — leaving the device permanently stuck on white and losing the real frame. Overlapping identifies also leave multiple uncancelled timers. Capture a stable pre-flash snapshot once per flash (and cancel/store the timer).

`resolve(deviceId)` is invoked synchronously outside any try/catch. If the resolver throws (e.g. a MAC with no registered address), the exception propagates out of `sendRaw`/`sendJson` and up into `PacingStream`'s constructor/`emit` interval callback (or into `identify`), crashing the caller or the timer callback instead of surfacing as a recorded transport error. Guard the resolution/send so resolution failures are recorded in `this.errors` like socket errors.

The sliding-window eviction assumes the injected `clock` is monotonic. A backward step (NTP/manual adjustment) makes `now - rearmAt[0]` negative so no entry ever satisfies `>= windowMs`, entries are never evicted, and rearm is permanently disabled; a large forward jump flushes all history and allows an immediate burst exceeding the intended budget. packages/govee/src/index.test.ts.content: Test-validity flaw: the toolkit side of this "parity" proof is `StubBindingStream`, a hand-written reimplementation of the exact same arm-settle / newest-wins / no-resend / supersede-counting logic that `PacingStream` (NativeStreamEngine) implements. A negative/non-finite `latencyMs` violates the `alignedShowTimeNs` contract ("subtracted, never added") — a negative value shifts show time forward and can crash `align()` via `BigInt`; a `confidence` outside [0, 1] silently propagates incorrect calibration quality downstream. packages/rekordbox-library/package.json.content: `rekordbox-connect` is declared as a hard runtime dependency, but the code treats it as optional: `src/options.ts` (lines 166-181) calls it "an optional runtime dependency", loads it via a dynamic variable specifier inside try/catch, and falls through to the pyrekordbox sidecar/blob derivation when it is absent. It also pulls in the native `better-sqlite3-multiple-ciphers` module (see yarn.lock), which is itself correctly declared optional here. Because it is listed under `dependencies`, `yarn/npm install` will attempt to build that native module and fail on platforms where the build is unavailable, even though the library can run without it (auto mode falls back in `service.ts`, line 136-140). To match the runtime behavior, move `rekordbox-connect` to `optionalDependencies` (it will then also be marked optional in yarn.lock's `dependenciesMeta`).

Only `main`/`types` are declared — there is no `files` allowlist nor an `exports` map. Without `files`, npm/yarn publish will include the whole package directory (source, tests, tsconfig) rather than just `dist`, since the repo-root `.gitignore` that ignores `dist/` does not apply to this sub-package. Without `exports`, the published module surface is unpinned and ESM deep imports (e.g. `@autolight/rekordbox-library/watch`) resolve relative to the package root instead of `dist`, so they break. Add a `files` allowlist and an `exports` map (the sibling `@autolight/config` package already follows this pattern).

packages/rekordbox-library/src/anlz.test.content: This test codifies acceptance of an ANLZ path that is absolute and lives *outside* the configured share. `resolveAnlzSet` (line 92 of anlz.ts) deliberately falls back to the stored absolute path when the share-relative form does not exist, and that value comes straight from the `djmdContent.AnalysisDataPath` column in master.db with no share containment check. If that DB value is ever attacker/corruption controlled (e.g. a crafted or shared library file), the resolver will happily report facts (path/size/mtime) for arbitrary filesystem locations, and any downstream reader that opens `dat.path` would read outside the share directory. Please confirm this behaviour is intended; if not, the resolver should confine the result to `sharePath`, and this test should assert that an out-of-share absolute path is rejected rather than treated as `anlz-ok`.

The injected `stat` seam returns facts only for paths ending in `.DAT`. This means the test cannot prove the seam is actually used for the audio existence check: the assertion `["audio-missing", "anlz-partial"]` would still hold if `resolveAnlzSet` ignored `statFile` for the audio path and ran the real `fs.statSync` against the non-existent `/virtual/share/a.mp3`. The test also never asserts that the injected size/mtime are propagated (`dat?.sizeBytes`/`mtimeMs` are unchecked here). Make the seam cover the audio path as well and assert the propagated facts so the test fails if the seam is bypassed, e.g. `const stat: StatFile = (p) => /\.(DAT|mp3)$/.test(p) ? { sizeBytes: 10, mtimeMs: 5 } : undefined;` then assert `resolved.audio?.exists` and `resolved.dat?.sizeBytes`.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/anlz.test.content: The only combined status case exercised with `audio-ok` is `audio-ok` + `anlz-ok`. The combinations `audio-ok` + `anlz-missing` and `audio-ok` + `anlz-partial` are never tested (all missing/partial cases pass no `audioPath`, so audio is `null` and its status is omitted). These are realistic states (audio present but a half-written or removed ANLZ set) and are exactly where an ordering/precedence bug or a crash in sibling derivation would hide. Add at least one case with a real audio file plus an absent/partial ANLZ set and assert the ordered statuses.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/anlz.ts.content: `swapSuffix` only recognizes `/` as the path separator. `join()` (and the stored absolute fallback) produce platform-native paths, so on Windows `slash` is always -1 and the `dot <= slash` guard becomes inert. In that case any dot that is not the file extension — e.g. a dotted directory segment in `/share/PIONEER/v1.2/ANLZ0000` — is treated as the extension and the sliced path becomes corrupted, yielding wrong `.EXT`/`.2EX` paths and therefore wrong `anlz-partial`/`anlz-ok` statuses. Using the `node:path` helpers removes the separator assumption.

This swallows every errno as "not found". Permission/resource errors (EACCES, EMFILE, EIO, ENOTDIR) are indistinguishable from ENOENT, so they are silently reported as `anlz-missing` / `anlz-partial` and the caller cannot tell a genuinely absent file from an unreadable one. Since a missing file is already modeled as a status, non-ENOENT errors should be surfaced (rethrow or return a distinct signal) rather than converted to a missing status. Note this also does not verify the path is a regular file, so a directory at `datPath`/`audioPath` is reported as existing.

Two concerns with this expression: (1) it stats `joined` (and possibly `stored`) to make the decision, then `facts(datPath, statFile)` re-stats the chosen path, so the DAT is stat'ed twice per row and the decision is based on a snapshot that can differ from the recorded facts (TOCTOU). Prefer resolving the path once and reusing the stat result. (2) `isAbsolute(stored)` is true on POSIX for the documented normal case (stored paths carry a leading `/` but are share-relative), so the absolute-wins fallback probes the filesystem root (`/PIONEER/...`) whenever the share-relative file is absent; the intended fallback should be triggered by an actually absolute stored path, not by the leading-separator convention.

A stored `analysisDataPath` containing `..` (an edited/unexpected DB row) escapes the share directory, and the resolver will stat and report files outside it as `anlz-ok`. Consider validating that the resolved path is contained within `sharePath` before trusting it.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/beat.test.content: The monotonicity test claims to cover "inside and outside the grid", but the generated grid has 128 beats (indices 0..127 → musical beats 1..128) while the loop only reaches beat 80 (`i <= 160` → `i/2`). The upper out-of-grid extrapolation region (beat > 128) is therefore never exercised, so a monotonicity regression in the "after the last anchor" nearest-tempo branch would go undetected. Extend the range past the top of the grid (beat 128 requires `i > 256`).

The out-of-grid samples only reach -0.25..1.25 of the grid span, and the out-of-grid error of a nearest-segment extrapolation grows linearly with distance from the ends. An extrapolation bug that is small within ±25% of the span (e.g. using the wrong end segment's tempo) can stay under the 1e-6 s tolerance here and survive the round-trip property. Consider widening the offset range (e.g. -2..3) so the extrapolation branches are meaningfully stressed.

`expect(Number.isFinite(accumulator)).toBe(true)` only rejects NaN/Infinity; any finite-but-wrong mapping (e.g. a constant value, or an off-by-one beat shift) still satisfies it. Combined with the fact that the timing budget is the only other assertion, this benchmark can pass while the mapping itself is broken. Add a correctness assertion on a known point, e.g. `expect(beatToSourceSeconds(grid, 1 as Beat)).toBeCloseTo(grid.beats[0]!.sourceTimeMs / 1000, 9)` (or accumulate and compare against a reference result).

The 250 ms wall-clock budget is calibrated to a specific host (comment claims 86 ms) and measures cold-JIT code on a shared CI runner. On slower/contended machines this assertion fails for environmental reasons unrelated to any regression, making the suite flaky. Prefer a much looser bound (or warm up before timing) so the test only catches order-of-magnitude regressions rather than host speed.

Exact float equality on a `seconds * 1000` product is brittle and inconsistent with the neighbouring `toBeCloseTo(1473, 9)` assertion for the same conversion. It happens to be exact today, but it will break if the conversion/rounding strategy changes even slightly. Use the same tolerant comparison as the second case.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/beat.ts.content: `raw.bpm` is copied into `BeatAnchor` without validation. A corrupt PQTZ file can supply `bpm === 0`, a negative value, `NaN`, or `Infinity`; consumers that derive beat/bar durations from the anchor's bpm (e.g. `60000 / bpm`) will then produce `Infinity`/`NaN` durations far from this boundary. Validate a finite, positive bpm here so corrupt data is surfaced instead of silently propagated.

Neither direction validates its scalar argument: `seconds` here, and `beat` inside `beatToSourceSeconds`, can be `NaN`/`Infinity` (or negative). With `NaN`, every comparison in `anchorPosition`/`beatCaret` is false, so the binary search collapses to segment 0 and the function returns `NaN` (or an arbitrary value) instead of failing fast. Add a `Number.isFinite` guard (plus a range check where negative time/beat is invalid) at the top of both functions.

if (!Number.isFinite(seconds)) throw new RangeError(`seconds=${seconds}, expected a finite number`);
  const ms = seconds * MS_PER_SECOND;

This also triggers for single-anchor grids (`beats[p + 1] ?? a` makes both spans 0) and for duplicate/equal anchor times or indices. In all those cases the mapping collapses (no longer monotonic or invertible), contradicting the documented contract in the header, and corrupt grids get masked rather than surfaced. Consider throwing (or otherwise rejecting) a grid that cannot support the requested mapping, e.g. requiring >= 2 strictly increasing anchors.

An unsorted grid or duplicate anchors silently select the wrong segment and return an incorrect time/beat instead of raising an error. packages/rekordbox-library/src/db.test.t.content: This assertion depends on row ordering that the queried SQL does not guarantee. `songPlaylistRows` executes `... WHERE PlaylistID = :id ORDER BY TrackNo`, but the fixture inserts both p1 membership rows with `TrackNo: 1` (see test-fixtures.ts membership). With equal sort keys, SQLite's tie order is unspecified (it happens to be rowid order for a plain table scan today), so this can become flaky if an index/plan changes. Either make the fixture use distinct TrackNo values for p1, or assert on a set/ordered-by-id result rather than an exact sequence.

The write-rejection check is too permissive to prove the write was actually refused. `toMatch(/readonly|read-only|query_only/i)` can be satisfied by incidental driver wording, and `counts().tracks` would be unchanged even if `CREATE TABLE autolight_write_probe` had partially succeeded (creating a table does not change the djmdContent count). Strengthen it by asserting the probe table was never created, e.g. query `sqlite_master` for `autolight_write_probe` (and expect no row), or assert `probe.error` matches the specific read-only error code rather than a broad regex.

This branch cannot actually distinguish the intended cipher failure path. When the module is present, `openWithCipher` still swallows a constructor/decrypt failure and returns `undefined`, so `openReadOnly` throws the same `cipher-module-missing` error as when the module is absent; asserting only `toBeInstanceOf(LibraryDbError)` therefore passes for either case and gives no real coverage of the cipher-present path. Assert the concrete code (or otherwise exercise a real cipher-open failure) so a regression in `openWithCipher` is not silently accepted.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/db.ts.content: Search input is wrapped as `%${search}%` without escaping LIKE metacharacters (`%`, `_`, and the escape char), so user text such as `100%`, `a_b` or `%%` broadens matches far beyond a literal substring. Worse, this diverges from the sidecar reader, whose `matchesSearch` uses a plain `String(...).includes()` comparison (sidecar.ts:335-340), so the same query returns different row sets (and a different `total`) depending on which reader is active — exactly what the DS-15 cross-check is meant to keep identical. Escape the wildcards and align both readers' semantics (or document the divergence).

packages/rekordbox-library/src/db.ts.content: Routing `Attribute` through `numberOrNull` means any non-`number` value (a TEXT-typed attribute column, a driver returning strings) collapses to `0`, so folders (1) and smart playlists (4) are silently reported as `"playlist"`. The `?? "playlist"` fallback also masks genuinely unknown attribute codes instead of surfacing them. Coerce the raw value directly and keep the fallback for truly unknown codes (or make unknown a distinct kind).

`text()` only accepts a real `string`; any numeric/BigInt ID (a driver or sidecar returning `ID`/`ContentID` as a number) is turned into the `""` fallback. `mapTrackRow`, `mapPlaylistRow`, `songPlaylistRows` and `historyTrackCounts` all use `text(row["id"], "")`, whereas `service.ts` and `sidecar.ts` consistently use `String(row["ID"] ?? "")`. That inconsistency makes the same row map to `""` here but `"101"` there, so `trackRow(id)` lookups and `tracksForEntries` membership resolution can silently return empty results for the TypeScript reader while the sidecar path works. Use `String(...)` (or extend `text()` to coerce numbers) for identity columns.

`numberOrNull` returns `null` for anything that is not a JS `number`. SQLite is dynamically typed, so numeric-looking columns can legitimately come back as strings (TEXT-declared columns such as BPM/Length/Rating/FileSize/SampleRate/BitRate/Seq/TrackNo) or as BigInt, and every such value is silently dropped to `null` rather than reporting a schema mismatch — the library would just show blank BPM/rating/duration with no error. Accept numeric strings/BigInt (e.g. coerce and reject non-finite results) or fail loudly on unexpected column types.

`historyTrackCounts` is only referenced by `db.test.ts`; it is not part of the `LibrarySource` interface (so `SidecarReader` has no equivalent) and `LibraryService.history()` computes the same count via a separate `songHistoryRows(...).length` path. This leaves two parallel counting implementations for the same data, one of which is unreachable from production code. Either expose it on `LibrarySource` and use it in the service, or drop it.

packages/rekordbox-library/src/driver.ts.content: Untrusted caller-supplied key is interpolated directly into a PRAGMA statement. A passphrase containing a single quote (e.g. `p'wd`) produces a malformed/broken statement, and crafted input such as `x'; PRAGMA journal_mode=...; --` can inject additional pragmas/SQL. Escape/validate before use, or use a driver API that accepts the key as a value.

`openWithCipher` returns `undefined` for EVERY post-import failure, including a wrong key, a corrupt/undecryptable database, or a present-but-unloadable native binding. Because the caller cannot distinguish "module absent" from "open failed", `openReadOnly` unconditionally reports `cipher-module-missing` here whenever the module IS installed but the key/file is bad. The caller then silently falls back to the sidecar reader even though the real problem is decryptability. Have `openWithCipher` distinguish module-absence from open-failure (e.g. a discriminated result or throw a typed error) and surface the real cause.

`openWithNodeSqlite` maps any non-driver-failed error (corrupt/truncated file, permission denied, locked file, I/O error) to `not-a-database`, and this block then relabels all of them as "is encrypted", discarding the original cause. A corrupt or unreadable plain SQLite file is thus misreported as encrypted, diverting the caller. Note also the `existsSync` check above races the open (TOCTOU): the file can be deleted/replaced between the check and `open`. Preserve the underlying `describe(error)` message / `cause` and only claim encryption when the failure is genuinely consistent with an encrypted database.

This security-critical check can silently drift between the two drivers and the fragile row-shape fallback may misread the flag if a driver returns a different shape. Extract a single shared helper (e.g. `assertQueryOnly(handle, dbPath)`) used by both paths.

The DS-22 confidences for `lighting-ipc-id` (0.95), `agent-api` (0.9) and `history-table` (0.8) are never checked, so a regression in the resolver's confidence table passes silently. A transient `uv` failure at import time (cold start, PATH not yet populated) permanently disables the only two tests that prove the key derivation and base85 decoder match pyrekordbox, with no signal at all. packages/rekordbox-library/vitest.config.content:
An alias is registered for *every* filesystem entry in `packages/` without verifying that the entry is a package directory containing `src/index.ts`. The canonical root `vitest.config.ts` deliberately guards this (`readdirSync(workspaceSrc, { withFileTypes: true }).filter((e) => e.isDirectory())`). Two failure modes follow from the missing guard:
1. Any non-directory entry or scratch directory in `packages/` (e.g. a stray `README.md`, `.DS_Store`, `packages/tmp/`) registers a bogus key such as `@autolight/README.md`.
2. A package whose entry point is not `src/index.ts` still gets an unconditional `@autolight/<name>` alias pointing at a non-existent path, which *shadows* the real workspace/node_modules resolution instead of falling back to it, surfacing as a confusing 'failed to resolve' error rather than a clear module-not-found.
Filter to real package directories (and ideally assert `src/index.ts` exists) so the alias only covers legitimately importable workspace packages.

`readdirSync(workspaceSrc)` at module load has no error handling: if `packages/` is missing or unreadable (permissions, partial checkout, config run outside the monorepo), the whole config evaluation throws before a single test is collected, producing an opaque failure that is hard to diagnose. Consider wrapping the scan (or validating the directory) and failing with an explicit, actionable message.

A slow drip-fed response keeps resetting the inactivity timer, so a hung server can hold the request open indefinitely; combined with the unbounded `body += chunk` accumulation below there is no cap on bytes or wall-clock time. packages/rekordbox-live/src/ax-provider..content: `remainingSeconds` is a countdown (time left), not a playhead position, and it is substituted for `elapsedSeconds` here and then reused for both `playheadSeconds` and the grid beat lookup. For a deck where only the remaining-time field is readable (ax.ts returns elapsed=null, remaining=non-null and marks the reading readable), this reports the countdown as the playhead (e.g. a 2:30 remaining shows playheadSeconds=150) and computes a beat far past the end of the track, while still labelling quality `estimated`. Keep the two fields distinct and only derive a playhead from remaining when a track duration is known; otherwise the deck should not emit a playhead.

`lastPollAtNs` is advanced before the permission check and before any tree is parsed, so a poll rejected for missing Accessibility permission still counts as "the last poll". After `setPermission(true)`, the next ingest that arrives within `intervalMs` of that rejected poll is silently dropped despite carrying valid data, delaying live updates by up to a full interval. Also note the comment claims in-flight coalescing, but `ingestTree` is synchronous and there is no in-flight tracking — this is purely an elapsed-time rate limit. Move `this.lastPollAtNs = at;` after the permission check (and update it only when a poll is actually processed).

`stateFor` is called by the read-only `getDecks()` accessor, yet it mutates shared mapper state via `mapper.update`. Worse, when `reading?.title` is falsy this passes `track: null`, which DeckGenerationMapper treats as an unload and *increments `generation`* and clears the stored track. Because `getDecks()` runs `stateFor` for unreadable decks too (whose title is often null), merely reading the deck list can bump the generation and make downstream consumers believe the track was unloaded/replaced, then bump it again when the next readable poll restores the title. A transient missing title on a readable deck has the same effect. Derive deck snapshots without mutating generation (only `ingestTree` should drive the mapper), and don't send `null` for a title that is merely unreadable.

Entries in `readings` (and `grids`) are never removed when a deck disappears from the dumped AX tree. `getDecks()`/`latestReadings()` keep returning the vanished deck with its last reading so consumers continue to see a deck that no longer exists in rekordbox; the stale grid can also produce a bogus beat if the same deck id is later reused. Evict readings/grids for decks absent from the current tree (marking them stale) instead of retaining them indefinitely.

Re-granting permission only flips the flag. When `granted` becomes true the status is left as `unavailable` (and stale readings/`lastPollAtNs` are retained), so the provider keeps reporting "Accessibility permission not granted" until the next successful `ingestTree`. Transition the status on re-grant (e.g. back to `starting`) and reset `lastPollAtNs` so the first post-grant poll is not coalesced away.

A tree that always contains a "Pause" (or "Cue") control, or a single transport toggle whose label lists both, forces `playing=false` even while a deck is playing. This does not read the toggle's actual state (AX/UIA checked/selected/TogglePattern). Prefer the toggle's checked state, and avoid treating mere presence of a "Pause"/"Cue" label as "not playing".

`timeToSeconds` applies a negative sign, so a remaining-time string like "-2:48" becomes `remainingSeconds = -168` instead of `168`. Because `isRemaining` also matches unsigned labeled remaining nodes, `remainingSeconds` has an inconsistent sign depending on how the UI renders it. Two concrete consequences: (a) the field no longer represents a remaining-time magnitude, and (b) it inverts `refineAxReading`'s "remaining decreases" checks — a signed countdown goes -168 -> -167 (i.e. numerically *increases*), so playing is never inferred from remaining for signed values. Downstream consumers that treat it as a magnitude (e.g. `ax-provider` using `remainingSeconds` as an elapsed fallback) then pass a negative value on. Normalize remaining to a positive magnitude and align the comparison direction, or make the sign explicit in the field semantics.

`all` is the fully flattened tree, so every node whose role matches `/deck|player/` — including a nested `role='player'` descendant of a deck container — becomes its own container, and the `/group|pane/` fallback matches many unrelated panels. The same deck can therefore produce multiple readings whose time nodes overlap, with colliding or renumbered `deckId`s (see `deckIndexOf`). Identify deck containers at one well-defined level (e.g. direct children of the deck area) and de-duplicate before reading.

The fallback derives deck identity from positional index in the container list. Since that list can contain nested/extra containers (see the container filter above), any such node shifts the numbering and produces incorrect `deckId`s and sort order rather than a stable identity. Additionally, `indexOf` returns -1 when the node is absent, silently yielding `deckId === 0`. Derive the deck number from an explicit label/attribute, and guard against a missing sibling instead of emitting a bogus id.

When both fields are present but no motion is observed (or `previous` is undefined), this returns `readable: true` while `playing` is left as whatever `current.playing` was — often `null`. That produces an inconsistent `{ readable: true, playing: null }` reading that callers treat as authoritative (the provider emits it and labels `playing` as only "estimated"). Either explicitly fall back to `current.playing`, or keep `readable` false when play/remaining state cannot be determined.

The binary search assumes `grid` is sorted ascending by `sourceTimeMs` and free of duplicate/gap entries, but nothing validates that. With an unsorted or duplicated grid the search silently returns a plausible-looking beat number (or 1 at the boundary) instead of `null`, corrupting the playhead mapping. Validate monotonicity (bail to `null`) or document/enforce the precondition at the call sites.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/composite.te.content:
The test name promises a lock "below the 15 ms target", but the only assertion is the quality label. `stateFor` sets `playheadSeconds` quality to `"derived"` whenever `state.locked` is true, independent of the residual error, so a correlation that locks with a large playhead error (or that merely flips the label) still passes — the 15 ms contract is never verified.

Worse, the pushed audio is systematically misaligned with the provider timebase: `end` is derived from the previously emitted `playheadSeconds` *before* `now += 100_000_000n`, but `tick(now)` then advances the clock, so `correctByAudio`/`referenceWindow` builds its reference window one tick (~100 ms = 5 samples at 50 Hz) ahead of the live slice that was just pushed. The lock therefore tests a shifted reference, not the real alignment.

Also `* 50` and `128` duplicate `envelopeRateHz` and the window size; if those options change the test silently breaks. Suggest aligning the slice to the tick timestamp (or computing it after advancing `now`) and asserting the actual residual error against `lockThresholdMs`/confidence instead of only the label.

`quality.channelFader` is statically `"exact"` in `stateFor` for every deck, and this test never ingests a `channel-fader` event, so the assertion only re-checks a constant and would not catch a broken channel-fader path. Ingest a `channel-fader` event and assert the resulting `deck.channelFader` value (and its label) so the fader path is actually exercised.

`resolveTrack` ignores the `query` argument and `listOpenFiles` returns a constant path, so the LOAD + open-files resolution path under test never exercises the `matchLibraryAudio` + query-driven resolution (canonicalPath/title/artist) that production uses. A regression where the resolver keys off the wrong query field, or where the open-file filter drops the path, would still pass this test. Consider driving the mock off `query.path` and asserting the resolved track fields.

`live` and `ref` are the same array, so `correlateEnvelopes` yields 1 whether or not the normalization is applied (an un-normalized dot product of an identical vector is also > 0.99). This assertion therefore cannot detect a missing or incorrect normalization. Use non-identical vectors (e.g. `ref.map((v) => v * 3)`) and assert the expected coefficient to actually validate the normalization.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/composite.ts.content: Root prefix matching has no path-separator boundary: `file.startsWith(root)` will accept `/music-other/track.mp3` for a configured root `/music`, admitting files outside the library and corrupting track resolution. The extension check lowercases `file` but this check uses the original case, so case-insensitive macOS paths can also silently fail. Compare against `root` with a trailing separator (or verify the next char is a separator) and normalize case consistently.

Nested ternary (three levels deep) to derive `track` violates the project rule forbidding nested ternaries and is hard to reason about. Extract a helper (e.g. `trackFromDeck(fallback)`) or use an if/else chain.

The `effectiveBpm` quality label is derived from the mere existence of a link tempo (`this.linkTempo()`), but `effectiveBpmFor` only uses the link value when it is fresh (< 2000 ms). If `linkTempo()` returns a stale sample (or a fresh one while the grid is absent so `effectiveBpm` ends up null), the value is actually grid-derived/estimated or null yet is labelled `derived`. The freshness decision must be shared with `effectiveBpmFor`. Additionally, `linkTempo()` is invoked twice per `stateFor` (once here, once inside `effectiveBpmFor`); if the callback returns a changing value the label and the value can disagree — read it once and pass it through.

Deck-to-file attribution is purely positional: the first unassigned candidate is handed to whichever pending deck is iterated first, with no check that the open file corresponds to the pressed deck. With simultaneous LOAD presses on both decks (or when only one new file appears), a file can be attributed to the wrong deck, mislabelling track/resolution. Consider correlating by press order/timing or exposing the deck association to the resolver.

When no open file can be resolved, this emits a synthetic track id `unresolved:<deck>:<at>`, but the deck keeps `hasTrack = true` with `resolution = null`, so the very next `stateFor` (from `tick`/other events) yields `{ id: "unknown" }`. The emitted track id therefore changes from the synthetic value to `unknown` for the same logical track, causing spurious track-change churn downstream. Use a stable id for the unresolved state.

`compositeFuseAxPlayhead`/`ingestAxPlayhead` only guard null/NaN and unconditionally rebase the anchor (and clear `locked`). Freshness is delegated to the caller, so a stale or out-of-order AX playhead can move the estimate backwards or forwards without the rate-limited slew used in `correctByAudio`, defeating the "never steps backwards while playing" guarantee. Add an age-based freshness/monotonicity guard here (or require the caller to pass freshness) rather than relying on call-site discipline.

The link-tempo freshness test does not reject future timestamps: if `link.atNs > atNs` (clock skew between the Link peer and the local clock) the difference is negative and always passes `< 2000`, so a future sample is trusted. Also `2000` is a magic number that should be a configurable/constant value. Use an explicit `age >= 0 && age < timeout` check.

`updateHz` is effectively hardcoded to 60 whenever `envelopeRateHz > 0` (the default), so the reported live update rate never reflects the actual emission/correlation rate. If a placeholder, wire it to the real tick/broadcast frequency or a named constant so it doesn't mislead hosts.

The lock decision compares sub-sample offsets against `lockThresholdMs` (default 15 ms), but at `envelopeRateHz` (default 50 Hz) the correlation offset is quantized to 20 ms/sample. `Math.abs(offsetMs) <= lockThresholdMs` can therefore only be true at zero lag, making the configured tolerance unreachable and causing `locked` to flip while the playhead is still up to one sample (20 ms) off. Either make the threshold at least one sample period or compare in sample units.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/contract-sui.content: The awaited `received.promise` has no timeout and `provider.stop()` is outside any `try/finally`. If a loopback datagram is dropped, `await received.promise` blocks forever (until the global vitest timeout), and if any assertion above throws, the bound UDP socket is never closed, leaking it into subsequent tests. The same pattern exists in the prolink test below. Wrap the wait+assertions in `try { ... } finally { await provider.stop(); }` and race the promise against a timeout so a missed datagram fails fast with a clear message instead of hanging.

`void track;` is a no-op that discards the contract-supplied track while an internal `trackCounter` synthesizes the track id. Because the harness never maps the contract's `track.id`, prolink's track-identity/generation mapping is not actually exercised against the contract's track ids, and the discard hides that gap. Prefer deriving the PRO DJ LINK trackId deterministically from `track.id` (or add an explicit comment explaining why the contract track is intentionally unused).

`127.0.0.1:${port ?? 0}` silently falls back to port 0 if `port` is ever null (bypassing the earlier non-null assertion). Sending to port 0 would make the datagram unreachable and, combined with the unbounded `await received.promise`, hang the test with a misleading failure. Capture the port once after the assertion and fail loudly if it is missing rather than silently defaulting to 0.

The guard `check(provider.getStatus() !== undefined, ...)` only records a message; the very next line(s) then dereference the value unconditionally (`provider.getStatus().state`). If a provider ever returns `undefined` (the check exists precisely because that is considered possible), the suite throws here and aborts, discarding all accumulated `failures` — directly contradicting the module contract stated at the top of the file ("returns the failures it found instead of throwing"). Bind the status once and guard the dereference.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/contract-sui.suggestion_code:
const status = provider.getStatus();
    check(status !== undefined, "status missing after start");

packages/rekordbox-live/src/contract-sui.content: More generally, the suite body is not wrapped to catch exceptions. Any throw from `provider.start()`, `subject.loadTrack()`, `subject.advance()` or `subject.malformed()` (e.g. a real socket provider that fails to bind, or the intentionally-leaky subject throwing) escapes out of `runProviderContractSuite` instead of being appended to `failures`. The red-run test relies on the suite returning a non-empty list (`expect(failures.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)`), so a throwing subject makes that test error rather than report the intended failure. Consider catching per-step and pushing a failure string.

This assertion does not actually exercise the bounded queue. `ProviderBase.emit()` already clamps `queueDepth` with `Math.min(1, this.queueDepth + 1)`, so for every provider in this package the value can never exceed 1 and the check is tautological; additionally the loop only advances virtual time and never feeds new updates, so for harnesses whose `advance()` emits nothing the depth is just a leftover from the earlier `loadTrack` and nothing is measured at all. A provider with a genuinely unbounded queue would not be caught. Drive a burst of updates without draining and then assert the bound.

The comment states deck 2 "must stay at generation 0 and not borrow deck 1's track", but the assertions only verify a state exists and that its title differs from "Generation A". A leaked `id`/`artist` from deck 1, or a wrong/borrowed generation on deck 2, goes undetected. Assert its own track identity (id/title/artist) rather than merely "not Generation A".
packages/rekordbox-live/src/contract-sui.suggestion_code: check(deckTwo?.track?.id === "gen-c" && deckTwo?.track?.title === "Deck Two", "deck 2 did not report its own track text");

packages/rekordbox-live/src/contract-sui.content: `onDeckState` and `onConnection` return unsubscribe functions (see `DJLiveProvider`), but both return values are discarded here. The listeners are never removed, so they survive `provider.stop()` and any reuse of the same provider instance accumulates callbacks, causing cross-suite contamination and a memory/resource leak. Keep the unsubscribers and invoke them when the suite finishes.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/follow.ts.content: Hardcoded business values: the version remedy embeds the literal version `7.2.19` and the date `2026-10-12` directly in the user-facing detail. These drift independently of `supportedVersions` (macOS `["7.2.8","7.2.17","7.2.18"]`, Windows `["7.2.10"]`) and of the upstream coverage, so the assistant can emit stale/misleading remediation guidance (the date is already in the past). Derive the message from a maintained constant/source of truth (or drop the version-specific date) instead of inlining literals.

Destination extraction is unscoped and last-write-wins: the regex matches any IPv4:port substring on any line containing "osc", and `destination` keeps whatever the last such line held. A config with more than one OSC-related address (e.g. an input/listen port such as `osc_input = 127.0.0.1:4461` after `osc_dest = 127.0.0.1:4460`) silently reports the wrong destination, which then produces a false `wrong-destination` setup state (or masks a genuinely wrong one). Scope the match to the destination key so only the intended line can set `destination`.

const dest = /osc[a-z_-]*\s*[:=]\s*((?:\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}:\d{2,5})\b/i.exec(line);
    if (dest) destination = dest[1] ?? null;
