packages/rekordbox-live/src/follow.ts.content: `subdiv` is only recognized when the entire remainder is exactly the case-sensitive string `beat/subdiv/<n>`. Any casing variation or trailing/extra segment yields `subdiv: null`, and the caller in rkbx-osc.ts then falls through to the path `switch` where the address is dropped into `unknownAddresses` — subdivision-based follow silently stops working with no error surfaced. Consider matching case-insensitively and/or tolerating surrounding segments (or reporting an explicit parse failure) so a malformed subdiv address is observable.

The state mapping only covers the five currently-known step ids and its final fallback silently maps any other failed step to `"no-packets"`. Because `failed` is the first step that fails, adding/reordering a step (or any id mismatch) will produce a wrong state and a remedy that quotes a different step's detail. Prefer mapping via an explicit `Record<RkbxSetupStep id, state>` or deriving the state from the step itself instead of a hand-maintained ternary chain with a catch-all.

Prolink takes precedence over AX based only on `peerPresent` and a non-null `beat`, ignoring `prolink.playing`. A paused/stale remote beat therefore overrides live AX playback (and reports its own `playing:false` to consumers). Per the file's stated intent ("prolink beats win when a peer emits; AX elapsed wins when readable"), please confirm this is desired; if the remote is paused, the AX reading is the honest live source and should win. At minimum exclude `prolink.playing === false` from the prolink branch.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.test..content: This "agree within threshold → no diagnostic" assertion is vacuous. `now += 1_000n * 1_000_000n` advances the clock by 1000 ms, but the default `staleMs` is 500 ms, so `rkbx-osc` (last seen at the earlier timestamp) is filtered out by `isFresh` inside `checkDisagreement`. With only one fresh provider left, `checkDisagreement` returns early (`fresh.length < 2`) and `drainDiagnostics()` is empty regardless of the playhead delta or the `disagreeBeats` threshold. The test therefore passes even if the threshold/agreement logic were completely broken. Advance less than `staleMs` and re-ingest the other provider so both states stay fresh and the near-equal spread is genuinely evaluated.

`now` is module-level mutable state captured by the `clock` closure, and every test in the file mutates it. This makes the suite order-dependent: any test that forgets to reset `now` at its start (the `describeStatus` test already does not) will inherit the previous test's timestamp and silently change freshness/hold-window behavior. Prefer resetting the clock in a `beforeEach` (or creating a per-test clock) so timing state can never leak between tests.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.test..existing_code:
let now = 1_000n * 1_000_000_000n;
const clock = (): bigint => now;

packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.test..content: This only weakly validates latest-wins. Pushing states for seconds 1/2/3 without flushing, then calling `drainPending()` asserts coalescing but immediately discards the result, so the later `expect(received).toEqual([4])` holds simply because a fresh `push(latest)` was made after the map was cleared — it would pass even if `flush()` forwarded every pushed state instead of the coalesced one. Consider asserting `drainPending()`/`flush()` output directly (e.g. expect the listener to receive the single coalesced value) so the forwarding path is actually exercised.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.content: The disagreement check filters providers only by `isFresh`, never by whether the field is actually supplied. For the `playheadSeconds` group there is also no null guard (unlike the explicit `effectiveBpm` guard below), so a provider that emits `playheadSeconds === null` is still compared: `beatsBetween` computes `Math.abs(a.playheadSeconds - b.playheadSeconds)` and JS coerces `null` to `0`, producing spurious large-spread diagnostics (or masking the real pair when the spurious pair dominates `spread`). Filter the `fresh` set per field by `supplied(...)` (or bail when either `playheadSeconds` is null).
packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.existing_code: const fresh = perProvider.filter((c) => isFresh(c.state, "playheadSeconds", atNs, this.options.staleMs));

packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.content: `Number(atNs - receivedAtNs)` assumes provider and engine clocks are synchronized. A future `receivedAtNs` (clock skew, or provider timestamp ahead of the engine) yields a negative delta that always satisfies `<= staleMs`, so an out-of-date value is treated as fresh forever. Also note `ingest` silently drops any packet whose `receivedAtNs` is lower than the stored one, so genuine out-of-order updates are discarded and never become the authority. Clamp the age to `>= 0` and/or reconcile clocks explicitly.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.existing_code:
if (state.quality[field] === "stale") return false;
  return Number(atNs - state.receivedAtNs) / 1e6 <= staleMs;

packages/rekordbox-live/src/fusion.ts.content: `start()` awaits each provider sequentially inside the loop; a provider whose `start()` never settles will block every later provider from starting and will hang the caller indefinitely. Starting providers is independent work, so await them with `Promise.all` (or at least race each with a timeout) to avoid one bad provider stalling the whole manager.

`stop()` tears down subscriptions and stops providers but does not cancel timers already queued through `schedule` (nor does `restart` consult `this.started`). A restart scheduled before shutdown still fires afterwards, calling `provider.stop().then(() => provider.start())` — resurrecting a provider and mutating `statuses`/`restarts` after the manager is stopped, which leaks resources and produces invalid state transitions. Track scheduled timer handles/handlers and cancel or no-op them in `stop()` (e.g. guard the callback with `if (!this.started) return;`).

`restart()` has no per-provider in-flight guard. Two `failed` statuses arriving before the scheduled callback runs (or the recursive `this.restart(provider)` in the `.catch` below firing while a prior attempt is still pending) will each increment `restarts`, schedule duplicate timers, and consume the restart budget twice for a single failure. Track an in-flight flag/set keyed by `provider.id` and ignore re-entrant restart requests until the current attempt settles.

`Promise.all([...this.restartsInFlight])` snapshots the set once. A restart chained from a failure `.catch` (which calls `this.restart` → adds a new promise + schedules a new timer) is added *after* the snapshot, so `settleRestarts` can resolve while a recursively scheduled restart is still pending — tests/shutdown will observe incomplete failover. Loop until the set is empty (draining newly added entries) instead of awaiting a single snapshot.

The `reason` union declares `"quality"` but no code path ever emits it; `pick()`/`emitSwitch` only ever pass `acquired`, `higher-authority`, or `stale-takeover`. Consumers matching on `"quality"` switches will never fire. Either implement the quality-driven switch (e.g. when the holder's quality degrades relative to a challenger) or drop the unused member to keep the contract accurate.

`this.options` is built by spreading the whole `opts` object (typed `{ now } & Partial<FusionOptions>`), so the non-`FusionOptions` `now` callback is copied into `options` and then leaked by `getOptions()` (`{ ...this.options, authority: [...] }`), returning an object with an unexpected `now` property. Destructure `now` out before spreading, or spread only the known option keys.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.test.t.content: Vacuous assertion: `at1x`/`at10x` are built from a single-event fixture, and index 0 always receives `baseNs` (i = 0 → `baseNs + BigInt(round(0))`) regardless of `rate`. This line therefore passes even if the `rate` argument were completely ignored, so the test does not actually cover "virtual clock" rate handling. Either use a multi-event fixture and assert the inter-event delta, or rely entirely on the dedicated §128 test below.

The step/full consistency check compares only `receivedAtNs`, so any divergence in the remaining DeckState fields (track, playing, playhead, source, etc.) between `replayFixtureStep` and `replayFixture` would go undetected. Compare the full state instead.

This fixture path is hardcoded and duplicated verbatim in the next test (line ~59), so a version/platform bump requires editing two places and they can silently drift. Additionally, the `readdirSync` loop assumes every entry is a directory containing `capture.json`; a stray file (e.g. a README or `.DS_Store`, both present elsewhere under this tree) makes `readFileSync` throw ENOENT and fails the whole suite with an opaque error. Hoist the path into a shared const and filter entries to those that actually contain a `capture.json`.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.test.t.suggestion_code: for (const action of readdirSync(dir).filter((e) => existsSync(join(dir, e, "capture.json")))) {

packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.test.t.content: `toMatchObject` only asserts `provider` and tolerates any additional keys in `raw`, so it cannot detect unexpected output fields or a regression in raw retention. The test also never verifies that `row` is retained, nor that `title`/`artist`/`sourceIds` were mapped into `state.track`. Assert the exact object to make the "unknown-field retention" contract meaningful.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.ts.content: `axFractionalBeat` is imported here but never referenced in this file (it is already surfaced via the `export * from "./ax.js"` barrel below). This is dead code and will trip unused-import lint. Remove the import.

`rate` is used as a divisor with no validation. `replayFixture(fixture, 0)` makes `i === 0` compute `0 / 0 = NaN`, so `BigInt(Math.round(NaN))` throws `RangeError: Cannot convert NaN to a BigInt`, and for `i > 0` it divides by zero. A negative rate produces negative/descending `receivedAtNs`, breaking the monotonic virtual-clock invariant callers rely on. Guard against non-positive/non-finite rates.

`String.prototype.replace` with a string argument replaces only the FIRST occurrence, so a normal range such as "7.x.x" becomes "7..x" and `version.startsWith("7..x")` is never true — every such range silently fails the gate. Additionally, prefix matching on the truncated range over-matches (e.g. "7.2.x" vs a hypothetical "7.2.0-rc"). Consider an explicit range parser/regex instead of stripping a single literal 'x'.

The comment above the schema states each expected event carries an `expectedBy` naming its human author, but the schema marks it `.optional()`. As written, `parseFixture` accepts fixtures with zero attribution, contradicting the documented fixture-lint contract (§T-QA-03). Either make it required (`z.string().min(1)`) or update the comment.

The step generator eagerly computes the ENTIRE replayed array on first advancement (via `replayFixture`) before yielding, so it is not actually incremental; a large fixture is fully materialized instead of one event per step. It also hardcodes rate `1`. If truly stepwise/streaming semantics are intended, iterate lazily without building the intermediate array.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.ts.content: Loop state is hardcoded to inactive and `master` to null regardless of the snapshot. `CompositeSnapshot` carries no loop/master fields, so any live loop or master-deck change is silently misreported as `{ active: false }` / `null` on every emit. If loop/master fidelity is a requirement for the composite provider, extend the snapshot; otherwise document the known limitation explicitly.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.ts.existing_code: loop: { active: false, startSeconds: null, endSeconds: null, beatLength: null },

packages/rekordbox-live/src/index.ts.content: The inline row type (`{ rekordboxId: string; canonicalPath?: string; title?: string; artist?: string }`) is duplicated verbatim three times in this function alone (and again in `CompositeSnapshot.row` and `DecodedMessage`). Extract a shared `LibraryRow`/`RowIdentity` type to prevent the copies from drifting.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/lighting-ipc.content: This assertion is too weak to prove the decode-failure path. `Buffer.from(str, "base64")` is lenient and never throws, so `decodeLightingCaptureBase64("!!!not-base64!!!")` does not hit the `catch` branch (`capture is not base64`) at all — it silently strips the invalid characters to `notbase64`, decodes 6 garbage bytes, and `decodeLightingCapture` then fails on a bogus huge frame length. `frames` ends up empty, so this test passes even though the intended error-reporting path is never exercised. Also assert `malformed` is non-empty so the rejection is actually verified.

The contract suite is run against a provider created with `fixtures: []`, which the sibling test establishes yields `capability() === "MISSING"` and `onStart()` → `unavailable`. The suite never checks the start/lifecycle path: it reaches `"live"` solely because `ingestEvent()` unconditionally calls `setStatus({ state: "live" })`, bypassing `onStart`. As written, a provider whose start logic is completely broken (e.g. never reports `unavailable`, or fails to transition correctly) would still pass. Exercise the suite with a READY provider (non-empty `fixtures`) and/or add explicit assertions that the MISSING provider reports `unavailable` with the owner `reason`/`remedy` after `start()`.

`"live"` is only asserted after `replayAll()`. A provider that transitions to live solely as a side effect of replay (and leaves `start()` stuck at `"starting"`), or one that never exposes a terminated state on `stop()`, would still pass. Assert the status immediately after `start()` (e.g. `"starting"`/`"unavailable"` expectations) and after `stop()` so the state machine is actually pinned down.

`fixture()` hardcodes `condition: "one-deck"` regardless of the `action` argument, so the `"loop-roll"`/master/loop/hotcue test produces an action/condition pair (`loop-roll-one-deck`) that does not correspond to any real matrix cell. Any downstream validation or path derivation that depends on the action↔condition pairing is therefore silently accepted rather than exercised. Let `fixture()` accept a `condition` parameter and pass a matching value from the call sites.

With only two frames this only checks the first inter-frame gap; dropped/reordered/duplicated intermediate frames, or incorrect cumulative `index * stepMs / rate` accumulation beyond the first step, would go undetected. Add a third event and assert all successive deltas (or the total span) so cumulative timing is validated, not just the first gap.

Inconsistent lifecycle status when only some (or none) fixtures decode. If `states.length > 0 && malformed.length > 0`, neither branch runs, so the provider stays in `starting` despite having emitted states. And in the `states.length === 0 && malformed.length > 0` branch, `markRejected` is a no-op when the current status is `starting` (see `ProviderBase.markRejected`: it only transitions from `live`/`degraded`), so a fully-undecodable replay also leaves the provider stuck in `starting`. Repro: commit one good fixture and one fixture whose `capture` is garbage, call `replayAll()` — states are emitted but `getStatus()` still reports `starting` forever. Handle the partial case explicitly and ensure the zero-decode case reaches a terminal state directly via `setStatus`.

Data loss: `ingestBytes` is fail-closed on ANY malformed frame. `decodeLightingCapture` deliberately skips bad frames and returns the decodable ones (`frames` + `malformed`), but this guard discards the entire buffer (returning early and dropping every valid frame) as soon as one malformed entry is present. Repro: feed a stream with 3 good frames and 1 corrupted frame — all 3 good states are silently dropped and only the error is reported. Ingest the decodable frames, then surface `malformed` (e.g., via `markRejected`) so a partial capture still yields states.

`rate` is used as a divisor without validation. `opts.rate ?? 1` accepts `0` (and negatives), producing `Infinity`/`-Infinity` from `Math.round(index * stepMs * 1_000_000 / rate)`, and `BigInt(Infinity)` throws `RangeError: The number Infinity cannot be converted to a BigInt`, aborting replay. Also note the passed `now` clock is ignored (`void clock`), so replay never honors real timestamps. Validate the rate before using it.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/lighting-ipc.suggestion_code:
const atNs = baseNs + BigInt(Math.round((index * stepMs * 1_000_000) / rate));
    // (add above: `if (!Number.isFinite(rate) || rate <= 0) throw new RangeError(...)`)
packages/rekordbox-live/src/lighting-ipc.existing_code: const atNs = baseNs + BigInt(Math.round((index * stepMs * 1_000_000) / rate));

packages/rekordbox-live/src/lighting-ipc.content: `this.replayed` grows unbounded and leaks provider state. `replayAll` resets it, but `ingestEvent` and `ingestBytes` only append (never trim/reset), so a long-running live stream grows the array without limit. Worse, `getDecks()` returns the internal mutable array instance, so any caller can mutate provider state (push/splice/sort). Return a defensive copy and bound/reset the buffer on ingest.

`raw["provider"]` is written unconditionally after unknown fields are copied, so a capture that legitimately contains a `provider` key has its value destroyed. This contradicts the module's stated guarantee that unknown JSON fields are "retained under raw, never dropped" (spec 9.5). Preserve the captured value (or namespace the injected metadata).

This `catch` is effectively dead code. `Buffer.from(capture, "base64")` does not throw on malformed base64 — it silently ignores invalid characters and returns a (possibly empty) buffer — and `new Uint8Array(...)` does not throw either. So the `capture is not base64` branch is unreachable for garbage input, which instead falls through to `decodeLightingCapture` and is reported as a truncated/bad frame. Validate the base64 shape explicitly (e.g., a regex/length check) if a dedicated error is intended.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.test.ts.content: The publish-wait loop recurses via `setImmediate` with no iteration cap or deadline. If `publish()` never produces a `setTempo` frame (e.g. the socket is closed, the write is dropped, or a future gating flag suppresses publishing), `published.promise` never settles and the whole suite hangs instead of failing with a clear message. Bound the loop with a deadline/attempt count and throw on timeout. Returning the matched line (see next comment) also lets the assertion validate the payload.

The only check is that the received text contains the substring `setTempo`; the actual value (126) is never asserted. A publish path that writes a wrong or malformed tempo (e.g. `setTempo: 0`, `NaN`, or a string) would still pass. Parse the frame and assert the full payload.
packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.test.ts.suggestion_code:
transport.publish({ tempo: 126 });
      // publish() was called above; assert the exact frame below instead of a substring match.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.test.ts.content: The transport is only stopped inside the `try` block; the `finally` closes only the fake server. If any assertion before `transport.stop()` throws, the client socket stays open and leaks into later tests. Worse, `stopFakeSidecar` calls `server.close()`, whose callback only fires once all existing connections have ended, so with the transport socket still open the `finally` itself can hang. Move `transport.stop()` into the `finally` (guarding against a double-stop) so teardown always runs.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/link.ts.content: Race: the 'error' handler clears `this.socket` unconditionally, unlike the 'close' handler which guards with `if (this.socket === socket)`. If this socket errors after a newer connection has replaced `this.socket`, the newer socket is clobbered to null (publishes silently dropped, status reports unavailable). Additionally `once("error")` removes the listener after the first error, so any subsequent 'error' on the same socket is unhandled and can crash the process. Guard the assignment and use `on` instead of `once`.

start()/stop() lifecycle is broken: (1) `this.socket` is assigned synchronously before 'connect' succeeds, so a second concurrent (or immediate) start() hits `if (this.socket) return` and resolves immediately, falsely reporting the transport as live while it is still connecting/failing. (2) If stop() runs while the socket is still connecting, `socket.destroy()` emits only 'close' (not 'connect'/'error'), so start()'s promise never settles — a permanently pending promise/resource leak. Track a connecting state and settle start() on 'close' as well, or reject when stopped mid-connect.

server.close() only completes once all existing connections are closed. If the client sidecar transport is still connected (a common test teardown order), the callback never fires and this promise hangs the test suite. The tracked `sockets` set should be destroyed here; note it is also not exposed on FakeSidecar, so expose it and destroy each socket before/while closing.

The fake sidecar does not keep a tail for partial lines: each raw TCP chunk is split on '\n' independently, so a published JSON object fragmented across chunks is recorded as multiple bogus entries in `received`. Tests then assert against corrupted data and can pass/fail independently of the real client behavior. Buffer the remainder like SidecarLinkTransport.ingest does (keep `tail` and prepend it).

The wire protocol carries the sidecar's own clock as `atMs`, but parseSidecarLine discards it and stamps `atNs` with the local receive time (`this.now()`), and ingest never consults `atMs`. Tempo/phase timing fed to the composite provider and adaptive clock is therefore skewed by transport latency with no correction, undermining time synchronization. Consider deriving the timestamp from `atMs` (with a local fallback/offset) rather than always using receive time.

Listener exceptions are not isolated: if one `onTempo` listener throws, the loop aborts, later listeners are skipped, and the exception propagates out of the 'data' event handler (uncaught exception that can crash the process). Wrap each listener call in try/catch (or defer notification) so a faulty consumer cannot break ingestion.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/manager.test.content: The entire test only ever asserts `fieldSources.playheadSeconds` (the winning provider label), never the merged value `fused.playheadSeconds`. This is a real gap in `FusionEngine`: a regression where `recompute()` labels `lighting-ipc` as the source but copies the challenger's `playheadSeconds` into the fused state (sources/quality and the value are resolved from different code paths, lines 172-181 vs 191) would still make every assertion here pass. Additionally, the switch-event check only verifies `reason` + `to`, so a wrong `field`, `deckId`, or `from` would go unnoticed. Assert the concrete value during the stale-hold steps (expect 10, i.e. lighting's value, not composite's 10.2/10.3) and after takeover (expect 10.4), and tighten the event assertion to include `from === 'lighting-ipc'` and `field === 'playheadSeconds'`.

The "Lighting wins" priority claim is never actually isolated from ingestion order: `lighting-ipc` is always ingested before `composite-flx4` in both cases (here and in the second `it`). Because the first candidate fed to `pick()` becomes the initial holder when both are fresh (fusion.ts:226-231), a regression that resolved priority by first-seen order instead of `rank()` would still pass. Add a case that ingests `composite-flx4` first (or emits composite then lighting in the same tick) and asserts lighting still wins, which is what proves rank-based priority.

The fixed 300 ms steps only bracket the `staleMs + switchHoldMs` window loosely (fresh at 300 ms, stale at 600 ms, takeover somewhere in (900, 1200] ms); they never pin the exact thresholds. An off-by-one or mis-set timeout still passes as long as it lands inside these coarse buckets — e.g. `staleMs` anywhere in (300, 600] or `switchHoldMs` in [300, 600] satisfies this sequence. Since `isFresh()` uses an inclusive `<=` (fusion.ts:74) and `pick()` switches at `>= holdNs` (fusion.ts:243), the boundary semantics are exactly what needs covering: assert freshness at age == staleMs and staleness at staleMs + 1 ns, and assert no takeover at switchHoldMs - 1 ns but takeover at switchHoldMs.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/master-field.content: This test cannot detect the regression its title claims. The test therefore still passes if that reset is deleted. Secondary issue: the title also claims the beat counter is cleared, but no beat packet is ever sent (so `buffer.beatCounter` stays 0) and `deck.beat` is never asserted. The test name claims the loop/roll is not carried across the mid-loop track switch, but no loop or roll state is asserted (only `generation` and `track.title`). Since `generation` is bumped by any track change, the assertion holds trivially and the 'without carrying the loop generation' behavior is never verified. Also, the track title and the playhead are changed together, so a change caused by the playhead cannot be distinguished from one caused by the title. Assert `after.loopRoll`/loop state after the switch to actually cover the intended behavior.

The per-field authority conflict is never actually exercised: `prolink` supplies no `pitchPercent` and `rkbx-osc` supplies no `sync`, so each asserted field has only a single candidate and the test would still pass if fusion simply took any present value instead of applying authority ranking. Worse, the title's 'fuses master from prolink' is never asserted, and per `DEFAULT_FUSION_AUTHORITY` (`rkbx-osc` at index 2 outranks `prolink` at index 3) the fused `master` would actually come from rkbx's `false`, contradicting the title. The test can therefore pass for the wrong reason. Re-ingest `composite-flx4` during the wait to keep it fresh (or assert the emitted switch reason is 'higher-authority').

This makes the tests order-dependent and cross-interfering: reordering or running them concurrently produces different timestamps and can change staleness/ordering behavior. packages/rekordbox-live/src/memory-reade.content: The lint assertion is too weak to be meaningful. `not.toEqual([])` only proves *some* failure string is produced; it does not verify that missing mandatory fields (`rekordboxVersion`, `platform`, `paths`, `verification`, …) are actually detected, nor which error/issue codes are reported. A regression where `lintOffsetsFile` returns a single generic error for every malformed input (or the wrong fields) would still pass. Assert on the specific linted keys/fields for at least one partially-populated object instead of only checking non-emptiness.

This scanner test is effectively tautological: it writes exactly the values the scanner is meant to discover and then asserts only the *field names* that were found. It never checks the discovered `base`/`offsets`, so a scanner that produced correct field labels at the wrong locations would pass. It also provides only a single observation, so the multi-observation verification branch in `scanMemoryOffsets` (the `rest`/filter path) is never exercised, and there is no negative case (e.g. a candidate value that must NOT be returned). Assert the concrete `{base, offsets}` tuples and add a second observation plus a non-matching value to guard against false positives.

The consent/version gates are only asserted at the `capability()` level. The disabled, no-consent and wrong-version providers are never started and never `poll()`ed, so a provider that still emits decks from the accessor despite a failing gate would not be caught here (only the no-consent case calls `start()`, and only its status is inspected). Start each gated provider and assert that `poll()` / `getDecks()` produce no data; also exercise `start()` on the READY provider to confirm it actually transitions to live.

The harness writes a constant playhead (0.5s) and BPM (128) on every `loadTrack`, and the generated `trackId` is computed but never asserted. As a result, regressions in playhead/time progression (e.g. a frozen or wrongly-reset playhead) and in track-id mapping will pass the suite undetected. Make the playhead/track id vary per generation (e.g. advance the virtual clock and assert `decks[0].playheadSeconds`/`track.id` follow), and add a `cleanup` that actually tears down state if the suite is expected to invoke it.

The slot layout (base `deck`/`region`, indices 0..3 mapped to playhead/bpm/masterDeck/trackId) is hardcoded independently here and again in the contract-suite `loadTrack`. If the offsets layout changes, one of the two sites can silently drift and the tests would no longer reflect the real schema. Extract a shared helper (or derive indices from the `offsets()` fixture) so both writers stay in sync with the declared pointer paths.

`pointerPathSchema` allows a multi-level `offsets` array, but `readMemorySample` only ever uses `offsets[0]`. Any real multi-level pointer path (dereference -> follow chain) silently resolves against a single flat slot, so it reads the wrong value and reports a corrupt playhead/BPM/trackId instead of failing. Either resolve the whole chain through the accessor or tighten the schema (`z.array(...).length(1)`) so unsupported paths are rejected at validation time rather than silently mis-decoded.

The cross-observation verification does not actually verify anything: (1) it only inspects `rest[0]` and ignores all remaining observations, (2) `bpm`/`trackId` candidates fall through to `return true` and are never checked, and (3) the playhead branch accepts a candidate when it equals `expectedSamples`, i.e. the *first* observation it was already matched against, so a stale/non-verifying path always passes. This defeats the stated `verify across a second observation set` guarantee and lets false-positive offsets be recorded as verified. Each candidate should be checked against every observation for its field (and bpm/trackId should be compared too), returning false on the first mismatch.

`path.sampleRateHz` is parsed but never used: `MemorySample` does not carry it and `stateFor` always converts with the provider-level `this.sampleRateHz` (default 44100). If the offsets file was verified at a different rate, the emitted `playheadSeconds` is scaled by the wrong factor, producing a consistently wrong playhead. Propagate the per-path rate into the sample (or into the provider when the offsets file is loaded) and convert with it.

`poll` only inserts/updates decks and never removes decks that are no longer present in `found`, so `getDecks()` keeps returning stale deck states for decks that vanished (e.g. a deck cleared in Rekordbox). Consumers have no way to know the data is old. Also the `live` status is published with hardcoded `updateHz: 0, ageMs: 0`, which misrepresents freshness and hides stalls from the status contract. Track the previous deck set, delete (and ideally emit/tombstone) decks absent from `found`, and report a real update rate/age derived from `at` vs. the last successful poll.

`playing` is hardcoded to `true` even though the memory reader has no play/pause signal, and `qualityFor()` marks `playheadSeconds`/`effectiveBpm`/`master` as `"exact"` unconditionally. When `playheadSamples`/`bpm` are null (no read) `playheadSeconds` defaults to 0 yet is still labelled `exact`, and `playing` is only labelled `derived` rather than unknown. Downstream observers cannot distinguish a real paused deck from a failed/absent read. Derive `playing` from actual state or report it as unknown, and set each field's quality based on whether the corresponding sample field was actually read (null -> unknown/absent).
`rate` is assigned and then only consumed by `void rate;`, so it is dead code. Remove both the local and the `void` statement (the conversion in `stateFor` reads `this.sampleRateHz` directly).

packages/rekordbox-live/src/os2l.test.ts.content: The TCP test has no `try`/`finally` cleanup path. If `await seen.promise` rejects (connection refused, server error) or any assertion between `start()` and the trailing cleanup throws, `provider.stop()` and `sender.destroy()` never run, leaking the listening server/socket and hanging the test until the Vitest timeout. Wrap the body in `try { ... } finally { sender.destroy(); await provider.stop(); }` (and destroy the socket on error) so the server is always torn down.

Two problems here: (1) the promise resolves on the *first* `data` chunk, not on the feedback line, and the assertion only checks `toContain('"feedback"')` — so a bug that emits the wrong `name`/`state` (or any other JSON containing `feedback`) would still pass. (2) There is no `sender.on("error", ...)` handler; a socket error between connect and destroy raises an unhandled `'error'` event and crashes the test. Assert the exact payload (`formatOs2lFeedback("program1", "on") + "\n"`) and register an error handler.

Assertions are too weak: `tail.length > 0` accepts any non-empty tail, so a splitter that drops/corrupts the partial object would still pass. `splitOs2lMessages` is documented to return the exact incomplete tail; assert it explicitly, e.g. `expect(first.tail).toBe('{"evt":"beat",');`, and also assert `first.garbage` is empty for this input.

This N/A filter keys on exact failure strings produced by the shared contract suite. The wording is owned by another module, so a benign message change makes the filter stop matching and the test fails for a misleading reason (and any real regression that happens to surface these specific strings is masked). If possible match on a stable code/identifier rather than the human-readable message, or pin the expectation to the suite's exported failure constants.

The test pins only pos 42 -> beatInBar 3, which is consistent with the provider's documented 4:4 convention (`pos % 4 == 0` marks the bar line). Because no boundary value is asserted, an off-by-one in `beatInBarOf` (e.g. treating pos 40 as beat 4 instead of 1) would not be caught. Add a bar-line case such as `pos: 40` -> `beatInBar: 1` to lock the convention.

A beat such as `{"evt":"beat","pos":1,"bpm":0}` produces `Infinity`/`NaN` for `playheadSeconds` (and a negative bpm produces a garbage playhead), which then propagates into the deck state. Reject/clamp non-positive bpm before computing.

Since `this.tail` is also cleared, the connection resynchronises only on the next chunk. Because this is an `else if`, any chunk that mixes malformed text with valid messages skips the transition to `live`. `markRejected` only downgrades an already `live`/`degraded` provider, so for the very first chunk `x\n{"evt":"beat","pos":1,"bpm":120}` the beat is applied and deck state is emitted while the provider stays in `starting` until a fully clean chunk arrives. packages/rekordbox-live/src/os2l.ts.content: Using `lastIndexOf(":")` breaks bare IPv6 hosts: `'::1'` is parsed as host `':'` and port `1`, so the server binds the wrong interface/port. In addition the parsed port is never range-checked against `OS2L_PORT_MIN`/`OS2L_PORT_MAX`, so out-of-range values (or `NaN` from a non-numeric suffix such as `'host:abc'`) are passed straight to `server.listen`. Parse `[host]:port` / bare host explicitly and validate the port falls within the advertised range.

Two error handlers are registered on the same server: this permanent listener plus the `server.once("error", reject)` below. On a listen failure both fire, so `setStatus({state:"failed"})` is called twice (and a third time from the catch in `onStart`), and because the permanent listener is never removed in `onStop` a late socket error after shutdown will overwrite the provider status again. Keep a single handler and detach it in `onStop`.

`sendFeedback` writes to every tracked socket without checking `writable`/`destroyed`. A socket that was reset or half-closed by the peer will emit `ERR_STREAM_DESTROYED`/`EPIPE`, which is only swallowed by the socket's `error` listener; guard the write (skip !socket.writable or cleaned-up sockets) so feedback is not silently lost.

`decodeOs2lText` re-implements the exact parsing `ingestChunk` performs lower in this file (splitting, `JSON.parse`, the same zod schema, and identical `bad OS2L ...` message formatting) but through a different code path (`safeParse` vs `try/catch`). Any schema or message-format change now has to be made in two places and the two can drift. Extract a single parse helper and have both entry points call it.

The `slot === 1 || ... || slot === 4` guard is always true for the finite numbers JSON normally carries, and the `null` return is only reachable for a non-finite `pos` (e.g. `1e999` parses to `Infinity`), in which case the bar position is silently reported as `null` instead of the message being rejected. Since `pos` is unconstrained in `os2lBeatSchema`, validate it as a finite/non-negative number in the schema rather than relying on this effectively-dead branch.

Inbound feedback frames are therefore counted as valid messages and trigger an `emit` while silently doing nothing. packages/rekordbox-live/src/osc.test.ts.content: The malformed-path test claims to prove `decodeOscDatagram` "reports malformed datagrams instead of throwing", but both negative inputs are shorter than 8 bytes, so they never reach the unguarded `readPaddedString(bytes, 0)` call in `decodeOscDatagram` (osc.ts:173, `bytes.length >= 8 ? readPaddedString(...) : ""`). That call sits OUTSIDE the internal try/catch, so a datagram of >= 8 bytes with no NUL terminator (e.g. `new Uint8Array([1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8])`) is still thrown at the caller, contradicting the documented contract. Add such a vector so the no-throw guarantee is actually exercised.

`notAnAddress` is misleading and the case is ineffective. The value is a valid OSC message whose address does begin with `/ok`, so decoding it just repeats the happy path and never covers the intended "non-address" malformed case. Also, this third assertion does not check `malformed` (it could be non-empty) and does not verify the decoded arg. Make the intent explicit and assert the full result, e.g. decode a datagram whose first token is not an address payload (`decodeOscDatagram(new Uint8Array([0x6f,0x6b,0x00,0x00])).malformed.length).toBeGreaterThan(0)`).

The args assertion is only executed when `vector.address !== undefined`. The bundle vector in the fixture (`timetag: 1`, `addresses: ["/a"]`, `args: [1]`) has no `address`, so its decoded argument is never validated at all — only the addresses are checked. A decoder that drops or corrupts a bundle element's arguments would still pass. Validate the args of every decoded message (e.g. iterate `decoded.messages` and compare their `args` against the vector), not just `messages[0]`.

Numeric args are asserted with `toBeCloseTo(Number(expected), 5)`, and the `argKinds` field declared in `OscVector` is never read. This makes the test blind to the OSC type-tag distinction (`i` vs `f`) and to string (`s`) arguments entirely — a decoder that emits floats for int tags, or mishandles `s`/`b` args, still passes since the fixture only carries numeric args and the int/float bytes are only checked for the two `roundTrip` vectors. Either assert `argKinds` against the decoded type tags or add string/typed vectors so the `s` encode/decode paths are covered.

The round-trip test unconditionally re-encodes EVERY `roundTrip` vector with `encodeOscMessage`, ignoring the `timetag`/`addresses` fields the interface allows. If a future `roundTrip` vector describes a bundle (the codec exposes `encodeOscBundle`), it would be encoded as a bare message and never validated as a bundle. Gate on the vector shape and call `encodeOscBundle` for bundle vectors.

Any package layout change makes the whole suite fail at import time with a raw ENOENT instead of a targeted assertion. Consider resolving via the package root (e.g. `import.meta.dirname` + a computed repo root, or a vitest alias/`import.meta.resolve`) so the failure is localized and the path is not coupled to the current directory depth.

packages/rekordbox-live/src/osc.ts.content: The top-level header pre-read runs outside the visitor's try/catch, so any datagram of >=8 bytes that does not contain a NUL within the buffer (e.g. `Uint8Array(8) {0x01,...}` with no 0x00, or a 4-7 byte NUL-terminated string whose 4-byte padding overruns) makes `readPaddedString` throw `RangeError("unterminated OSC string")` directly out of `decodeOscDatagram`. This violates the documented contract ("Malformed elements are reported, never thrown at the caller (S26)") and, since the only caller `ingestDatagram` (rkbx-osc.ts:193) does not wrap the call, an attacker can crash the caller with a single malformed UDP packet. The `bytes.length < 8` branch pushes the error into `malformed`, so the behavior is inconsistent between short and long un-terminated inputs. Prefer eliminating this duplicate read (see the unused `timetag` below) or at minimum wrap it in try/catch and push to `malformed`.

The 4-byte blob length prefix is bounds-checked, but the blob payload/padding is not: `at + 4 + len` is never validated against `data.length`. When `len` overruns the buffer, `data.slice()` silently truncates the blob and `at` is advanced past the end of the datagram, so the remaining args are no longer parsed at the correct offsets and the element is NOT reported in `malformed` — corrupting the parse instead of rejecting it. Validate the full padded length before slicing.

The bundle element loop condition `at + 4 <= data.length` silently ignores any residual 1-3 bytes left in the bundle (or a size prefix that cannot be fully read). A structurally malformed bundle is therefore accepted and reported as clean rather than added to `malformed`. After the loop, flag any leftover bytes.

`timetag` is read here but never used inside `visit` (the return value for the top level is recomputed separately at the end of `decodeOscDatagram`). This is dead code and is the root cause of the duplicated `#bundle`/timetag parsing; remove it (or have `visit` return the top-level timetag so the header is parsed only once).

Integers outside the int32 range fall through to the `f` (float32) branch, so e.g. `args: [5_000_000_001]` is encoded as a float tag, silently losing precision and round-tripping to a non-integer. Consider throwing for out-of-range integer arguments (or documenting the fallback) rather than emitting a precise-looking but lossy float32.

Playing detection is scaled incorrectly and mishandles slow pitch / backward seeks.

1) At 120 Hz the wall period is ~8.33 ms. Any `playRate` below ~0.6 (5 ms / 8.33 ms) makes the per-tick playhead advance smaller than `playingEpsilonMs`, so a *playing* deck falls into the pause branches, sets `pauseSinceNs`, and after `pauseHoldMs` is flipped to `playing = false` — slow-pitch playback is reported as paused.
2) A backward jump (backward seek while playing) hits `!forward && deltaMs >= epsilon` and immediately sets `playing = false`, so the deck is briefly reported as paused until the next forward tick re-arms it.

The epsilon must be relative to the expected movement (e.g. scaled by `playRate`, or derived from the tick period), and a backward seek should not by itself force the pause state.

`deckIdOf` returns 0 for any non-numeric buffer. The `"master"` buffer is stored under the string key `"master"`, so a seek detected while applying `/master/time` yields `deckId: 0` in the emitted `RkbxSeekEvent` instead of the actual master deck. The same bogus 0 propagates through `requestResolution` when `masterDeckId` is unresolved (`this.masterDeckId ?? 0`), producing resolution requests for a non-existent deck 0. Resolve the master buffer's owning deck (via `masterDeckId`) rather than falling back to 0.

When binding fails (or the socket emits an error before `bind` completes), the rejected promise is caught, status is set to failed, and the error is rethrown — but the dgram socket stored in `this.socket` is never closed. The socket (and the bound/attempted port, with `reuseAddr`) leaks, and `this.socket` stays set so a later `onStart` silently orphans the previous handle. Close the socket in the failure path before rethrowing.

The step window `[atMs - period, atMs]` is inclusive on both ends, so a step whose `atMs` lands exactly on a tick boundary is applied on two consecutive ticks (the tick equal to `atMs` and the following tick, whose lower bound is also `atMs`). This duplicates play/pause/seek/pitch/track datagrams in the generated stream (e.g. a step at `atMs = 0` fires at t=0 and again at t=period), breaking the deterministic replay guarantee. Make the window half-open (e.g. skip when `step.atMs < atMs - period` only for the previous tick, or track which steps were already applied).

packages/renderer/src/color.ts.content: `fixtureBytes` re-implements the numeric gamma transfer instead of delegating to `linearToSrgbByte`. Unlike `linearToSrgbByte`, this copy (a) has no `gamma > 0` guard, so a calibration gamma of 0 or negative is used directly (`1/gamma` becomes Infinity or negative), and (b) does not clamp the `pow` result before `Math.round(... * 255)`. It also propagates NaN silently (Math.min/Math.max pass NaN through, Math.round(NaN) => NaN, which a Uint8Array store then truncates to 0). packages/show-host/src/clock.ts.content:
`fire(0)` runs synchronously *before* `setInterval` is installed. Consequences:
1. Resource leak on auto-stop: if `options.ticks` is 0 or 1, `fire(0)` reaches `fired >= maxTicks` and calls `stop()`, but at that moment `timer` is still `null`, so nothing is cleared. The `setInterval` created on the next statement is then never cleared and keeps firing forever (each callback early-returns because `running` is false), pinning the event loop open permanently. The timeout-spin/hybrid strategies fire zero ticks and stop cleanly in this case.
2. Inconsistent tick numbering: `ticks: 0` still emits one tick here, unlike the other two strategies.
3. API hazard: because `onTick` is invoked synchronously inside `startClock`, a callback that references the not-yet-returned `ClockHandle` (e.g. `handle.stop()`) will hit a TDZ ReferenceError.
Install the interval first, then guard the initial fire, e.g. `timer = setInterval(...); if (maxTicks === undefined || maxTicks > 0) fire(0);` — that also lets `stop()` from `fire(0)` actually clear the interval.

The comment claims this branch 'degrades to timeout-spin shape', but it does not spin. Here `coarseMs = (expected - now) - spinMs`, yet the callback calls `fire(index)` immediately instead of busy-waiting until the anchored `expected`. Ticks therefore land up to `spinWindowMs` (default 1.5ms) early, and because `fire` floors jitter at zero the early phase error is silently hidden. Add the same spin tail used by timeout-spin before firing.

`fire(index)` calls the caller-supplied `onTick` and is followed by the recursive `arm(index + 1)` (and `setImmediate(step(...))` in the hybrid path). If `onTick` throws, the reschedule never runs, so the timeout-spin/hybrid clock halts permanently with no `stop()` call and no surfaced error — whereas the interval strategy simply fires again on the next interval. Guard the reschedule so a throwing callback cannot silently kill the tick stream.

Drift correction is one-directional: only `behind > next` is handled. When the interval timer fires slightly earlier than `nominalNs`, `behind < next`, yet the code still emits the future index immediately. `scheduledNs` is then in the future while `jitterMs` is floored to 0, so the early phase error is masked and the phase can walk ahead of the anchored schedule. Consider waiting until `scheduledNs` (or at least not emitting a tick whose scheduled time has not yet arrived) instead of firing regardless.

This test is named "tick clock defaults to the monotonic hrtime source" but `makeHost()` always injects `nowNs: () => now`, and `tick(nowNs)` takes the timestamp as a parameter. packages/show-host/src/invariants.ts.content: The single outer try/catch collapses every internal failure into code `finite-beats`, even though this is not a beat problem. Consequences: (1) a caller cannot distinguish an internal contract breach (e.g. `ctx === undefined` or a malformed sub-field) from a genuine non-finite beat; (2) because all checks run sequentially inside one try, an exception thrown by an early check (e.g. `Object.entries(ctx.pendingPerDevice)` when a sub-field is missing) silently skips every later invariant, so `out` contains only the misleading `finite-beats` report and all real diagnostics for that frame are lost. Consider isolating each check (its own try/catch) and adding a dedicated `INVARIANT_CODES` entry such as `"invariant-error"` for internal failures instead of reusing `finite-beats`.

`hostThreadId`/`rendererThreadId` are typed `number | string`, but this uses strict `===`. A numeric host id and its stringified renderer id (e.g. `1` vs `"1"`) are the same thread yet compare unequal, so a real same-thread violation is silently missed. The existing test only assigns identical types (`ctx.rendererThreadId = ctx.hostThreadId`) so this gap is not covered. Normalize both sides before comparing.

`actual ?? 0` conflates two distinct situations: a frame that genuinely carries 0 zones and a device that has no frame entry at all (`ctx.frameZones[deviceId] === undefined`). Both report `frame carries 0`, misreporting the observed value and making the diagnostic misleading. Branch on `deviceId in ctx.frameZones` so a missing frame is reported as such, and only render the numeric value when the entry exists.

`checkBeats` returns after the first non-finite beat, so a frame with multiple bad beats only ever produces one report (later bad beats are suppressed) and the message does not identify which beat/index is invalid. Also an empty `ctx.beats` array passes with no signal. Prefer accumulating violations (drop the early `return`) and including the beat index/value in the message so diagnostics are complete.

packages/show-host/src/snapshot.test.ts.content: Circular/tautological comparison. The bytes fed to the "recording transport" are produced by `frameBytesOf(snap)`/`cellsToFrames(snap)` from the *same snapshot* that was read off the wire, and the assertion then compares `cellsToFrames(snapshot)` of that identical snapshot back to `match.bytesByFixture`. Both sides derive from the same `HostSnapshot`, so the check can never detect an incorrect host frame — it only proves `cellsToFrames` is deterministic. Consequently `expect(transport?.records.length).toBe(recorded.length)`/`byKind("razer")` are also trivially true (one send per push). To actually test the claim, the recorded bytes must come from the host's pre-calibration logical frame (e.g. the renderer frame captured inside the host) rather than from the published snapshot.

The replayed snapshot is injected back into `seen`, the same array used to compute `published` below. Because `replay` is itself added to `published`, the later assertion `Math.max(...published.filter(t => t <= replayed)) === replayed` is guaranteed true and cannot fail, even if the renderer actually replayed a stale frame. Additionally `replay` is sourced from `latestPublishedSnapshot(...)` (which returns the max-tick snapshot), so it is by definition the latest published — the property under test is assumed, not verified. The test should observe the snapshot the reloaded renderer actually receives (a real replay path) and must not push it into the same list it is checked against.

"Zero frame gap at the transport" is not measured at a transport. No `RecordingTransport` is instantiated in this test; `transportTicks` collects `host.getMetrics().ticks`, so the loop below only proves the host's own tick counter increments by one. It never exercises transport-side frame continuity (the reload/drop is simulated purely by the `rendererLive` flag gating `seen`). The test name and comments overstate what is verified; either wire an actual recording transport and assert on its per-tick records, or rename to reflect that only host tick continuity is checked.

Dead fallback. `latest` and `wire` are both derived from the same `seen` array (`wire = snapshotsOf(seen)`), so when `latestPublishedSnapshot` returns `null` the `seen`-derived `wire` is empty and `wire[wire.length - 1]` is `undefined`. The documented fallback (`?? wire[wire.length - 1] ?? null`) can therefore never produce a value, masking the case where no genuine replay snapshot was observed at all. Capture the pre-reload snapshot before the dark window (or use a real replay source) instead of a fallback that is unreachable in practice.

No bounds check before writing. `cell.cellIndex * 3` (and +1/+2) are written into a `Uint8Array` sized to `fixture.cells.length * 3`; if a snapshot ever carries an out-of-range `cellIndex`, the typed-array store is silently ignored (no throw), so cells are dropped without any signal. In `frameBytesOf`/`cellsToFrames` this would let byte comparisons pass while real cells are missing, hiding host output that exceeds the fixture cell count. Guard `cell.cellIndex` against `[0, fixture.cells.length)` and assert/fail explicitly on an out-of-range index.

packages/show-host/src/snapshot.ts.content: `latestPublishedSnapshot` seeds `latest` with `snapshots[0]` and only replaces it on a strictly greater tick, so on equal ticks it returns the *earliest* element rather than the most recently received one. This violates the documented `latest wins` contract: a re-publish or resubscribe replay that appends a same-tick snapshot is ignored, and if the host tick counter ever resets/rolls over (new session or restart) a newer snapshot with a lower tick can never replace the stale one, pinning the UI to an obsolete frame. Consider comparing arrival order/element index as a tie-breaker (or handling tick resets) instead of relying on a monotonic tick alone.

`SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES` is a hardcoded copy of the `runtime.snapshot.maxBytes` default. `measureSnapshot` uses it as its default budget, but the host actually enforces the effective configured value (`options.config.maxBytes` in index.ts). If the runtime config is set to anything other than the default (range allows 16384..4194304), `withinBudget` is computed against the wrong limit — e.g. a 20 KB snapshot is reported within budget while the host would reject it at a 16 KB configured ceiling. Prefer threading the effective configured limit through rather than duplicating the default here.

`SNAPSHOT_UI_RATE_HZ` is exported but never referenced anywhere in the codebase; the publish rate actually comes from `runtime.snapshot.uiRateHz` / `options.config.uiRateHz`. packages/show-host/vitest.config.ts.content: The alias key `@autolight/${e.name}` is a plain string find. Vite/@rollup/plugin-alias matches string keys by exact match OR by a leading `key + "/"` prefix, so any subpath import of a workspace package is rewritten by prefix substitution into a nonsense path: `@autolight/simulator/dist/recording.js` becomes `<packages>/simulator/src/index.ts/dist/recording.js`, which never resolves and throws at import time. The hue search probes only 12 fixed +30° steps, and when none is valid the loop exits after the 12th shift wraps the hue back to its starting value — so the function returns the *original, un-repaired* hues with no indication that repair failed. Callers rely on the invariant: `planIdentity` (packages/show-planner/src/identity.ts:55) feeds the result straight into `globalDesign`, and the identity test only passes because it accepts a 0.06 slack below the configured threshold (identity.test.ts:79-81: `paletteMinDistance - 0.06`), which shows the contract is not actually met. packages/show-planner/src/types.ts.content: `mulberry32` derives its state from `parseInt(seedHex.slice(0, 8), 16)`. For any seed whose first 8 chars are not valid hex (e.g. the caller in recurrence.ts passes `` `motif-${seedHex}` ``, and `CompileInput.seedOverride` / `trackFingerprint`'s "id" branch can pass arbitrary strings), `parseInt` returns `NaN` and `NaN >>> 0` is `0`. Every such seed therefore silently collapses to the SAME PRNG stream, defeating seed determinism and masking malformed seed input. Consider throwing (or returning `NaN`) on invalid tempo and validating non-negative inputs at the boundary.

Use a `reduce` (or loop) to compute the max instead of an argument spread.

An out-of-order/stale install (plan gen N, then model gen N-1, or a late plan for an old generation) silently clobbers the newer artefacts while `tickWorld` keeps emitting `generation: world.generation`. Add a monotonic guard so a generation lower than the current one is rejected (or at least so plan and model cannot regress each other).

`trackDeck` rebuilds the scratch state on every call via `initialScratchState(prevBeat)`, so `observeRate` only ever sees the default `lastRate` and can record at most one reversal per call. The estimation path is chosen by `fresh` (gated on `estimatorOptions.seekThresholdMs`, default 150ms) while `clockHealth`/`motionFactor` use the independent `HEALTH_EXTRAPOLATE_MS` (500) / `HEALTH_HOLD_MS` (2000) thresholds, and `clockSource` is derived from `health`, not from the branch actually taken. With the defaults this happens to align, but a `DeckWorldOptions.estimator` override with `seekThresholdMs > 500` makes the `fresh` branch run `estimator.observe` while `health === "holding"`, so the tick reports `clockSource: "hold"` and a faded `motion` even though a fresh observation was used. To actually test that the rendered output after arbitrary history matches a fresh cursor, drive the real render path (`tickWorld` after `seekWorld`, i.e. ingest an identical observation into both a history world and a fresh world and compare `tick.cues`), not the pure seek helper. Also, `fresh.plan === null ? [] : ...` is a dead branch: `deckWorld` always calls `installPlan(world, 1, plan)` with a non-null plan, so `fresh.plan` is never null here.

packages/show-runtime/src/seek-equivalen.content: The phrase case is only checked for grid membership while `beat <= 192`, so the exact region the comment flags as unverified (beats past the last phrase, 192–200) degrades to a monotonicity-only check. `quantizeResume(beat, "phrase", grid)` returns `Math.ceil(beat/16)*16` there (e.g. 208 for 192.5), but a broken fallback (off-by-one multiple, wrong step, or even returning the unquantized `beat`) would still satisfy `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(beat)` and pass. `upcomingCues(p, 4, 1)` is only asserted to have length 1, so a wrong selection passes: returning the last cue, returning a cue at/before the current beat, or breaking the start-beat ordering would all still yield length 1. Assert the identity/order of the returned cue instead.

To assert "zero turn commands while armed" the recording must be driven through the simulator's armed-channel logic (e.g. via `GoveeLanSim` plus a capturing transport), not a plain recorder.

These assertions do not prove reappearance or identity change. `sim.replyIp()` computes its result from the *current live* `packetCount` (>= redesign `reappearAt`) rather than from an actual reply, and no reply is captured anywhere in this test, so it would pass even if the sim never emitted a datagram after reappearing. packages/storage/src/fastpath.test.ts.content: This assertion is a wall-clock p95 over 150 real file reads, so it is environment-sensitive: a loaded/slow CI runner (or a container with cold page cache) can push p95 over 100 ms and fail the suite non-deterministically, while passing locally. Prefer asserting through `fastPathBudget(budgetMs).pass` (same comparator as the code under test) and derive the budget from a shared constant/config, and/or carve the timing assertion out of the default run so a busy machine does not produce false failures.

The suite never verifies cache-key isolation, so a broken key would go undetected. Concretely, in "answers with typed misses" the `{ styleHash: house }` request is issued after the plain-request load has already populated the LRU with a `plan: null` entry; if `planKey()` dropped `styleHash` (or `artifactKey()` dropped `analyzerVersion`/`sourceFingerprint`), that request would be served from the stale entry and still report `miss === "no-plan"` with a non-null track — the assertions would pass anyway. `fastPathCacheSize() === 1` only proves one entry exists, not that entries are keyed by the request fields. Add a negative test: load two requests that must not collide (e.g. different `configHash`/`sourceFingerprint`/`styleHash`), and assert both are cold misses with `cacheHit === false` (and cache size 2).

This F-DATA-04 regression test points the artifact row at `/cache/real.json`, which does not exist, so `readFileSync` throws ENOENT and the loader reports `invalid-artifact` because the file is missing — not because its content is not a TrackModel. The test therefore conflates "file missing" with "content invalid" and would still pass if the missing-file path regressed independently of the invalid-content path. The only line that actually guards the F-DATA-04 regression is `typeof result.track !== "string"`. Point the row at an existing file whose contents are not a TrackModel (the next test already does this with `bogus.json`) and add a separate explicit case for the missing-file behavior.

Asserting literal message substrings (`compile from cached features`, `plan key mismatch`, `did not parse to a ShowPlan`, `/cache/real.json`) couples the tests to exact wording in `fastpath.ts` rather than to the miss classification contract. Any copy edit (e.g. the source's "no cached plan; compile from cached features (spec 138 step 2)") breaks these tests without an actual behavior change, and conversely they do not check that `detail` is consistent with the reported `miss`. Prefer asserting `miss` (and `track`/`plan` nullability) as the contract, and treat `detail` only as an optional diagnostic.

Since `extra` is typed `Partial<LogFields>`, a caller (or forwarded worker payload) can silently replace these, producing records that no longer reflect this logger or the spec-130 schema. The dedup key is only `${severity}:${message}`, ignoring contextual fields (`session`, `deck`, `track`, `fixture`, `event`). `timestamp` is derived from `monoMs` via `new Date(monoMs)`. The field name (and injectable `now`) implies a monotonic clock; if a caller injects `performance.now()` or another monotonic source, `monoMs` is not wall-clock epoch ms, so `timestamp` becomes a wrong (1970-based) time while still passing validation. Additionally, if `now()` returns an out-of-range value, `toISOString()` throws `RangeError`. Capture wall-clock time for `timestamp` independently (or document/enforce that `now` must be `Date.now`).

Required fields are validated individually above and then re-checked by this loop, so a single missing field yields two problems (e.g. `timestamp: missing or not an ISO date` plus `timestamp: missing`). This pollutes diagnostics and makes problem counts misleading. The core-field presence checks are redundant with the individual checks — drop this loop (or drop the presence clause from the individual checks).

The `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`CENTER` thirding is not a valid partition and produces incorrect/overlapping target sets for small fixture counts:

The ranges are `LEFT = [0, ceil(n/3))`, `RIGHT = [n - ceil(n/3), n)`, `CENTER = [ceil(n/3), n - ceil(n/3))`.

- n = 1: `LEFT = [0]` and `RIGHT = [0]` — the same cell is returned by two different targets, so an operation applied to both (or a `LEFT` + `RIGHT` mapping) is applied twice.
- n = 2: `CENTER = [1, 1)` is empty.
- n = 4: `CENTER = [2, 2)` is empty while `LEFT`/`RIGHT` each take 2 cells.

`CENTER` silently becomes empty and `LEFT`/`RIGHT` can overlap, so callers get wrong target sets with no error. Please guard the boundaries (e.g. compute `third = Math.floor(n/3)` and clamp/deriving `CENTER` from the leftover after `LEFT`/`RIGHT`, or handle `n < 3` explicitly) so the three sets are disjoint and cover the intended cells.

protocol-fixtures/serato/3.3.5/macos/loo.content: This fixture's only distinguishing frames are `/Status/Deck/Loop/LoopRollOn` = 1 (64 ms) followed by 0 (160 ms), but the expected state asserts only the `loop` object. In the decoder, `loop.active` is driven by `/Status/Deck/Loop/AutoLoopOn` (`remote-provider.ts` -> `publish()`: `active: acc.loop.autoLoopOn === true`), and the roll state lives in the separate `loopRoll` field (`loopRoll: acc.loop.loopRollOn === true ? {...} : null`). `SeratoRemoteProvider` emits `loopRoll` on the deck state, but the fixture schema (`seratoFixtureSchema.expectedEvents = deckStateSchema.omit({receivedAtNs:true})`, non-strict) has no `loopRoll` key, so it is silently stripped and never compared. Consequence: a decoder that ignores `/Status/Deck/Loop/LoopRollOn` entirely still replays to these exact states and this fixture stays green, i.e. the 'loop-roll' action is not actually tested. Assert the roll state so the toggle is verified (this requires the fixture/contract schema to carry `loopRoll`).

5 frames split into 2 bursts (0-64 ms, then 160 ms) yield exactly 2 events, so the count matches `compareSequences`' length check. However, the 160 ms burst carries only `LoopRollOn=0`, which changes no field this fixture asserts (`loop.active` stays false from AutoLoopOn, `beatLength` stays 0.5), so the two `expectedEvents` are byte-for-byte identical. The second event therefore verifies nothing the first did not, and the roll-off transition it was presumably added for is unverified. Because the event must remain (the wire emits a second state for the second burst), give it a distinguishing assertion rather than an exact copy of the first.

protocol-fixtures/serato/3.3.5/macos/pla.content: Fixture semantics are correct but implicitly depend on a decoder-side constant. The three frames at 0/20/120 ms are split by `SERATO_BURST_GAP_MS = 50` in `packages/serato/src/replay.ts`: frames 0 and 20 coalesce into one burst (one event), while the 100 ms gap to the 120 ms frame makes it a second burst (second event). So 3 frames → 2 events is intentional, not a dropped frame. The problem is that the committed expectation (`expectedEvents.length === 2`) is derived from a 50 ms heuristic rather than from protocol structure: if the gap constant is retuned to match the real Serato playhead cadence (~30-40 ms, exactly what HW-SER-01 is likely to reveal), this fixture and every sibling will silently decode into a different number of events and the hand-written expectations become wrong for a reason that looks like a decoder regression. Suggest recording the frame→burst→event mapping for this action (fixture note/README) and adding an assertion that the expected event count equals the number of bursts derived from `frameTimesMs`, so a gap-constant change fails at the fixture-window level instead of being misattributed to the provider.

The expected state for the `play` action is not physically derivable from the wire data it asserts. The burst timestamp is 120 ms (the third frame) and the burst start is 20 ms, so the playhead is expected to jump 0 s → 2 s (~4.1 beats at the asserted 124 BPM) in 100 ms while `playRate` stays 1. A pure play advances the playhead by rate × Δt ≈ 0.1 s; a 2 s change is only reachable via seek/scratch. Consequence: this fixture pins the decoder's contract for a transition the action it claims to cover cannot produce, and any later playhead-continuity/rate validation or seek-vs-play classifier would be exercised against impossible input (and either fail or be forced to accept a 2 s jump as "playing"). Suggest either using a rate-consistent marker (≈0.1 s at 120 ms) or documenting explicitly that playhead values in these scripted fixtures are synthetic markers rather than real times, so the fixture is not mistaken for a reference capture.

protocol-fixtures/serato/3.3.5/macos/rep.content: expectedEvents[1] asserts the loop is off (active=false, beatLength=null), but the capture contains no wire record that turns the loop off — the only loop records set AutoLoopOn=1 and BeatLength=4. The "off" state is produced solely by the decoder's implicit "clear loop on track-identity change" heuristic (`noteTrackFieldsChanged` in packages/serato/src/remote-provider.ts resets `loop: {}` when the filepath id changes). The fixture therefore bakes decoder behavior into the "expected Serato" baseline: it cannot detect a regression/change in that reset rule, and it asserts an end-state (loop cleared on replace) that real hardware has not confirmed (provenance: HW-SER-01 pending). Consider adding an explicit `/Status/Deck/Loop/AutoLoopOn = 0` record (with its frameTime) or a comment documenting that loop-off here is a decoder-side reset, not a wire assertion.

The capture delivers the replaced track's Title/Artist *before* its Filepath (all within one <50 ms burst). At that moment the decoder's accumulator still points at fixture-a, so this fixture's correctness relies entirely on burst coalescing publishing only one state per burst. If a frame-time gap ever reaches SERATO_BURST_GAP_MS (50 ms) between Title/Artist and Filepath, an intermediate state would be published with fixture-a carrying "Fixture C"/"Emulator", and this fixture's two expected events would neither cover nor catch that mis-association. Worth recording the dependency on Title/Artist/Filepath landing in the same burst so a future timing edit does not silently invalidate the expectation.

scripts/golden-update.mjs.content: The `--reason` value is never validated. If `--reason` is omitted, `reason` becomes `""`; if `--reason` is the last argument, `process.argv[reasonIdx + 1]` is `undefined` and the changelog line literally records `undefined`. In both cases the golden is still overwritten, directly violating the stated "never silent / deliberate update" guarantee. Reject the run when no non-empty reason is supplied.

scripts/golden-update.mjs.content: The golden file is overwritten here before the CHANGELOG entry is appended. If `appendFileSync` later throws (read-only dir, ENOSPC, permissions), the golden has already changed but no provenance entry is written — an untracked, silent update. Compute and validate everything (including the changelog line) before mutating, or write the changelog first / roll back on failure, so the two changes cannot diverge.

`reason` is interpolated verbatim into CHANGELOG.md. A value containing newlines (e.g. `--reason "x\n\n## forged entry"`) can inject arbitrary headings/sections and forge changelog history, corrupting the audit trail. Sanitize the reason (strip/replace newlines, collapse whitespace) or record it in a fenced/escaped form before writing.

The dynamic `import`, the `JSON.parse` calls for the reference files, and `planShow` can all throw. None of this is guarded, so a missing dist build, malformed reference JSON, or planner error aborts the script with a raw stack trace and non-obvious exit code instead of an actionable diagnostic. Wrap the work in try/catch (or a top-level `.catch`) and report a clear message with a controlled non-zero exit.

There is no locking around the update. Two concurrent invocations can interleave: `writeFileSync` on `planner-golden.json` is not atomic (a reader or parallel run may observe a truncated/partial file) and the two `appendFileSync` calls can duplicate or conflict, yielding a corrupted golden and/or inconsistent changelog. Guard with an exclusive lock file (or write-temp-then-rename) to serialize runs.

test-fixtures/analysis/live-deck2.trackm.content: Every beat in these fixtures carries `beatInBar: 1`, so no bar/downbeat structure is recoverable. Consumers treat `beatInBar === 1` as a genuine downbeat (downbeat-dependent structure/drop detection, phrase/quantize alignment, mix points), so with these grids every beat is reported as a downbeat and bar-aligned behavior is wrong; any regression that depends on real downbeats cannot be exercised. Please regenerate with a proper 1,2,3,4 cycle (or derive the downbeat explicitly) unless an all-ones grid is deliberately under test — in which case a comment/docs note should state that intent.

`phrases` is a byte-identical duplicate of `sections` (same entries, same `kind`/`rawLabel`/`startBeat`/`endBeat`/`confidence`). These are conceptually distinct views: `phrases` is the native PSSI-derived phrase list (which per `phraseSchema` must also carry `mood`, `bank`, `fill`, `fillBeat`, `raw`) while `sections` is fused structure. Keeping two identical copies is a maintenance hazard (silent divergence, double-counting by consumers iterating both), is ambiguous as to which is authoritative, and means phrase-specific paths are never exercised and any `sections`/`phrases` field-swap or PSSI-field bug passes unnoticed. Regenerate `phrases` from the actual PSSI source (with mood/bank/fill/raw), populate only the field the scenario intends to exercise, or remove the duplicated data rather than copying `sections`.

`sourceTimeMs` values carry floating-point artifacts from beat-time accumulation (e.g. 32323.999999999996, 16120.000000000002, 8079.000000000001) alongside exactly-integral neighbours. Because these fixtures are consumed by exact-comparison/golden tests, any assertion using strict equality or a serialized round-trip on grid times is brittle and can mask or spuriously trigger timing regressions. Generate/round times to a consistent precision (e.g. nearest millisecond) when producing the grid, or ensure all consumers/tests compare with a tolerance.

Segment boundaries are offset relative to the beat grid: `beatGrid.beats[].index` is 0-based (0..319) while every phrase/section uses 1-based `startBeat` values (first segment `startBeat: 1`, skipping index 0), and the last segment ends at `endBeat: 308`, leaving beats 308..319 unlabeled. Consumers that index the grid by `startBeat`/`endBeat` (e.g. cue/section-transition derivation) will shift every boundary by one beat and drop the final ~12 beats. Confirm whether these are 1-based musical beats (and convert consistently) or fix them to match the 0-based grid indices and cover the whole grid.

test-fixtures/analysis/live-homecoming.t.content: Every section/phrase carries the identical `confidence` of 0.9, `beatFeatures` and `musicalEvents` are empty, and 16 of the 19 `analysisCoverage2.inputs` are `absent` (only `fusion.structure`, `native.rekordbox.grid`, `native.rekordbox.pssi` are `present`). test-fixtures/analysis/reference-track.j.content: `analysisCoverage` is "full" while `readinessLevel` and `analysisCoverage2.level` are both "structured", and the input map only marks `source.audio`, `native.rekordbox.grid`, `native.rekordbox.pssi` and `fusion.structure` as `present` (everything else `absent`). `compute_readiness()` (analysis/src/autolight_analysis/readiness.py) therefore returns "structured", and the producer `_model()` (analysis/src/autolight_analysis/worker.py:435-438) explicitly enforces `analysisCoverage === readinessLevel === compute_readiness(inputs)` ("readiness is computed, never set by hand"). So this fixture could not have been emitted by the analysis worker; it violates a documented invariant. Neither the TS `superRefine` nor Python `validate_track_model` cross-checks `analysisCoverage` against the input map, so the inconsistency is silent. Set `analysisCoverage` to "structured".

test-fixtures/analysis/trackmodel-v2.fix.content: Coverage status contradicts the embedded native data. `analysisCoverage2.inputs` marks `native.rekordbox.cues` (and `native.rekordbox.waveforms`) as `absent`, yet `nativeAnalysis.rekordbox` contains a cue entry and `waveformFlags.hasWaveform` is `true`. A parity/readiness fixture whose input flags disagree with the data it carries can let tests pass while the coverage/readiness flags are wrong. This gridWarning cannot be produced by the current producer and encodes inconsistent coordinates. In `analysis/src/autolight_analysis/metrical.py` `metrical_vote`:
- `evidence` is emitted as `f"{name}:offset-median-{median}ms"` / `f"{name}:p95-{p95}ms"` (e.g. `beat-this:offset-median-60ms`), not the bare `beat-this:offset` used here.
- `beatRange` is set to `[1, len(native_times)]`, i.e. `[1,4]`; but the grid's beats are 0-indexed (`index` 0–3), so `[1,4]` exceeds the valid max index 3 (off-by-one coordinate mismatch).
- `compare_grids` short-circuits to no warning when `n < minAnchors` (default 32), so a 4-beat grid cannot yield any warning under default config.
The fixture therefore validates a warning shape/range the pipeline never emits; align the evidence string, `beatRange` coordinate base, and anchor count with the producer (or with an explicitly lowered `minAnchors`).

tsconfig.base.json.content: `target` is ES2022 but `lib` is ES2024. The explicit `lib` overrides the target-derived default library, so type-checking exposes ES2023/ES2024 APIs (e.g. `Array.prototype.toSorted`/`toReversed`, `Object.groupBy`, `Promise.withResolvers`, `Map.groupBy`) that are not guaranteed to exist on an ES2022 runtime. Such calls will type-check cleanly but throw `TypeError: ... is not a function` at runtime. Align `lib` with the runtime baseline (e.g. `ES2022`) or raise `target` to match the lib (and document the required runtime) so the type surface and runtime guarantees stay in sync.

vitest.config.ts.content: `readdirSync(workspaceSrc, ...)` runs unguarded at config load and every directory is blindly aliased to `<pkg>/src/index.ts`. Two problems: (1) if `packages/` is missing/unreadable the whole test run aborts with an opaque ENOENT before any test loads; (2) directories that are not real packages (or packages whose entry is not `src/index.ts`) get an alias pointing at a non-existent file, so a later import of that name fails with a confusing module-resolution error. Consider deriving the alias list from the packages' `package.json` (name + `exports`/`main`) or at minimum filtering to directories that actually contain `src/index.ts`, and wrap the scan so a missing `packages/` yields a clear error.

vitest.config.ts.content: The subpath regex only matches exactly one sub-segment and hard-codes the `.ts` extension: `^@autolight/([^/]+)/([^/]+)$` → `src/$2.ts`. Any deeper subpath (e.g. `@autolight/foo/a/b`), a directory-index subpath (e.g. `@autolight/foo/sub` backed by `src/sub/index.ts`), or a `.tsx` subpath will match and be rewritten to a non-existent file (first-match-wins, so it does NOT fall back to the string aliases), or not match at all — in which case the string-prefix `@autolight/foo` alias swallows it as a prefix and resolves the package barrel, exactly the T-TRU-04 failure this block was added to prevent. Also note this only works because `subpathAlias` is spread before the string aliases; a future reorder silently reroutes every subpath to the barrel. Broaden the pattern (e.g. `^@autolight\/([^/]+)\/(.+)$`) and/or resolve to the real file extension.

All three include globs end in `*.test.ts`, so any `.test.tsx` (or `.spec` variant) is silently not collected. The repo already has `.tsx` components (e.g. `apps/desktop/src/components/kit.tsx`), so a component test authored as `*.test.tsx` would run zero assertions while the suite still reports green. Include the tsx globs so those tests cannot be skipped unnoticed.
